title: Churn Prediction Model: How to Use Customer Data to Spot Risk Before It's Too Late
html:
In SaaS, churn doesn’t happen all at once. It builds up silently. A customer stops using one feature, then logs in less frequently, then goes quiet in support. And before you know it, they’re gone. At that point, it's too late to fix things—and too costly to ignore. That’s why a churn prediction model is one of the most important tools for any B2B SaaS company trying to build sustainable growth.

A churn prediction model is a way to forecast which customers are likely to cancel their subscription, based on how their behavior compares to patterns observed in past churned accounts. It gives customer success teams the ability to act before a customer disengages entirely. But building a model that works—one that flags risk early enough to do something about it—depends on the quality of the customer data you have, and how well you're able to connect it across your product and your CRM.

What we are going to cover today:

  • A churn prediction model helps B2B SaaS companies identify at-risk customers before they leave, using patterns in product usage and engagement to surface early warning signs.
  • Customer success teams become strategic when equipped with the right metrics, allowing them to anticipate churn, personalize outreach, and prioritize efforts based on real behavior—not guesswork.
  • June connects product analytics with CRM data, making it possible to build accurate health scores, track engagement trends, and create churn prediction models grounded in both user behavior and account context.
  • With features like embedded dashboards, June also helps companies share usage insights directly with their customers—turning data into a tool for re-engagement, accountability, and retention.

Customer Success and the Strategic Role of Churn Prediction

Customer success is where churn becomes visible. It's where usage is monitored, value is delivered, and relationships are maintained. But the best customer success teams aren’t just solving problems after they happen—they're anticipating them. And that shift from reactive to strategic customer success starts with the ability to read the signals.

Not all churn is the same. Some customers churn early because onboarding failed. Others churn after years because usage started to decay. And some don’t churn at all—they just stop growing. The role of customer success is to understand these patterns, recognize the early indicators, and intervene with the right approach. That might mean re-engaging a dormant user, unblocking a stuck team, or simply surfacing the value they’ve already received. But you can’t do any of that if you don’t know what’s happening in the first place.

A churn prediction model gives customer success managers a layer of visibility that transforms how they prioritize their work. Instead of guessing which accounts might be at risk, they have a clear signal. Instead of waiting for a red flag in QBR prep, they see the trend in real time. And instead of managing every account the same way, they tailor their actions based on behavior, engagement, and timing.

Why Churn Prediction Starts with Understanding the Right Signals

Most churn doesn't come as a surprise to the customer—it only comes as a surprise to the company. A churn prediction model helps close that gap. It tracks the subtle behavioral shifts that often lead to cancellation. The team that stops exploring new features. The account that plateaus in usage. The user who logs in but doesn’t actually get anything done.

These signals can vary depending on the product, the use case, or the customer segment, but they always exist. What’s needed is a system that helps surface them before they grow into full-blown risks, a system that ties together what customers are doing, what they’re not doing, and what that means in the broader context of their relationship with your company.

When done right, this doesn’t just help reduce churn—it helps drive better outcomes. Customers get more attention when they need it. Teams work more efficiently. And the entire experience becomes more proactive.

How June Helps Build Churn Prediction Models That Actually Work

This is where June comes in. June connects product analytics with CRM data to give SaaS companies a full picture of their customers—how they behave, how engaged they are, and how that aligns with their business context. It doesn’t just show you what users are doing inside the product; it shows you how that activity relates to deal size, lifecycle stage, user segments, and more.

This integration is what makes churn prediction models powerful. Product data tells you what’s happening in real time. CRM data gives you the context to interpret it correctly. When those two sources are aligned, you get a much sharper view—not just of who is using the product, but why it matters, and what’s likely to happen next.

June lets you define your own engagement signals—whether that’s feature usage, onboarding completion, or frequency of activity. You can build customer health scores based on these inputs, and track how those scores evolve over time. The CRM connection adds crucial detail, like renewal dates, company size, or team structure, giving you the insight needed to act precisely.

What makes June especially effective is that it’s not just a tool for internal analysis. With embedded dashboards, you can surface usage data directly to your customers. That means your users can see their own engagement—how active their team is, which features are being used, and whether they’re getting full value from the product. This visibility increases accountability and makes churn prevention a shared responsibility. Instead of telling your customers they’re at risk, you can show them—and help them course-correct before it’s too late.

Use Case: Spotting Risk in High-Value Accounts

Consider a large account worth $80K a year. For months, things looked fine—seats were filled, usage was steady, and support requests were minimal. But behind the scenes, one of the core teams stopped using a critical feature. Over time, their engagement declined, and by the time the QBR rolled around, the decision to cancel had already been made.

With June in place, that drop in usage would have triggered a flag. The customer success team would have seen that a key segment within the account was disengaging—and would’ve had the chance to reach out with a specific plan to re-engage that team. That could’ve been a well-timed training session, a change in onboarding process, or just a nudge to remind them of the value. The point is, the opportunity wouldn’t have been missed.

Use Case: Creating Reliable Health Scores for Renewals

Renewal time shouldn’t be a guessing game. But in many companies, health scores are either too simple or too disconnected from reality. They show “green” when things are actually fragile, or “red” when usage is just a little behind. That’s because the data underneath them is often incomplete.

June helps you build health scores that are grounded in real product behavior. You can assign more weight to strategic features, adjust based on team-level engagement, and bring in CRM fields like industry, account age, or expansion potential. This results in a much more reliable view—so when you enter renewal conversations, you know exactly what’s going on in the account and how likely they are to stay.

Use Case: Driving Expansion Through Predictive Insight

Churn prediction isn’t only about preventing loss—it’s also about spotting opportunity. If a certain segment is engaging more, using new features, or inviting more teammates, that’s a signal too. It means the account is warming up for a bigger conversation.

June allows you to track these signals in the same system. Instead of separating growth and retention, you treat them as two outcomes of the same process: understanding what your users are doing and helping them do more of it. This turns product analytics into a strategic engine, not just for churn prevention, but for revenue growth.

Final Thoughts on Churn Prediction Models

Churn is part of any SaaS business. But surprise churn doesn’t have to be. A well-designed churn prediction model—built on connected product and CRM data—gives you the power to act before the damage is done. And it gives your customer success team the tools to stop managing symptoms and start addressing the root causes.

June helps you build that model, monitor it in real time, and act on it in meaningful ways. Whether it’s surfacing usage insights through embedded dashboards or flagging early signs of disengagement, June turns churn prediction into a practical, proactive process.

It’s not about eliminating churn altogether. It’s about making sure that when it happens, it never comes as a surprise.

title: B2B SaaS Growth Strategy: How Vertical SaaS Companies Win with Retention, Specialization, and Embedded Insight
html:
As the SaaS ecosystem matures, the playbook for growth is evolving.

Gone are the days when “build it for everyone” was a viable strategy. The next generation of SaaS companies is thriving not by going broad, but by going deep.

These are vertical SaaS businesses—companies laser-focused on serving a specific industry or function with tailored, workflow-driven software. And for them, the most effective B2B SaaS growth strategy is built not just on acquisition, but on retention, expansion, and deep product insight.

What we'll cover today:

  • Vertical SaaS companies grow by going deep, not broad, focusing on retention and specialization rather than mass acquisition. Their users are often non-technical, so product adoption and long-term engagement become core to a winning B2B SaaS growth strategy.
  • June helps vertical SaaS businesses track meaningful product usage and customer behavior, combining product analytics with CRM data to surface real engagement patterns across teams, departments, or projects.
  • Beyond internal insights, June enables companies to deliver usage data back to their customers as part of onboarding, success reviews, or embedded dashboards—helping customers see their own progress and increasing the product's perceived value.
  • Use cases include tracking adoption in specialized workflows, identifying churn risks early, and surfacing expansion opportunities by analyzing segment-level engagement—making June a key driver of retention and growth in vertical SaaS.e

Vertical SaaS Is Reshaping How SaaS Companies Grow

Unlike horizontal platforms that offer broad functionality across different customer types, vertical SaaS companies are built around the nuances of specific industries—construction, legal, logistics, healthcare, hospitality, and so on. They solve domain-specific problems in a way generalist tools can’t. But this focus comes with a different set of challenges.

Vertical SaaS often sells to non-technical users. Their customers care less about fancy analytics and more about whether the product solves real operational pains. This means the growth strategy must go beyond traffic and signups—it has to drive real, observable value, quickly and consistently. That’s why retention becomes the most important growth lever, and why having the right data—not just to measure internal success, but to fuel customer-facing insights—is crucial.

Why Retention Is the Centerpiece of Vertical SaaS Growth

In vertical SaaS, churn doesn’t always mean switching to a competitor. It often means going back to manual workflows, spreadsheets, or outdated tools. Customers leave not because they found a better product—but because they didn’t find enough value in yours.

This makes retention and product engagement mission-critical. Understanding how each team, user, or project interacts with your product is the only way to ensure that customers stay. And that understanding can’t be surface-level. It has to be connected to context—who’s using what, why, and where.

That’s where June comes in. By combining product analytics with CRM data, June provides vertical SaaS companies with rich, actionable insights at both the user and account level. But more than that, it helps companies translate these insights into value—both internally and externally.

June Helps You Generate Insights—Then Share Them with Your Customers

One of the most powerful but often overlooked growth levers in vertical SaaS is the ability to present meaningful usage data back to your customers. It’s not just about customer analytics—it’s about helping them understand how they’re using your product and what that means for their own operations.

June gives vertical SaaS businesses this superpower. It enables them to take product usage data and turn it into customer-facing insights, embedded into dashboards, reports, or onboarding reviews. This could be something as simple as showing a logistics customer how many tasks they completed this month compared to last, or as advanced as surfacing usage trends by department in a distributed enterprise client.

These insights add tremendous value, especially for customers who don’t have in-house analytics capabilities. They also help drive trust, transparency, and accountability—which are critical in industries where software adoption is still catching up. When your product helps your customer look smarter or manage better, it becomes that much harder to replace.

June makes this possible by offering clean, real-time product data that’s enriched with CRM context. Whether you want to build a health report for your CS team or a usage dashboard for your customer, June provides the infrastructure to do both without complexity.

Use Case 1: Measuring Product Adoption in a Specialized Workflow

One of the hardest parts of building for a vertical is knowing whether the product is being adopted as intended. You’re not tracking generic behaviors—you’re tracking specific workflows tied to industry context. For example, in a logistics SaaS, it might be about route creation. In real estate, it could be listing views or client follow-ups.

June allows product teams to define what meaningful adoption looks like, track it across accounts and teams, and then turn that information into insight. This helps improve onboarding, prioritize feature development, and reduce time-to-value for every new customer.

Use Case 2: Spotting Churn Risk Before It Happens

In vertical SaaS, every customer matters. Losing a single high-value account can be a major setback. But these customers rarely leave overnight. They disengage slowly—first by skipping steps, then by using the product less, then by going quiet.

June helps detect these patterns early. Its product analytics surface user behavior trends that can be linked to CRM data, making it easy for customer success teams to identify which teams are at risk and why. From there, they can act—before a renewal becomes a resignation.

Use Case 3: Fueling Expansion Through Segment-Level Insight

In many vertical SaaS scenarios, expansion revenue doesn’t come from convincing a company to buy more—it comes from helping them see where they’re already succeeding and scaling that success. One location is thriving with your product? Time to bring in the others. One department is fully onboarded? Let’s go to the next one.

With June, you can group users by business unit, geography, or project, and analyze their engagement in a meaningful way. This lets your team pitch expansions with evidence, not assumptions—and lets customers feel like they’re building on a working foundation, not starting from scratch.

Why June is the Growth Engine Vertical SaaS Didn’t Know It Needed

June was built for companies that don’t just want data—they want clarity. Especially in vertical SaaS, where customer relationships are more nuanced and product adoption is more variable, June gives teams the tools to understand what’s really going on. More importantly, it helps them act on that understanding: to increase client retention, expand faster, and deliver insights back to the customer.

And because June integrates product data directly into your CRM, your entire company—from sales to customer success—can operate with shared intelligence. You don’t need separate reports or siloed dashboards. You just need to ask the right questions, and June helps you find the answers.

A New Kind of Customer Intelligence for B2B SaaS

The most effective B2B SaaS growth strategy today is not about acquiring more—it’s about going deeper. It’s about understanding what makes your best customers successful and using that insight to replicate it across your user base. For vertical SaaS, this is even more critical. Your customers won’t always tell you what’s working or not—but their product usage will.

June gives your team the tools to listen, learn, and act. It becomes the nervous system that connects product, success, and growth—all through the shared language of data.

title: Understanding Customer Segment Analysis in B2B SaaS and Vertical SaaS
html:
In the world of B2B SaaS and Vertical SaaS, especially when selling to mid-market or enterprise-level clients, not all customers are equal.

One account might generate over $100K in annual revenue, but internally it could be made up of multiple departments, teams, or locations—each with different usage patterns, needs, and engagement levels.

That’s where customer segment analysis becomes crucial. Customer segment analysis refers to the process of breaking down a customer account into smaller, meaningful units—such as teams, projects, business units, or regions—so that the company can analyze and engage them more precisely.

This goes beyond traditional account-based views and offers a much more dynamic and actionable understanding of how a product is used.

TL;DR:

  • Customer segment analysis helps B2B SaaS and Vertical SaaS companies—especially those selling to mid-market and enterprise—understand usage patterns at a more granular level, like team, department, or region within the same account.
  • Segmenting customers based on who they are (CRM data) and what they do (product data) is essential for identifying churn risks, unlocking expansion opportunities, and personalizing engagement.
  • June connects product analytics with CRM data, allowing CS teams to create and monitor custom segments that reflect real organizational structures and behavior.
  • With June, SaaS companies can prevent churn earlier, drive smarter upsells, and improve how they engage with every part of a large customer—not just the account as a whole.

Applying Segment Analysis to Product Analytics

In B2B SaaS, product analytics typically focus on aggregate data at the company level. However, this level of abstraction often hides important signals.

A customer might look healthy overall, while one of its core teams is disengaging and at risk of churning. Or a single project may be driving most of the value, leaving room to expand to other underutilized areas.

Segment analysis enables SaaS companies to detect these patterns. Instead of tracking just the account's overall activity, you look at usage trends by team, department, location, or even use case. This level of detail is essential when trying to drive engagement, retention, and upsell conversations with precision and confidence.

Common Ways to Segment Customers for Analysis

Segmentation works by grouping users or accounts based on who they are and what they do. Identity-based segmentation is about the customer’s characteristics: industry, company size, business model, department, geography, or role.

Behavior-based segmentation is based on what they actually do inside your product: how often they log in, which features they use, how many team members are active, or whether their engagement is growing or shrinking over time.

At the enterprise level, segmentation should happen not only across your customer base but within each individual account. For example, you might break down a single $100K ARR customer by region (EMEA vs. US), by department (Marketing vs. Product), or by project (internal testing vs. external rollout).

This is essential if you want to understand what’s working, what’s not, and how to engage with each group differently.

Why Traditional SaaS Dashboards Don’t Cut It

Most SaaS tools focus their customer analytics at the account level.

This may be fine in early-stage companies or when selling to SMBs, where each customer equals one use case and one team. But it falls short when selling into larger organizations.

When a company has 200 seats but only 20 are active—and all of them come from the same team—you need to know exactly which team that is, and whether others have even started adopting the product. Traditional CS tools aren’t built for this level of granularity.

That’s where June comes in.

How June Helps You Segment and Analyze Customers More Intelligently

June integrates product usage data with CRM systems like HubSpot, Salesforce, and Attio, giving you a full picture of your customers—not just what they’re doing, but who they are.

This integration allows you to tie product data (like feature usage or activation milestones) directly to CRM data (like company size, location, deal size, or lifecycle stage), enriching your customer records with both quantitative and qualitative insights.

With June, you can build and monitor custom segments that reflect how your business actually works.

Want to understand which enterprise customers in the fintech vertical are engaging with your new feature? Done. Curious to know which departments inside your largest customer are lagging behind in activation? You can see that, too.

June helps you move from a single static view of each customer to a dynamic, multi-layered and strategic understanding that matches your go-to-market reality.

Group-Level Segmentation: A Critical Step for Enterprise SaaS

June is specifically designed to help CS teams operate at the group-of-customers level.

That means it’s not just about seeing data per user or per account—it’s about building views that mirror how your customer accounts are structured internally. You might want to group users by their team, business unit, country, or project. Once grouped, you can track their engagement, compare trends across segments, and trigger alerts or workflows based on specific behaviors.

June is working to give customers even more flexibility here—allowing them to define, edit, and monitor customer groups based on their own rules.

Whether you define a “segment” by email domain, CRM property, product behavior, or any combination of those, June will give you the tools to analyze performance, forecast risk, and identify opportunities at a much finer grain.

Use Case: Identifying At-Risk Segments Before It’s Too Late

Say you have a $200K ARR customer with 150 users across five departments. One team starts logging in less frequently and stops using key features.

Without segment analysis, that drop-off could go unnoticed because the overall account health still looks okay. But with June, you can set up alerts for any segment showing signs of disengagement.

This allows your CS team to intervene early and save the account—before churn happens.

Use Case: Finding Opportunities to Expand Within a Large Account

If one team is using your product daily and another hasn’t even onboarded, that’s a signal.

With June, you can pinpoint which departments or locations are underutilizing your product and which ones are driving the most value. That makes your expansion conversations easier—and more data-driven.

You’re not just saying “we think you should buy more seats,” you’re showing that one group is thriving and another could benefit from the same approach.

Use Case: Tailoring Engagement by Segment Needs

Different teams inside the same company often have different goals and workflows.

With June, you can adapt onboarding experiences, success metrics, and engagement playbooks based on each segment’s behavior and context. That allows you to move from a one-size-fits-all success model to something much more adaptive and effective—especially in complex, multi-stakeholder accounts.

Why Segment Analysis Will Shape the Future of Customer Success

As SaaS companies scale and move upmarket, the challenge shifts from landing customers to growing and retaining them. And that means understanding them at a deeper level. Segment analysis is the only way to do this effectively.

It lets you track what matters, where it matters, and tailor your actions accordingly.

June helps make this approach possible by combining product data and CRM data into one clear picture, organized around the way your customers actually use your product—not how your CRM says they do.

For B2B SaaS companies working with large, complex clients, this capability is no longer optional. It’s the foundation of a modern customer success strategy.

title: Retention Rate vs. Churn Rate: Understanding the Metrics That Define SaaS Growth
html:
In a subscription-based model, long-term success depends on keeping existing customers engaged while minimizing the number of users who leave. Two key metrics define this dynamic: retention rate and churn rate.

While they measure opposite sides of the customer lifecycle, they are deeply interconnected, offering insight into customer satisfaction, revenue stability, and overall business health.

Understanding both metrics—and using them together—helps companies fine-tune their customer success strategy, predict risks, and identify opportunities for growth. With the right tools, such as product analytics and CRM integration, SaaS businesses can move beyond simply tracking these metrics and start proactively managing them.

Let'see together how.

TL;DR

  • Retention rate and churn rate are two critical SaaS metrics that measure opposite sides of customer success—retention tracks customers who stay, while churn tracks those who leave. Together, they provide a full picture of business health.
  • A high retention rate leads to predictable revenue and long-term growth, while a high churn rate signals disengagement, poor adoption, or gaps in customer success strategies. Industry benchmarks vary, but strong B2B SaaS companies aim for retention above 85% and churn below 5-7% annually.
  • Integrating product data with CRM insights is essential to tracking and improving retention and churn. Understanding how customers engage with the product allows teams to predict risks, intervene early, and create targeted retention strategies.
  • June helps SaaS businesses proactively manage retention and churn by combining real-time product analytics with CRM workflows, allowing customer success teams to detect risks, engage customers effectively, and identify expansion opportunities.

What is Retention Rate in B2B SaaS?

Retention rate measures the percentage of customers who continue using a product over a specific period. It is a direct indicator of how well a company keeps its customers engaged and satisfied. High retention means customers find ongoing value, while low retention suggests issues with adoption, onboarding, or overall experience.

The formula to calculate retention rate is straightforward:

Retention Rate = ((Customers at End of Period – New Customers) / Customers at Start of Period) × 100

For example, if a SaaS company starts the quarter with 1,000 customers, gains 200 new customers, and ends the quarter with 1,050 customers, the retention rate would be:

((1,050 – 200) / 1,000) × 100 = 85%

Retention benchmarks vary based on industry and customer size. In B2B SaaS, companies with small and mid-sized business (SMB) customers often see retention rates between 70-80%, while enterprise-focused SaaS companies typically aim for retention rates above 85-90% due to longer contracts and deeper product adoption.

Strong retention rates are associated with sustainable growth, predictable revenue, and higher customer lifetime value (LTV). Companies that consistently retain customers can invest more confidently in expansion, product development, and customer success initiatives.

What is Churn Rate and How is It Calculated?

Churn rate is the percentage of customers who cancel their subscription over a given period. While retention rate focuses on those who stay, churn rate tracks those who leave. This metric reveals weaknesses in the customer experience and highlights areas where businesses must improve to reduce customer attrition.

The formula for churn rate is the inverse of retention:

Churn Rate = (Customers Lost During Period / Customers at Start of Period) × 100

For example, if a SaaS company starts the quarter with 1,000 customers and loses 100 customers by the end, the churn rate would be:

(100 / 1,000) × 100 = 10%

In the B2B SaaS industry, benchmarks vary depending on the target customer segment. SMB-focused SaaS companies often experience higher churn, with rates ranging from 5-7% per month, while enterprise SaaS businesses typically see churn rates closer to 1-2% per month or 5-7% annually. A lower churn rate indicates better customer retention, stronger product adoption, and a more stable revenue stream.

Reducing and analysing churn is crucial because the cost of acquiring a new customer is significantly higher than the cost of retaining an existing one. Even a small decrease in churn can have a significant impact on revenue growth, making churn prevention a top priority for customer success teams.

Retention Rate vs. Churn Rate: Two Sides of the Same Coin

Although retention rate and churn rate measure different aspects of customer behavior, they are deeply connected. A high retention rate naturally results in a low churn rate, and vice versa. Together, they provide a complete picture of customer loyalty, engagement, and the overall health of a SaaS business.

Retention and churn are influenced by the same factors, including onboarding process, customer engagement strategies, product usability, and proactive customer success interventions. Companies that focus on improving retention simultaneously reduce churn, creating a cycle where satisfied customers continue using the product, refer others, and increase their overall lifetime value.

While retention measures success, churn acts as a warning signal. If retention starts declining, churn will increase, signaling that customer expectations are not being met. By tracking both metrics in parallel, SaaS companies can identify trends early, take action to resolve potential issues, and improve long-term growth.

How June Helps SaaS Businesses Improve Retention and Reduce Churn

Understanding retention and churn is one thing—managing them effectively is another. June provides a seamless way to track, analyze, and act on customer data, helping SaaS businesses reduce churn and increase retention through real-time insights.

With June’s integration of product analytics and CRM data, customer success teams gain a complete view of each customer’s engagement and health score. Instead of relying on guesswork, teams can see exactly how users interact with the product, which features they adopt, and where they struggle. This visibility enables proactive outreach, ensuring that customers receive support before they disengage or cancel.

For churn prevention, June helps teams identify customers who show signs of decreasing engagement, enabling early intervention with personalized messages, additional training, or feature recommendations. By tracking customer behavior over time, teams can predict churn risks before they materialize, making it easier to prevent revenue loss.

On the retention side, June allows teams to monitor accounts that are ready for expansion opportunities, helping companies maximize revenue from their existing customer base. By recognizing usage patterns that indicate readiness for upselling or cross-selling, June ensures that expansion efforts are well-timed and data-driven rather than purely sales-driven.

Why June is Essential for a Customer Success Tech Stack

Customer retention and churn prevention require more than just tracking numbers. They demand a structured, data-driven approach that combines real-time insights with strategic interventions. June simplifies this process by integrating product analytics with CRM workflows, ensuring that customer success teams always have the right data at their fingertips.

By using June, SaaS businesses can:

  • Detect early signs of churn and intervene before it’s too late.
  • Track retention trends and adjust strategies based on real customer behavior.
  • Identify expansion opportunities and engage customers when they’re most likely to upgrade.

Rather than reacting to churn after it happens, June enables SaaS companies to proactively manage customer relationships, strengthen retention strategies, and create a more predictable revenue stream.

Retention Rate vs. Churn Rate in B2B SaaS

Retention rate and churn rate are two of the most important metrics in B2B SaaS.

They define customer loyalty, revenue stability, and long-term growth potential. While retention rate highlights success, churn rate serves as a warning system, showing where improvements are needed.

By integrating real-time product analytics with CRM data, SaaS businesses can gain deeper insights into customer behavior and take strategic action to improve both metrics. June provides the tools needed to track engagement, prevent churn, and maximize retention efforts, ensuring that customer success teams can operate with efficiency and precision.

In an industry where customer retention is the key to sustainable growth, investing in the right tools and strategies is essential. With June, SaaS companies can move beyond tracking retention and churn to actively managing and improving them—driving stronger relationships, higher revenue, and long-term success.

title: Analytical CRM: Turning Data into Actionable Customer Insights
html:
Customer relationship management (CRM) has evolved far beyond being just a repository for contact details and sales records. Today, SaaS companies require a data-driven approach to customer interactions, one that moves past static records and instead offers deep analytical insights into customer behavior, engagement, and growth potential. This is where analytical CRM becomes a game-changer.

Unlike operational CRMs, which primarily focus on managing daily interactions, analytical CRMs process large volumes of customer data to uncover trends, predict behavior, and optimize customer success strategies. They enable companies to shift from reactive management to proactive engagement, ensuring that every touchpoint is informed by data rather than assumptions.

What we'll cover today:

  • Analytical CRM helps SaaS companies turn customer data into actionable insights, enabling better retention, engagement, and expansion strategies by leveraging real-time analytics.
  • Integrating product usage data into an analytical CRM provides a complete view of customer behavior, helping teams predict churn, optimize onboarding, and identify upsell opportunities based on actual engagement.
  • Key use cases include churn prevention, expansion opportunities, and improving onboarding, ensuring that customer success efforts are proactive rather than reactive.
  • June enhances analytical CRM by combining product analytics with customer success data, allowing SaaS teams to track customer health, automate engagement workflows, and maximize revenue through data-driven decision-making.

What Makes Analytical CRM Different?

An analytical CRM system goes beyond traditional customer records, incorporating real-time insights from multiple data sources. It brings together historical interactions, engagement patterns, behavioral trends, and predictive analytics to help businesses make smarter decisions about customer retention, upselling, and expansion strategies.

To function effectively, an analytical CRM must process and interpret a wide range of customer data. This includes basic information such as company size and industry, but more importantly, it leverages real usage data, customer support history, renewal likelihood, and health scores. By integrating this information into a single, cohesive system, businesses can develop a deeper understanding of their customers and personalize interactions based on real needs and behaviors.

The Role of Product Data in Analytical CRM for SaaS

For SaaS businesses, product usage data is one of the most valuable assets in an analytical CRM. While traditional CRM systems track customer interactions through email, calls, and meetings, they often lack visibility into how customers actually engage with the product. This leaves customer success teams with an incomplete picture, making it harder to anticipate churn risks, identify expansion opportunities, or personalize outreach.

Integrating product data into an analytical CRM bridges this gap, allowing businesses to see exactly which features customers use most, where they struggle, and how deeply they are engaged. When combined with customer success records, sales data, and support interactions, this insight creates a full 360-degree view of each account, ensuring that every decision is backed by accurate, real-time information.

By leveraging product data within an analytical CRM, SaaS companies can move from reactive decision-making to predictive, strategic customer management. Understanding how customers use the product is not just about improving the user experience—it’s about driving retention, expansion, and long-term customer success.

Key Use Cases for an Analytical CRM in SaaS

One of the most impactful applications of an analytical CRM with integrated product data is predicting and preventing churn. Many SaaS businesses struggle with retaining customers, often realizing there’s a problem only when a renewal is at risk. By analyzing real usage patterns, engagement trends, and support activity, customer success teams can detect early warning signs of disengagement and intervene before a customer decides to leave.

Another critical use case is identifying expansion and upsell opportunities. Not all customers use a product to its full potential, and many may be ready to upgrade without realizing it. By analyzing how users interact with different features, businesses can pinpoint accounts that would benefit from an expanded plan, additional seats, or advanced functionality. This ensures that upsell conversations happen at the right time, based on customer needs rather than arbitrary sales cycles.

An analytical CRM also plays a key role in enhancing onboarding and customer success strategies. By tracking how new users engage with the product, teams can adjust onboarding processes to reduce friction, accelerate time-to-value, and ensure early adoption. If certain accounts struggle to complete onboarding steps, automated workflows can trigger additional guidance, tutorials, or outreach to keep them on track.

How June Helps SaaS Companies Enhance Analytical CRM

June provides a seamless way to integrate real-time product analytics with CRM data, ensuring that SaaS companies can track customer health, engagement trends, and expansion opportunities in one place. By enriching an analytical CRM with usage insights, June helps customer success teams move from guesswork to precision, ensuring that every interaction is based on actual customer behavior.

With June, customer success managers can detect churn risks early, automate personalized engagement workflows, and pinpoint upsell or cross-sell opportunities based on real usage data. Instead of relying solely on sales interactions or support tickets, teams gain a holistic understanding of how customers are engaging with the product and can tailor their approach accordingly.

By combining analytical CRM capabilities with June’s real-time customer insights, SaaS businesses can create a data-driven customer success strategy that improves retention, maximizes revenue, and enhances customer relationships.

Conclusion: Analytical CRM for Customer Analysis

An analytical CRM transforms customer data into actionable insights, allowing SaaS companies to predict churn, optimize onboarding, and drive expansion with confidence. By integrating product usage data, businesses gain a complete view of customer engagement, ensuring that customer success efforts are targeted, proactive, and highly effective.

With June, SaaS companies can unlock the full potential of analytical CRM, ensuring that every customer interaction is backed by real-time insights and predictive analytics.

In a competitive landscape where retention and growth are essential, investing in a smarter, data-driven approach to customer relationship management is the key to long-term success.

title: MCPs: the AI plugin that might actually stick
html:
Over the past few weeks, MCPs have gone viral.

If you haven’t tried one yet, imagine this:

You’re in an AI chat.

You ask it to summarize your Gmail inbox, generate a Figma file, or message someone who liked your latest LinkedIn post.

And it just… does it.

No integrations. No agents.
Just type in a chat—and your tools come to life.

This is what MCPs (Model Context Protocol) do. And they’re likely the next infrastructure layer for AI.

What’s an MCP?

MCPs are plugins that let AI talk to real-world software.

Think of them like chat-native APIs.
You don’t write code. You don’t switch tabs.
You just ask, and the AI makes the calls in the background.

They're built to give AI superpowers—access to live data, tools, and actions.

MCPs are:

  • simple to install
  • instantly usable
  • incredibly versatile

They work across productivity tools, design tools, dev tools, CRMs, marketplaces—you name it.

Why they matter

Today’s AI tools are smart, but mostly passive.

MCPs flip the script. They give AI the ability to act.

That changes a few things:

  • Chat becomes the control layer for your tools
  • You automate real workflows without setup
  • You no longer need agents, scripts, or connectors

This is why it feels like USB-C for AI—a universal adapter that works everywhere.

And it’s not just a toy project.

Last week, Zapier launched their own MCP.
That’s 6,000+ apps now accessible from a chat window.

That’s a signal.

6 examples you can try today

Here’s a curated list of MCPs that are already mind-blowing.
Each one is usable today, no config needed.

# MCP What it does Link
1 Figma MCP Codes and renders a Figma file with 80% accuracy Try it
2 Gmail MCP Summarizes your inbox and drafts urgent replies Try it
3 Browser MCP Finds and summarizes web pages on demand Try it
4 GitHub MCP Reviews code, suggests changes, drafts PRs Try it
5 Airbnb MCP Ranks listings based on your preferences Try it
6 Shopify MCP Auto-generates product pages with AI content Try it

What they don’t do (yet)

MCPs aren’t perfect.

Most are still early and built on brittle assumptions.

Good write-up here by Stefan Faistenauer on what can go wrong.

A few common weak spots:

  • Many MCPs are hardcoded and break if APIs change
  • There’s no persistent memory across steps
  • The model still needs to understand what you want

So they’re not quite agents.
But they’re also a lot easier to use than agents.

And they’re evolving fast.

Why I’m bullish

Every few years, a new abstraction layer changes how we build.

MCPs feel like one of those shifts.

They let AI act.
They connect to the real world.
And they’re usable by anyone—not just developers.

Even if something replaces them, the core idea won’t go away:

Chat will become the interface to everything.

That’s why we built fleurmcp.com, it’s the easiest way to explore and install MCPs on Claude.

Would love to hear:
Which MCP use case blows your mind the most?
And which one would you want to exist next?

I started a thread here.

title: Customer Success Framework: Structuring Retention and Expansion for SaaS Growth
html:
Customer success is not a reactive function—it is a structured approach that ensures users find continuous value in a product, leading to long-term retention and revenue expansion. A well-defined customer success framework provides a repeatable strategy for engaging customers, preventing churn, and identifying opportunities for growth. Without a structured framework, companies risk operating in silos, applying inconsistent strategies, and missing critical moments in the customer lifecycle.

For B2B SaaS businesses, a strong customer success framework must cover both retention and expansion. Keeping customers engaged and satisfied ensures they continue renewing, while identifying expansion opportunities allows companies to maximize revenue from their existing customer base. To build an effective framework, teams must leverage data, integrate product and CRM insights, and create structured engagement playbooks that drive action at the right time.

TL;DR

  • A structured customer success framework ensures predictable retention and expansion, helping SaaS businesses proactively engage customers, reduce churn, and identify growth opportunities instead of reacting to issues.
  • Working strategically with clear frameworks and operational systems is critical, allowing customer success teams to scale efficiently, prioritize accounts, and automate engagement based on real customer data.
  • Integrating product analytics with CRM data provides a complete view of customer health, enabling teams to track engagement, intervene early, and personalize retention and expansion strategies based on actual usage patterns.
  • June helps SaaS companies implement effective customer success frameworks, combining real-time insights with automated workflows to improve retention, drive upsells, and make customer success efforts both scalable and data-driven.

Why Customer Success Needs Structure and Strategy

Customer success, when left unstructured, often becomes reactive—teams spend more time responding to churn signals rather than proactively preventing them. A strategic approach, built on clear frameworks and operational systems, ensures that customer success teams work efficiently, focusing on long-term retention rather than short-term issue resolution. Without a defined methodology for engaging customers, tracking health metrics, and scaling interventions, efforts become fragmented, leading to inconsistent customer experiences.

A structured approach allows teams to prioritize accounts based on real data, standardize engagement playbooks, and automate critical processes to improve efficiency. With the right operations, tools, and data integration in place, customer success becomes a predictable, repeatable function that directly impacts revenue growth. Instead of working in a reactive manner, teams following structured frameworks can anticipate customer needs, deliver value proactively, and create a scalable success model that grows with the company.

Building a Retention Framework for Customer Success

Retention is the foundation of customer success. Without it, expansion opportunities shrink, revenue becomes unpredictable, and churn eats away at growth. A retention framework ensures that customers remain engaged, satisfied, and consistently see the value of the product.

The first step in creating a retention framework is defining customer health indicators. This requires tracking how customers interact with the product, identifying patterns that correlate with long-term success, and monitoring early warning signals that suggest disengagement. A structured approach involves segmenting customers based on their engagement levels, ensuring that those at risk of churn receive proactive support before they consider leaving.

Once customer health is clearly defined, the framework should outline key engagement milestones. Onboarding is the first critical phase, where customers must be guided toward their first moment of value as quickly as possible. A structured onboarding experience, with personalized touchpoints and proactive guidance, significantly reduces early churn. Beyond onboarding, continuous check-ins, feature recommendations, and value-driven conversations ensure that customers remain active and informed.

Proactive intervention plays a critical role in retention. Tracking behavioral data allows customer success teams to identify customers who are showing signs of disengagement and take action before they churn. If a customer’s activity drops or they stop using core features, an automated or personalized outreach should be triggered to re-engage them with relevant content, additional support, or alternative use cases that reinforce value.

The final piece of a retention framework is measurement and iteration. A data-driven approach allows teams to analyze retention trends, refine engagement strategies, and continuously optimize processes based on what is working. By integrating product analytics with CRM data, customer success teams can connect product usage trends with business context, ensuring that retention strategies remain both proactive and scalable.

Designing a Customer Success Expansion Framework to Drive Revenue Growth

Expansion is the next logical step once retention is stabilized. A strong expansion framework ensures that customer success teams systematically identify growth opportunities within the existing customer base, whether through upselling, cross-selling, or increasing overall adoption of advanced features.

A structured expansion framework begins with understanding customer potential. Not all customers are immediate candidates for upsells, so identifying the right accounts based on product usage, engagement patterns, and business needs is essential. The goal is to focus on customers who are already finding success with the product but could benefit from additional features, higher-tier plans, or expanded team adoption.

Timing is critical in expansion. Customers must experience success before they consider investing further in the product. The framework should establish trigger points that signal when an account is ready for expansion. If a customer consistently engages with a feature that is limited in their current plan, they may be open to upgrading. If a team reaches the maximum number of seats or usage limits, expansion conversations become natural rather than forced.

Expansion strategies should be deeply integrated into customer lifecycle management. Regular success reviews provide an opportunity to align the product’s roadmap with the customer’s evolving needs. Expansion should feel like a natural next step rather than a sales pitch, reinforcing how the product can drive even greater efficiency, collaboration, or revenue growth.

A strong expansion framework also incorporates customer advocacy and referrals. Customers who are already deriving value from the product become powerful advocates who can introduce the product to new departments, subsidiaries, or partner organizations. Structuring referral and expansion programs ensures that satisfied customers become growth drivers, turning organic advocacy into a repeatable part of the business strategy.

Why Product and CRM Data Integration is Key to a Successful CS Framework

A retention and expansion framework is only as strong as the data that informs it. Without a clear, centralized view of customer health, product engagement, and past interactions, teams operate with incomplete insights, leading to missed opportunities and inefficient engagement efforts.

Integrating product analytics with CRM data creates a unified view of the customer journey. Instead of tracking product engagement in one system and customer history in another, teams can see the full picture in one place, allowing for smarter decision-making, automated workflows, and more personalized interactions.

For retention, this integration ensures that customer success managers can identify disengaged users early, understand why they might be struggling, and intervene with the right messaging. For expansion, product usage data highlights which customers are primed for additional investment, making upsell conversations data-backed and relevant rather than speculative.

Automated workflows powered by integrated data also improve efficiency. If a customer stops engaging with a core feature, an automated email can offer targeted content or a troubleshooting guide. If an account reaches usage limits, the CRM can prompt a CSM to initiate an expansion conversation at the right time. With real-time data integration, customer success efforts become both scalable and highly effective.

How June Helps Build and Execute a Customer Success Framework

June plays a crucial role in helping customer success teams operationalize their retention and expansion frameworks. By seamlessly combining product analytics with CRM data, June provides the insights needed to track customer health, engagement trends, and expansion potential in real time.

For retention, June enables teams to identify early churn risks, automate re-engagement efforts, and ensure that customers receive timely, relevant support. By surfacing real-time usage data, teams can proactively reach out to at-risk customers before it’s too late, reinforcing value and keeping engagement levels high.

For expansion, June helps companies pinpoint which customers are ready for upsells or additional features, ensuring that outreach is both timely and contextually relevant. Instead of relying on generic sales tactics, teams can use real usage data to drive expansion conversations that align with customer needs.

By providing a unified, data-driven approach to customer success, June ensures that retention and expansion efforts are not based on assumptions but on real customer behavior. This allows SaaS businesses to build frameworks that are both scalable and effective, driving higher engagement, stronger renewals, and increased revenue.

Final Considerations

A structured customer success framework is essential for ensuring long-term customer retention and expansion.

Without it, engagement strategies remain inconsistent, and growth opportunities go untapped. The key to success lies in leveraging data effectively, and with June, customer success teams can move beyond reactive management to a proactive, strategic approach that maximizes both retention and expansion.

title: SaaS Customer Retention: Strategies for Long-Term Success
html:
Customer retention is the foundation of any successful SaaS business. While acquiring new customers is important, the real driver of sustainable growth lies in keeping existing customers engaged, satisfied, and continuously finding value in the product. Unlike one-time transactions, the SaaS model thrives on recurring revenue, making it essential for businesses to focus on reducing churn and ensuring customers remain loyal over time.

Retention is not just about preventing cancellations—it’s about deepening customer relationships, increasing product adoption, and identifying opportunities for expansion. A strong retention strategy helps businesses improve revenue predictability, reduce acquisition costs, and build long-term customer advocacy. Without a well-defined plan to keep customers engaged, even the best SaaS products risk losing users to competitors or disinterest.

TL;DR

  • Customer retention is essential for SaaS growth, ensuring predictable revenue, reducing acquisition costs, and driving expansion through upsells and cross-sells. A strong retention strategy leads to long-term customer relationships and increased lifetime value.
  • SaaS companies scaling from $3M to $10M ARR should prioritize retention, as high churn at this stage can slow growth and reduce efficiency. More mature businesses beyond $10M ARR rely on retention and expansion to maximize revenue.
  • Integrating product data with CRM systems is key to an effective retention strategy, allowing customer success teams to track engagement, identify churn risks, and automate proactive outreach based on real-time customer behavior.
  • June helps SaaS companies improve retention by combining product analytics with CRM insights, enabling teams to monitor customer health, detect early warning signs, and personalize engagement to maximize customer lifetime value.

Why Customer Retention is Essential for B2B SaaS

Retention is directly tied to the financial health of a SaaS company. Customers who stay longer contribute more revenue over time, increasing lifetime value (LTV) while reducing the pressure to constantly acquire new users. Companies with strong retention rates also experience greater opportunities for upselling, cross-selling, and expansion revenue, further strengthening their financial position.

Beyond revenue, retention fuels product growth and advocacy. Engaged customers provide valuable feedback, contribute to product improvements, and often become brand ambassadors, bringing in referrals and strengthening the company’s reputation. In contrast, a high churn rate can stall growth, making it difficult to scale effectively.

The SaaS model depends on long-term relationships. Customers who see continuous value in the product are less likely to leave, creating a stable foundation for growth. A well-executed retention strategy ensures that customers don’t just stay—they thrive, advocate, and expand their usage over time.

Which SaaS Companies Should Prioritize Retention—and When?

While customer retention is important for all SaaS businesses, its significance varies depending on the company’s growth stage, market position, and business model. Early-stage startups often focus more on acquiring new users to establish product-market fit, but as they scale, retention becomes the key factor in driving profitability and sustainable growth.

For SaaS companies transitioning from $3M to $10M ARR, retention should be a top priority. At this stage, businesses have usually validated their market and built an initial customer base. Now, the focus should shift to ensuring those customers remain engaged, renew contracts, and expand their usage over time. A high churn rate at this stage can slow down growth, making it harder to achieve predictable revenue and reducing the efficiency of sales and marketing investments.

More mature SaaS businesses—those beyond $10M ARR and looking to scale efficiently—depend heavily on expansion revenue from existing customers. At this level, the cost of acquiring new customers is often higher than the cost of retaining and expanding existing ones. Prioritizing retention allows these companies to maximize the value of their customer base while reducing reliance on aggressive acquisition strategies.

Regardless of stage, any SaaS business with a high cost of acquisition, long sales cycles, or complex customer onboarding should invest heavily in retention strategies. The longer it takes to acquire and onboard a customer, the more critical it becomes to keep them engaged for the long term.

Key Strategies to Improve Customer Retention in B2B SaaS

Retaining customers requires more than just providing a good product. It involves proactive engagement, data-driven insights, and a deep understanding of customer needs. Successful SaaS companies implement structured strategies to ensure that users remain engaged from onboarding through long-term adoption.

A strong onboarding process is the first step. When customers experience immediate value, they are far more likely to stay. A guided onboarding journey ensures that users understand how to get the most out of the product, reducing frustration and increasing early adoption. Companies that personalize this process based on customer use cases and goals create stronger connections from the very beginning.

Beyond the onboarding process, continuous engagement plays a critical role in retention. Customers need regular touchpoints that reinforce the product’s value. Automated check-ins, educational content, and feature recommendations help maintain engagement, ensuring that users do not drift away over time. Well-timed in-app messages and personalized email sequences can provide guidance based on real usage patterns, keeping customers active and informed.

Proactive customer success efforts also help prevent churn before it happens. By tracking early warning signals such as decreased usage, lower login frequency, or reduced engagement with key features, teams can intervene before a customer decides to leave. A retention-focused strategy should include structured outreach efforts that re-engage inactive users and address potential issues early.

Expansion opportunities further strengthen retention by ensuring that customers continue to grow within the product. When users see additional features that align with their evolving needs, they are more likely to stay invested. Introducing upsell and cross-sell opportunities at the right time enhances the customer experience while increasing revenue. This approach works best when expansion conversations are data-driven, ensuring that recommendations feel relevant rather than forced.

The Role of CRM and Product Data Integration in Customer Retention

One of the biggest challenges in improving retention is gaining a complete view of the customer journey. Many SaaS companies struggle with fragmented data, where customer interactions, product usage, and support history exist in separate systems. Without a unified approach, retention efforts become reactive, making it difficult to engage customers effectively.

By integrating product data with CRM systems, companies create a centralized view of customer health, engagement trends, and risk indicators. This integration allows teams to track how users interact with the product, identify behavior patterns, and personalize retention strategies based on real insights. When customer success managers have access to both product usage data and account history, they can engage with precision, ensuring that outreach efforts align with each customer’s specific needs.

A connected data approach also enables automation. Instead of waiting for churn risks to become apparent, automated workflows can trigger engagement efforts based on predefined signals. If a user’s activity declines, a targeted intervention can be sent immediately, offering support or guidance to re-engage them. If an account is showing signs of expansion readiness, sales and customer success teams can receive automated prompts to start a strategic conversation.

By bridging the gap between product analytics and CRM insights, companies can move beyond guesswork and create a retention strategy that makes customer success both proactive and scalable.

How June Helps SaaS Companies Improve Customer Retention

June plays a crucial role in helping SaaS companies track customer engagement, identify churn risks, and automate retention efforts. By seamlessly integrating product analytics with CRM data, June provides real-time insights that empower customer success teams to take action before it’s too late.

With June, businesses can monitor customer health scores, track feature adoption, and receive automated alerts when engagement drops. This ensures that customer success managers can intervene at the right moment, offering support or re-engagement strategies tailored to each customer’s needs. By understanding how users interact with the product, companies can personalize retention efforts, making each interaction more relevant and impactful.

Beyond churn prevention, June helps SaaS businesses identify expansion opportunities by surfacing insights on high-value accounts that are ready for upselling or cross-selling. Instead of treating retention and growth as separate strategies, June enables customer success teams to create a unified approach that maximizes both.

Final Thoughts on Customer Retention

Customer retention is about continuously delivering value, strengthening customer relationships, and identifying opportunities for expansion. A well-executed retention strategy ensures that customers remain engaged, satisfied, and willing to invest more in the product over time.

By integrating product data with CRM systems, companies can gain a holistic view of the customer journey, enabling proactive engagement and data-driven decision-making. June helps businesses turn insights into action, ensuring that retention strategies are both scalable and effective.

Companies that invest in smart retention strategies, powered by real-time analytics and automation, position themselves for stronger growth, higher revenue, and lasting customer relationships.

title: The power of a founding myth: why every great startup has one
html:
How iconic tech companies craft compelling origin stories to stand out and build lasting brands.

People love stories.

And in startups, a founding myth is one of the most powerful ways to create an emotional connection with your audience. A great founding myth anchors a company’s identity in people’s minds. It reinforces what makes the company unique. And it aligns perfectly with the value it delivers.

Some founding myths are 100% real. Some were small moments that got amplified. Some are entirely crafted.

It doesn’t matter. The strongest brands in tech have them.

Why founding myths matter

Think of a founding myth as the startup equivalent of a national origin story. It provides context, builds credibility, and makes the company memorable. More than just a catchy anecdote, a great myth weaves the company’s identity into a broader narrative that resonates deeply with customers, employees, and investors.

It also serves a practical purpose: differentiation. Startups operate in fiercely competitive markets. When products start to look the same, and features can be copied overnight, what sets a company apart is not just what it does, but the story it tells.

A compelling myth answers:

  • Why does this company exist?
  • What problem was it born to solve?
  • What is the emotional connection between its origin and its mission today?

Classic examples of founding myths

Amazon

Jeff Bezos started Amazon in a tiny office, personally packing and shipping books. His first desk? A door he put some legs on.

The image of the scrappy entrepreneur, working late nights to build the world's largest bookstore, reinforces Amazon’s ethos of frugality and operational efficiency.

→ You get the best price on Amazon because it has always been built for scale and optimization.

Uber

The story goes that Travis Kalanick got the idea for Uber in Paris after struggling to find a cab. The Paris backdrop wasn’t accidental—it suggests a level of sophistication and exclusivity.

→ Uber was born as a luxury black car service, setting the stage for its premium positioning.

Notion

Notion’s founders set up shop in Kyoto, a city known for craftsmanship, simplicity, and thoughtful design. This reinforces the idea that Notion is more than just a productivity tool—it’s a carefully constructed, elegant user experience.

→ Notion isn’t just software. It’s a tool built with intention and artistry.

Shaping a founding myth

If you don’t have a founding myth yet, don’t panic. Myths aren’t always a single moment of inspiration—they can be crafted over time. The best ones highlight the values the company stands for.

Steps to craft your own myth:

  1. Identify a defining moment – When did the idea click? Was there a struggle or breakthrough that shaped the company?
  2. Find the emotional core – Why does this story matter? What does it say about your mission and how you operate?
  3. Make it memorable – A good story sticks because it’s simple, visual, and easy to retell.
  4. Repeat it everywhere – A myth is only powerful if people hear it over and over again. Use it in interviews, fundraising pitches, and even on your website.

Why this matters more than ever

In today’s startup ecosystem, where competition is fiercer than ever, a strong narrative can be the difference between being just another product and becoming an enduring brand. It’s not just about what you build—it’s about how people remember you.

So ask yourself: What’s your story?

title: Customer Health Dashboards: The Key to Proactive Customer Success
html:
Customer success teams thrive on data. Without a clear view of how customers interact with a product, identifying engagement trends, renewal risks, and expansion opportunities becomes nearly impossible. A customer health dashboard solves this challenge by consolidating key metrics into a single, actionable interface. When properly designed, it allows customer success teams to proactively engage accounts, increase retention, and identify growth opportunities before they slip away.

A well-structured dashboard is not just a collection of random data points—it is a strategic tool that helps teams make informed decisions. By integrating product usage insights with CRM data, companies can track customer behavior in real time, ensuring that every interaction is guided by data rather than assumptions. The result is a more efficient customer success operation that anticipates needs, strengthens relationships, and drives long-term revenue growth.

What we'll cover today:

  • A customer health dashboard is essential for proactive customer success, providing real-time insights into engagement, retention risks, and expansion opportunities by tracking key product usage and customer sentiment data.
  • Integrating product analytics with CRM data ensures a complete view of customer health, allowing teams to anticipate issues, personalize outreach, and strategically engage users based on real behavior rather than assumptions.
  • A well-structured dashboard includes metrics on feature adoption, usage trends, customer satisfaction, and upsell potential, enabling customer success teams to act before risks turn into churn and to identify expansion-ready accounts.
  • June helps customer success teams build smarter dashboards by connecting product and CRM data, automating engagement workflows, and providing actionable insights to maximize retention, engagement, and revenue growth.

What is a Customer Health Dashboard?

A customer health dashboard is a real-time visualization of customer engagement, product adoption, and overall account health. It provides a structured way for customer success teams to monitor account activity, detect early warning signs of churn, and capitalize on upsell and expansion opportunities.

Rather than relying on scattered reports or manual tracking, a dashboard aggregates essential data in one place, ensuring that customer success managers (CSMs) have everything they need to take action. A well-organized dashboard does not simply display numbers—it tells a story about how a customer is experiencing the product, whether they are finding value, and what steps can be taken to strengthen the relationship.

The most effective dashboards are not static. They evolve alongside customer needs, incorporating new data sources and refining insights to ensure that engagement strategies remain relevant. This adaptability ensures that customer success teams remain proactive, rather than reactive, in managing relationships.

How to Build a Customer Health Dashboard for Your CS Team

Creating an effective customer health dashboard starts with understanding the key metrics that define success. The goal is to provide a real-time snapshot of customer engagement, satisfaction, and potential risk factors.

Organizing the dashboard begins with segmenting customers based on their lifecycle stage. New users require different monitoring than long-term customers, and accounts nearing renewal should have distinct indicators that highlight their likelihood to continue or churn. By structuring the dashboard around these different stages, teams can apply the right strategies at the right time.

Another critical factor is choosing the right data visualization. Simply listing numbers does not create clarity. A well-designed dashboard should highlight trends, comparisons, and key thresholds that indicate whether an account is healthy or requires immediate attention. Graphs, progress indicators, and predictive scoring models make it easier to identify patterns at a glance and prioritize actions accordingly.

The most important element, however, is ensuring that the data is always up to date and actionable. A static dashboard with outdated insights does more harm than good. By integrating product usage data within the CRM tech stack, teams can track engagement in real-time and trigger automated workflows that address issues before they escalate.

What Data Should Be Included in a Customer Health Dashboard?

The effectiveness of a customer health dashboard depends on the quality and relevance of the data it tracks. Customer engagement metrics, such as logins, session duration, and feature adoption, offer a clear view of how actively a customer is using the product. A drop in these indicators may signal decreasing interest or frustration, requiring immediate intervention.

Beyond engagement, customer sentiment data provides another layer of insight. Tracking support ticket volume, survey responses, and net promoter score questions helps gauge customer satisfaction and potential churn risk. If a previously engaged account suddenly starts submitting more support requests or provides lower feedback scores, it may indicate underlying friction that needs to be addressed.

Expansion and upsell opportunities should also be incorporated into the dashboard. If an account consistently uses high-value features, it may be a strong candidate for an upgrade. Tracking usage patterns alongside CRM data allows customer success teams to identify accounts ready for expansion and engage them at the right moment with relevant offers.

By combining product data with CRM insights, a customer health dashboard becomes far more than just a reporting tool—it transforms into an active engagement engine that helps teams maximize revenue potential while improving customer satisfaction.

Why CRM and Product Data Integration is Critical for Customer Health Dashboards

One of the biggest mistakes companies make when building customer health dashboards is relying solely on either product data or CRM data, rather than integrating both. While product usage insights reveal how customers engage with the platform, CRM data provides the broader context of the relationship, including past interactions, contract details, and historical trends.

Without this integration, customer success teams operate with incomplete information. A customer might appear highly engaged in the product, but if they have previously raised major concerns in support tickets or renewal discussions, their true customer health score could be lower than the usage data alone suggests. On the other hand, an account flagged as a renewal risk might be a prime expansion opportunity if product engagement is increasing.

By synchronizing real-time product data with customer relationship insights, companies can ensure that every engagement is targeted and data-driven. Automated alerts can be triggered when a customer reaches a usage milestone, experiences a drop in engagement, or submits a survey response indicating dissatisfaction. This allows teams to respond proactively rather than waiting for problems to surface.

How June Helps Build Smarter Customer Health Dashboards

June enables customer success teams to create data-rich customer health dashboards that combine product analytics with CRM insights. By providing real-time engagement tracking, usage trend analysis, and customer health scoring, June helps teams anticipate churn risks, identify expansion opportunities, and drive proactive engagement strategies.

With June, customer success managers gain a complete picture of each customer’s journey, ensuring that renewals and upsells are based on actual behavior rather than assumptions. Automated workflows ensure that when key events occur—such as a drop in usage, an increase in support requests, or a milestone achievement—teams are immediately notified and can take action.

Beyond engagement tracking, June enables teams to personalize customer outreach based on real usage patterns. Rather than sending generic check-ins, CSMs can deliver targeted, meaningful interactions that reinforce value and strengthen customer relationships.

Final Thoughts on Customer Health Dashboards

When built correctly, a customer health dashboard provides real-time insights that empower teams to engage customers more effectively, prevent churn, and drive expansion. By integrating product data with CRM records, businesses can ensure that their customer success efforts are always informed by accurate, actionable data.

With June, customer success teams can unlock the full potential of customer health dashboards, ensuring that every interaction is timely, relevant, and strategically aligned with business goals. By leveraging real-time customer analytics and automation, companies can move beyond reactive customer management and create an experience that maximizes retention, engagement, and revenue growth.
