title: From Onboarding to Retention: Customer Success Strategies That Keep SaaS Users Engaged
html:
Customer success is at the core of any B2B SaaS company's growth strategy. It goes beyond answering support tickets or ensuring renewals—it’s about proactively guiding customers toward value, increasing engagement, and driving long-term retention. The most effective customer success strategies are built on a combination of personalized onboarding, targeted engagement, and seamless integration between product analytics and CRM data. By leveraging insights into customer behavior, businesses can design experiences that keep users engaged while also identifying expansion opportunities.

A structured and data-driven approach ensures that customers progress smoothly from sign-up to full product adoption without friction. When executed well, customer success isn’t just about preventing churn—it becomes a key driver of expansion and advocacy.

What we'll cover:

  • Effective customer success strategies focus on proactive engagement through personalized onboarding, targeted in-app messaging, and continuous value reinforcement to drive retention and adoption.
  • Integrating product data with CRM systems provides a complete view of customer behavior, allowing teams to automate relevant touchpoints, identify risks early, and trigger upsell opportunities at the right moment.
  • Customer analytics play a crucial role in shaping engagement strategies, helping teams track user behavior, introduce features contextually, and refine onboarding experiences to prevent churn.
  • June enables customer success teams to execute scalable, data-driven strategies by combining real-time product analytics with CRM insights, ensuring that every interaction is meaningful and aligned with customer needs.

Tailoring the Onboarding Experience to Maximize Success

The first few interactions a customer has with a product set the tone for the entire relationship. A tailored onboarding experience ensures that customers quickly reach their first moment of value, reducing the risk of early drop-off. This requires a deep understanding of how different user segments interact with the product, which can only be achieved through customer data tracking and behavioral analysis.

A structured approach starts with an automated yet personalized onboarding process that walks customers through the key features they need to succeed. Instead of overwhelming them with too much information upfront, progressive disclosure introduces functionalities gradually, keeping the experience intuitive and digestible. Personalized demos can further reinforce the value proposition, helping users understand how the product aligns with their specific workflows and goals.

A well-designed onboarding checklist provides clear milestones for users to follow, ensuring they stay on track. This structured approach not only boosts engagement but also helps customer success teams identify users who may need additional guidance. By tracking progress through product analytics, teams can intervene proactively if a customer is falling behind.

Keeping Users Engaged Beyond Onboarding

The onboarding phase is just the beginning. To maintain momentum, customer success teams need to keep users engaged through ongoing communication and contextual guidance. Email sequences post-sign-up serve as a continuous touchpoint, reinforcing best practices, introducing advanced features, and guiding customers toward deeper product adoption.

In-app messaging provides another powerful tool for engagement. Rather than relying solely on email, well-timed in-app prompts and walkthroughs help users discover key features organically. Gamification techniques, such as badges and progress bars, can make the user experience more interactive, encouraging completion of onboarding steps and ongoing product exploration.

A knowledge base embedded directly within the product gives users a self-serve option to find answers quickly, reducing frustration and improving retention. When customers feel supported at every stage, they are far more likely to continue engaging with the platform rather than seeking alternatives.

Introducing Secondary Features to Exceed Expectations

Once users become comfortable with the core functionality, the next step is to introduce secondary features strategically. By going beyond the essential use case and helping customers discover new capabilities, customer success teams can increase stickiness and prevent churn. Rather than overwhelming users with every feature at once, secondary tools should be presented contextually, based on their behavior and engagement history.

This approach ensures that users continue to see evolving value in the product, rather than plateauing in their experience. By aligning secondary feature introductions with customer workflows, companies can keep engagement levels high and reinforce long-term adoption.

Optimizing Retention and Expansion Opportunities

Customer success isn’t just about keeping users engaged—it’s also a key driver of revenue growth through strategic upselling and expansion. Tracking product usage data allows teams to identify the right moments to introduce premium features or higher-tier plans. If a customer consistently uses a feature with limitations, a well-timed upgrade suggestion can feel natural rather than intrusive.

Surveys embedded within the app provide an opportunity to gather insights directly from users, ensuring that expansion opportunities align with their needs. Similarly, feature request collection helps customer success teams understand which improvements would add the most value, creating a feedback loop that strengthens customer satisfaction.

Referrals and reviews also play a critical role in the expansion phase. Encouraging satisfied customers to share their experiences not only increases customer advocacy but also reinforces their own investment in the platform. Word-of-mouth remains one of the most powerful growth drivers, especially in competitive SaaS markets.

Identifying and Preventing Churn with Data-Driven Insights

Even with a well-executed onboarding and engagement strategy, some customers will inevitably show signs of disengagement. Tracking user behavior provides an early warning system, allowing customer success teams to step in before a customer decides to leave. If a customer stops using key features or significantly reduces their activity, a proactive check-in can help identify pain points and offer solutions.

Exit surveys for customers who do churn provide valuable insights into why they left and what could have been improved. Rather than treating churn as an unavoidable loss, it should be viewed as an opportunity to refine processes, optimize engagement strategies, and continuously enhance the customer journey.

The Role of CRM and Product Data Integration in Customer Success

One of the most significant challenges in customer success is gaining a complete view of the customer journey. Many companies struggle with disconnected data, where product usage insights exist separately from CRM records. This fragmented approach leads to missed opportunities, inefficient outreach, and a lack of personalization in customer interactions.

By integrating product data directly into CRM systems, customer success teams gain a holistic perspective on customer health, engagement trends, and expansion potential. This unified data source ensures that every customer interaction is informed by real behavior, rather than assumptions or outdated records.

When customer success teams have access to real-time insights within the CRM, they can track how individual users engage with the product, identify common friction points, and automate personalized follow-ups based on actual usage patterns. This makes retention more strategic, allowing companies to guide users through the customer journey with precision and relevance.

How June Empowers Customer Success Teams

June plays a crucial role in making data-driven customer success strategies both actionable and scalable. By seamlessly integrating product analytics with CRM data, June provides real-time visibility into customer engagement, adoption trends, and retention risks.

With June, customer success managers can quickly identify accounts that need proactive attention, ensuring that users who are struggling receive timely support. The platform also enables automated, personalized engagement workflows, allowing teams to scale customer success efforts without losing the human touch.

Beyond retention, June helps teams uncover expansion opportunities by surfacing data on feature usage and engagement levels. By recognizing which customers are ready for upsells or additional services, companies can strategically introduce new offerings at the right time, increasing revenue without aggressive sales tactics.

Final Thoughts on Customer Success Strategies

Customer success in SaaS is no longer just about solving problems—it’s about building proactive, data-driven relationships that drive long-term engagement and growth. By personalizing onboarding, leveraging automation, integrating product analytics with CRM, and continuously optimizing engagement strategies, companies can create customer experiences that foster retention and encourage expansion.

With platforms like June, customer success teams gain the insights needed to make strategic decisions at every stage of the customer journey. When customer success is executed with precision, supported by real-time data, and designed to evolve with user needs, it becomes a powerful engine for sustainable business growth.

title: Thoughts on the AI evolution
html:
Artificial intelligence has been on a rapid trajectory—from simple tools that needed explicit instructions to fully autonomous agents capable of making decisions. What started as a way to summarize text or generate SQL from plain English has transformed into a new paradigm: agentic AI.

I believe this shift is not just about better models but about how we, as builders and users, adapt and push AI’s boundaries. Each phase has unlocked new possibilities, not just because of improvements in technology, but because ambitious founders experimented, iterated, and proved what was possible. Every major AI evolution has led to successful startups pioneering the next big thing.

AI as a tool

The first wave of AI was all about direct inputs producing direct outputs. You had to prompt it precisely to get the result you wanted. This was particularly useful for structured tasks—summarization, translation, and generating SQL queries from plain English.

OpenAI’s early Codex, for example, turned human language into functional SQL, making databases far more accessible. Similarly, startups like Copy.ai built AI-powered content generation tools that automated human creativity. But at this stage, AI wasn’t truly "thinking"—it was responding. The intelligence still relied heavily on the user’s instructions.

AI as an assistant

The next phase saw AI moving beyond one-off interactions into more integrated, interactive assistants. Instead of simply producing an output, AI became part of a workflow, continuously helping users with tasks.

For instance, Cursor embedded AI inside development environments, making coding more intuitive. But these assistants still required significant human direction. They reduced friction, but they didn’t independently make decisions.

Still, they relied heavily on user direction. They helped, but they didn’t act on their own.

AI as an agent

Then came AI that could not only assist but act. AI agents execute tasks end-to-end, taking automation to another level.

A breakthrough example is Devin AI, the world’s first AI software engineer, capable of coding and debugging on its own. This was a major shift—AI wasn’t just enhancing human capabilities; it was beginning to replace manual effort entirely.

The rise of agentic AI

Now, AI is moving beyond executing predefined tasks to dynamically figuring out what needs to be done next. Instead of following a fixed script, agentic AI can adapt in real time.

Anthropic’s Claude is one of the leaders in this space, aiming to build AI that not only completes requests but can also determine what’s necessary to achieve a broader goal. This marks the beginning of AI managing complex processes with minimal human intervention.

The race to find new use cases

With the rise of agentic AI, we’re seeing an intense competition among founders to discover the next breakthrough use cases. Investors are placing massive bets, sometimes funding AI startups at sky-high valuations—even before they’ve proven product-market fit.

I think this is both an incredible opportunity and a dangerous trap. Some of these AI startups will fail. A lot of capital will be lost. But for the ones that succeed, the upside is enormous.

Take Lovable.dev as an example. This text-to-functioning-app editor skyrocketed to $17M in ARR in just six months. The appeal is clear: you simply type the app you want, and Lovable generates the necessary code and deploys it for you. This kind of AI-native experience would have been unimaginable just a few years ago.

What enabled this shift?

Several key factors have driven AI’s rapid evolution:

  • Better models → More capable AI like GPT-4, Claude, and multimodal systems that handle images, text, and actions.
  • Better infrastructure → Vector databases, AI memory, and improved orchestration frameworks have made complex AI applications more viable.
  • Successful experiments → Startups testing the limits of AI have demonstrated what’s possible, inspiring others to follow suit.

Why does this matter?

Each AI evolution doesn’t replace the last—it builds on it. AI assistants didn’t kill AI tools, and AI agents haven’t made assistants obsolete. Instead, every step forward has unlocked new, higher-value use cases.

I believe we’re just at the beginning of agentic AI. The most exciting part isn’t what AI can do today—it’s what people will build with it next. The startups that master this new paradigm will define the next era of AI-powered work. Soon, instead of asking AI to perform a task, we’ll just define a goal—and AI will figure out how to achieve it.

The race is on.

title: Tech-Touch Customer Success: Scaling Engagement Without Losing Impact
html:
Customer success in SaaS has traditionally been associated with high-touch, one-on-one interactions where dedicated managers guide customers through every stage of the journey.

While this approach works well for enterprise accounts, it quickly becomes unsustainable as a company scales. This is where tech-touch customer success comes in—a model that leverages automation, product analytics, and CRM integration to engage customers efficiently at scale.

For growing B2B SaaS businesses, a tech-touch approach allows customer success teams to deliver value to a large number of customers without direct human intervention at every step. By combining personalized automation with data-driven insights, tech-touch customer success ensures that even lower-revenue accounts receive proactive guidance, timely support, and strategic engagement. When implemented effectively, it enhances adoption, retention, and expansion while freeing up human resources for high-priority accounts.

What we'll cover today:

  • Tech-touch customer success helps B2B SaaS companies scale engagement efficiently by using automation, product analytics, and CRM integration to support a growing customer base without relying on constant human interaction.
  • Automation plays a key role in proactive customer success, ensuring that customers receive timely onboarding guidance, feature adoption nudges, and engagement reminders based on real-time behavior rather than manual outreach.
  • Integrating product data with CRM systems is essential for making tech-touch strategies effective, allowing customer success teams to track usage trends, identify risks, and trigger personalized engagement workflows that feel relevant rather than generic.
  • June enables SaaS businesses to execute a smart tech-touch approach by combining product analytics with CRM insights, ensuring that customer success teams can drive retention, expansion, and engagement with data-backed automation.

The Role of Automation in SaaS Customer Engagement

In a tech-touch model, automation becomes the foundation of engagement. Instead of relying on CSMs to manually track usage patterns, respond to risks, and guide customers through milestones, technology steps in to deliver personalized, contextual interactions at scale. This can include automated customer onboarding processes, product adoption nudges, in-app messaging, email campaigns, and proactive outreach triggered by specific customer behaviors.

The key to making automation work is ensuring it feels personal and timely rather than generic or reactive. When customer actions trigger well-designed, data-driven interactions, businesses can maintain engagement without overwhelming customers with unnecessary communication. Instead of waiting for customers to request support, tech-touch strategies anticipate needs, offering solutions at the right time based on real usage data.

This approach allows businesses to provide consistent, scalable customer experiences, ensuring that every customer—regardless of size—receives structured guidance and meaningful touchpoints that drive value realization.

Tech-Touch vs. High-Touch Customer Success

While high-touch customer success focuses on deep relationships and frequent personalized interactions, tech-touch takes a more automated, data-driven approach. High-touch models rely on dedicated CSMs working closely with customers, often through direct calls, meetings, and customized success plans. This is typically reserved for high-value accounts where maximizing retention and expansion potential justifies the cost of dedicated resources.

Tech-touch, on the other hand, is designed for scalability. It works best for mid-tier and lower-tier accounts that do not require frequent one-on-one engagement but still benefit from structured, proactive support. Instead of relying on individual CSMs, it leverages automation, product analytics, and CRM-driven workflows to deliver relevant, targeted interactions.

A hybrid model often works best, where high-touch is reserved for strategic customers, while tech-touch ensures that the broader customer base remains engaged, educated, and supported. The success of this model depends on how well data is used to personalize automated interactions, making customers feel valued without requiring constant human oversight.

A Framework for Succeeding with Tech-Touch Customer Success in B2B SaaS

Implementing a tech-touch model requires a structured framework that combines automation, data intelligence, and seamless CRM integration. The first step is understanding customer segmentation, ensuring that the right engagement strategy is applied based on revenue potential, usage patterns, and risk indicators. Customers with predictable, straightforward use cases can thrive with tech-touch approaches, while more complex, high-value accounts might require additional human involvement.

The second pillar of success lies in automated engagement workflows. These workflows should be designed to guide customers through key lifecycle stages, from onboarding to expansion. Timely product walkthroughs, milestone-based email sequences, and in-app messaging ensure that customers receive the right information at the right time, reducing friction in adoption.

Beyond automation, data-driven insights play a crucial role in ensuring tech-touch strategies are effective. Product usage metrics help identify which customers are engaged and which might need additional support, while CRM setup & integration provides a unified view of each customer’s journey. Without these insights, automation risks becoming impersonal or irrelevant.

Finally, continuous optimization and iteration ensure that tech-touch engagement remains effective. By monitoring customer responses, refining workflows, and adjusting based on behavioral trends, SaaS businesses can ensure that automated engagement remains meaningful rather than mechanical.

Product Data Integration with CRM: A Critical Component of Tech-Touch Success

One of the biggest challenges in scaling customer success is ensuring that automation remains intelligent and personalized. This is where product data integration with CRM tech stack becomes invaluable. When customer success teams have access to real-time product usage data within their CRM, they can trigger automated workflows based on actual customer behavior rather than static timelines or assumptions.

With deep integration between product analytics and CRM, customer success teams can track feature adoption, identify inactive users, and automatically initiate engagement workflows that address specific customer needs. For example, if a customer hasn’t used a key feature within a certain timeframe, an automated message can provide guidance or offer a relevant case study. If a customer’s engagement spikes, a targeted expansion opportunity can be introduced at the right moment.

This integration eliminates blind spots and ensures that even tech-touch strategies remain highly contextual, data-driven, and impactful. Instead of sending generic check-ins or irrelevant messages, companies can tailor outreach based on real usage trends, reinforcing value at every step of the customer journey.

How June Helps Scale Tech-Touch Customer Success

June provides the product analytics and CRM integration capabilities needed to execute a successful tech-touch strategy. By offering real-time insights into customer engagement, feature adoption, and behavioral trends, June helps SaaS companies design smarter automation workflows that feel personal and relevant.

With June, customer success teams can track customer health scores, identify risks, and automate interventions that keep users engaged. Whether it’s surfacing inactive accounts for re-engagement, flagging expansion opportunities, or tracking which customers are ready for renewal conversations, June ensures that tech-touch strategies remain proactive rather than reactive.

By bridging the gap between product analytics and CRM workflows, June enables scalable, automated customer engagement that doesn’t compromise on quality. Instead of relying solely on manual touchpoints, companies using June can implement data-backed customer success strategies that drive retention and growth—at scale.

Final Thoughts on Tech-Touch Customer Success

Tech-touch customer success is not about replacing human interactions—it’s about scaling engagement intelligently. By leveraging automation, data-driven insights, and CRM-product analytics integration, SaaS companies can deliver proactive, personalized customer success experiences without requiring constant human involvement.

June provides the tools to execute a tech-touch model that works, ensuring that every customer interaction is informed, timely, and aligned with their product journey. When done right, tech-touch customer success becomes a powerful driver of retention, expansion, and long-term customer satisfaction.

title: Customer Success Planning: Turning Product and CRM Data into Engagement, Retention and Growth
html:
Customer success is more than just a department—it’s a structured, ongoing effort to ensure customers achieve their desired outcomes with a product. For B2B SaaS companies, where long-term retention is the foundation of sustainable growth, having a clear and well-defined customer success plan is essential.

A customer success plan provides a structured approach to guiding customers from onboarding to full adoption, ensuring that engagement remains high and opportunities for expansion are identified early. Without a plan in place, customer success teams operate reactively, addressing issues as they arise rather than proactively driving value and growth.

A strong customer success plan does not just focus on preventing churn. It serves as a roadmap for customer engagement, retention, and expansion, aligning internal teams with customer needs and ensuring that each interaction contributes to a long-term partnership. Creating and executing such a plan requires a combination of customer analytics, strategic engagement tactics, and seamless integration between product data and CRM systems.

What we'll cover today:

  • A structured customer success plan is essential for SaaS companies to proactively guide customers from onboarding to retention and expansion, ensuring they continuously derive value from the product.
  • Customer analytics play a critical role in shaping an effective plan, helping teams track engagement trends, anticipate risks, and refine strategies based on real-time data rather than assumptions.
  • Integrating product data with CRM systems provides a complete view of customer health, enabling customer success managers to personalize outreach, optimize engagement efforts, and improve retention rates.
  • June empowers customer success teams with actionable insights, combining product usage analytics with CRM data to drive smarter decision-making, automate proactive interventions, and measure the success of engagement strategies.

What is a Customer Success Plan and Why Does It Matter?

A customer success plan is a structured framework designed to help customers maximize their experience with a product. It outlines the key touchpoints, success milestones, and ongoing strategies that ensure customers not only use the product but derive measurable value from it. The purpose of this plan is to align the customer’s goals with the company’s ability to deliver on them, creating a mutual path to success.

Without a clearly defined plan, customer interactions become fragmented. Some customers might receive high-touch support while others are left navigating the product on their own.

A structured approach ensures that every customer receives the appropriate level of guidance, whether through dedicated CSMs, automated engagement strategies, or periodic value-driven check-ins. It also allows customer success teams to track progress, measure impact, and make informed decisions about retention and expansion opportunities.

Key Elements of a Customer Success Plan

A well-designed customer success plan includes several core components. The first is engagement, which involves guiding customers through onboarding, training, and product adoption.

Engagement should be proactive, ensuring that customers feel supported and confident in their ability to use the product effectively. Success teams should work closely with customers to understand their business goals and align product capabilities with those objectives.

The second element is retention, which focuses on maintaining customer satisfaction over time. This includes monitoring product usage, identifying risk signals, and implementing strategies to prevent churn. Retention efforts should be data-driven, relying on customer health scores and behavioral analytics to anticipate and address issues before they escalate. Regular check-ins, feature recommendations, and personalized interactions all contribute to higher retention rates.

The final component is expansion, which refers to increasing the value customers get from the product through upsells or cross-sells, and deeper adoption of advanced features. Expansion happens naturally when customers recognize the long-term benefits of a product and see clear opportunities to enhance their operations through additional capabilities. A customer success plan should include structured outreach efforts to introduce new features and identify potential growth opportunities within existing accounts.

How to Create a Customer Success Plan

Developing an effective customer success plan starts with understanding customer needs. This requires gathering insights from sales handoffs, onboarding sessions, and early product interactions to build a customer profile that includes business objectives, use cases, and potential challenges. Once the foundation is set, the plan should outline key milestones that indicate successful adoption. These milestones should be measurable, tracking whether customers are progressing toward their expected outcomes.

The next step is defining engagement strategies. Some customers may require high-touch interactions with dedicated CSMs, while others may benefit from self-serve onboarding experiences supported by automated workflows. Defining the right level of engagement ensures that resources are allocated efficiently while maintaining strong customer relationships.

Retention strategies should be built into the plan from the start. Rather than waiting for renewal periods to assess customer health, ongoing monitoring and proactive interventions should be integrated into the process. By continuously tracking product usage and sentiment, customer success teams can anticipate risks and address concerns before they lead to churn.

Expansion efforts should also be strategically planned. This involves identifying the right timing for introducing additional features or services, ensuring that upselling and cross-selling efforts feel organic rather than forced. Expansion should always align with customer needs, reinforcing the value the product delivers.

Leveraging Customer Analytics to Build a Stronger Plan for CS

Customer analytics play a critical role in shaping a customer success plan. Data-driven insights help teams understand which behaviors correlate with long-term success and which signals indicate risk. By analyzing patterns in product usage, engagement trends, and customer feedback, teams can make informed decisions about where to focus their efforts.

Tracking how customers interact with specific features helps refine engagement strategies. If certain workflows are underutilized, customer success teams can introduce targeted education efforts to drive adoption. Similarly, analyzing renewal trends can highlight the factors that contribute to high retention rates, enabling teams to replicate successful strategies across the customer base.

With real-time customer analytics, success teams can shift from a reactive model to a proactive one. Rather than waiting for customer complaints or drop-offs in engagement, teams can intervene at the right moments, ensuring that customers stay engaged and continue to see value in the product.

The Role of CRM and Product Data Integration in Customer Success Planning

Integrating product usage data into CRM systems transforms how customer success teams operate. Instead of relying solely on past interactions or account history, teams can access real-time insights that reflect how customers are actively using the product. This integration allows for a holistic view of customer health, combining support tickets, engagement levels, and feature adoption into a single, actionable dataset.

With this level of visibility, customer success managers can prioritize outreach based on actual usage patterns, ensuring that at-risk customers receive the attention they need while highly engaged accounts are introduced to relevant expansion opportunities. Automated workflows can also be triggered based on key behaviors, such as sending proactive guidance when a customer hasn’t engaged with a critical feature or offering targeted recommendations based on usage trends.

This seamless integration between CRM and product analytics removes the guesswork from customer success planning, allowing teams to build strategies that are rooted in actual customer behavior rather than assumptions.

How June Helps Customer Success Teams Execute Their Plan

June plays a pivotal role in helping customer success teams operationalize their success plans by providing real-time product analytics integrated with CRM data. With June, customer success managers gain a clear view of how customers interact with the product, enabling them to track engagement trends, monitor health scores, and identify opportunities for both retention and expansion.

By surfacing actionable insights, June allows teams to tailor engagement strategies, ensuring that outreach efforts are personalized and data-driven. The ability to connect customer usage data with CRM records ensures that every interaction is contextual and meaningful, strengthening customer relationships and improving retention rates.

Beyond engagement, June helps teams measure the effectiveness of their success plans. By analyzing customer behavior before and after interventions, teams can continuously refine their approach, ensuring that strategies evolve alongside customer needs. This makes customer success planning an ongoing, adaptive process rather than a static set of guidelines.

Final Thoughts on Customer Success Planning

Customer success planning is essential for B2B SaaS companies looking to drive engagement, retention, and growth. Without a structured plan, customer success teams risk operating reactively, addressing issues as they arise rather than proactively guiding customers toward long-term success.

By incorporating engagement strategies, retention efforts, and expansion initiatives, companies can create a framework that ensures customers receive ongoing value.

Leveraging customer analytics, integrating product usage data into CRM systems, and using platforms like June allows teams to build a plan that is both data-driven and highly actionable. The ability to anticipate customer needs, optimize engagement efforts, and measure success ensures that customer success teams are not just problem solvers, but strategic drivers of growth.

title: How I grew to 60K followers on LinkedIn (and what you can learn from it)
html:
Thank you!

I just passed 60,000 followers on LinkedIn. In 2024 alone, my posts generated 18 million impressions, leading to 22,000 directly attributed website sessions. And while it’s hard to track exact numbers, we suspect LinkedIn has contributed to hundreds of thousands in ARR.

Here’s what I’ve learned from this journey—and how you can grow on LinkedIn too.

LinkedIn is a lead generation machine for B2B SaaS

For most B2B SaaS companies, LinkedIn is an incredible opportunity. Why? Because in B2B, it takes an average of six touchpoints before someone signs up for a product. Most people don’t buy on the first interaction.

LinkedIn enables exactly that: multiple touchpoints, varied interactions, and a natural way to build relationships over time. One day you share an industry insight, the next a customer success story, then maybe a feature announcement or a piece of content. Happy customers may chime in, creating instant social proof—like a live testimonial wall.

Even better, LinkedIn’s organic reach isn’t dependent on ad budgets. People engage because they’re genuinely interested. And despite what some say, LinkedIn is FAR from saturated.

Is LinkedIn saturated? Nope.

310 million people log into LinkedIn every month, but only 3 million post weekly—that’s just 1% creating content. LinkedIn isn’t even in the top 15 social media apps in terms of active users. If you think it’s too late to build an audience, think again.

After three years of consistent posting, I’ve seen the platform change. New creators emerge, some disappear. But the fundamentals remain the same. Here are five things that helped me grow—and that I rarely see people talk about.

1. Nail your positioning

LinkedIn isn’t overcrowded, but people’s minds are. You need to stand out.

Your goal is to own a specific spot in people’s minds. When they think of you, they should immediately associate you with a topic.

How do you find your positioning? Start with topics where you have legitimacy. If you were a PM at Intercom, people will care about your product management insights. If you built a successful startup, people want to hear about that.

For me, my three core topics are:

  • Product management before product-market fit
  • The challenges of a startup journey
  • AI done right

Great creators have a personal positioning:

  • Lenny Rachitsky? "Deeply researched product, growth, and career advice"
  • Elena Verna? No-bs B2B growth marketing.
  • Justin Welsh? How to build a one-person business.

Positioning takes time. Test topics, see what resonates, iterate. Once you find your lane, refine it—update your bio and profile visuals to reinforce it.

2. Speak to your target audience

LinkedIn takes effort, so remember why you’re doing it: business growth.

Your content should align with your audience. June’s audience, for example, includes founding teams, CSMs, and RevOps at early-stage companies. When I write about product, startups, and AI, I tailor it for them.

Many influencers attract huge followings but little business. Some do it intentionally; others don’t. If your goal is business impact, pick topics your ideal customers care about. They don’t have to be about your product, but they should resonate with your audience.

Great examples:

  • VCs write about how to build great startups—then offer funding.
  • Justin Welsh writes about LinkedIn success—then sells courses on it.
  • Adam Robinson shares methods to grow revenue—then sells a product that converts visitors into leads.

Find the intersection between what you’re passionate about and what aligns with your business.

3. Be human

LinkedIn is professional, but too many people act too professional. Or cringe.

At work, you don’t speak in jargon-filled corporate talk. Don’t do it on LinkedIn either. The best creators show personality. People can tell when a real human is behind an account, sharing real thoughts and experiences.

Things that work for me:

  • Engaging in 1:1 conversations—I try to reply to every comment.
  • Writing like I talk—casual, direct, sometimes even “lol.”
  • Humor, sarcasm, and the occasional cringe.

One tip: check your LinkedIn feed and drop fun, thoughtful comments on the top five posts. Do this daily. It becomes a habit—and helps build relationships.

4. Quality > Quantity

You’ve heard this before, but here’s what it really means: LinkedIn rewards GREAT posts, not good ones.

The algorithm works by pushing high-engagement posts to a wider audience. If your content is just “good,” it won’t go far.

To create standout content:

  • Keep a backlog of ideas. If an idea still excites you weeks later, it’s worth writing about.
  • Write drafts. Rewrite, refine, and iterate until it’s strong.
  • Post when it’s ready—not just to hit a quota.

How often should you post? As often as you can maintain high quality—whether that’s once a week or daily doesn’t matter.

5. Keep testing new formats

People judge posts by their format. What worked last year won’t always work today.

At first, plain text posts dominated. Then the “Justin Welsh method” (problem > agitate > tease solution) took over. Then carousels. Then videos. Now single images are trending. LinkedIn constantly evolves.

To stay ahead, experiment. Change up your content style, try new formats, and surprise your audience.

The other truth about creating on linkedIn

Some things no one tells you:

  • It’s a grind. Some days you won’t feel like posting. Prep ahead so those days aren’t so hard.
  • Your reach will fluctuate. Some weeks your content will soar; other times, it’ll tank. It’s frustrating, but normal.
  • The platform constantly changes. LinkedIn is a moving target. If your reach drops, don’t panic—experiment until you find what works again.

Final thoughts

LinkedIn has been an incredible platform for me. It’s helped me connect with thousands of people, grow my business, and share insights that resonate.

If you’re just starting or looking to grow, I hope these learnings help. And if you’ve figured out things I haven’t—drop a comment, I’d love to hear.

Thank you all for being part of this journey 💜

title: The Customer Onboarding Process: A Customer Success Perspective
html:
Customer onboarding is one of the most critical phases in the customer journey. It sets the foundation for engagement, retention, and long-term growth.

For customer success teams, this process is more than just introducing users to a product—it’s about ensuring that new customers quickly realize the value of their investment. A smooth and strategic onboarding process reduces churn, accelerates product adoption, and strengthens customer relationships from day one.

In B2B SaaS, where recurring revenue depends on long-term engagement, onboarding plays an even bigger role. A poorly executed experience can lead to confusion, low adoption, and ultimately, customer dissatisfaction.

On the other hand, a well-structured process ensures that customers not only understand the product but integrate it seamlessly into their daily workflows.

TLD;DR

  • Customer onboarding is the foundation of long-term retention and engagement in B2B SaaS. A well-structured onboarding process ensures that customers quickly realize value, reducing churn and increasing product adoption.
  • Data-driven onboarding is far more effective than a one-size-fits-all approach. Customer analytics help customer success teams track engagement, identify friction points, and personalize the experience to meet each customer’s needs.
  • Integrating CRM and product analytics improves onboarding by providing a unified view of customer behavior. With real-time insights, teams can proactively address low engagement, automate follow-ups, and guide customers toward key milestones.
  • June helps customer success managers streamline onboarding with actionable insights. By tracking product usage and customer interactions, June enables proactive engagement, ensuring that customers stay on track and reach their first moment of value faster.

The Anatomy of an Effective Customer Onboarding Process

A well-designed onboarding experience should feel intuitive, structured, and proactive. From the first touchpoint, customers need clarity on how the product solves their specific challenges. A successful onboarding process is not just about technical setup but also about guiding customers toward their first meaningful outcomes.

For customer success teams, this means balancing education with personalization. The process should start with a clear understanding of the customer’s business goals, ensuring that every step is aligned with what they hope to achieve. From initial product walkthroughs to personalized training sessions, each interaction should reinforce how the product delivers measurable value. The transition from sales to onboarding should also be seamless, with customer data flowing effortlessly between teams to prevent any loss of context.

Onboarding is not a one-size-fits-all approach. Some customers may need more hands-on guidance, while others prefer self-serve resources. The ability to segment customers based on their needs and engagement levels helps ensure that each account receives the right level of support. Continuous check-ins and feedback loops are also essential, allowing customer success managers to adjust the process based on real-time customer insights.

Why Customer Analytics is Essential for Onboarding

An effective onboarding process is built on data, not guesswork. Customer analytics helps teams understand how new users interact with the product, whether they are completing key milestones, and where they might be struggling. By tracking onboarding metrics, customer success teams can proactively address roadblocks before they become larger issues.

Visibility into engagement patterns allows teams to optimize onboarding workflows, ensuring that customers stay on track. If data shows that certain users are dropping off at specific stages, adjustments can be made to improve clarity or provide additional support. Customer analytics also helps identify which onboarding tactics are most effective, allowing teams to refine their approach based on actual results.

For customer success teams, having real-time access to onboarding data is invaluable. It means being able to intervene at the right moments, offer personalized guidance, and create a smoother path to product adoption. Without these insights, onboarding becomes a reactive process rather than a strategic driver of success.

How CRM and Product Data Integration Enhances Customer Onboarding Processes

Seamless integration between product data and CRM systems significantly improves the onboarding experience. Customer success teams need a unified view of each account, combining product engagement insights with customer profiles, previous interactions, and business objectives. Without this integration, valuable information is often scattered across different platforms, leading to inefficiencies and missed opportunities.

By connecting CRM tech stack and product analytics, teams gain a holistic understanding of customer behavior. They can track how new users engage with the product, identify where they may need additional support, and ensure that onboarding is aligned with their specific goals. This integration also facilitates automation, allowing for timely follow-ups, personalized recommendations, and proactive interventions when necessary.

In B2B SaaS, where customer relationships are complex and involve multiple stakeholders, a connected data ecosystem ensures that onboarding remains smooth and efficient. It enables customer success managers to operate with greater precision, making data-driven decisions that lead to higher adoption and long-term satisfaction.

How June Supports Customer Success Managers in Onboarding Processes

June plays a crucial role in helping customer success teams streamline and enhance the onboarding process. By integrating product analytics with CRM data, June provides a real-time view of how customers interact with the product from the very first day. This visibility allows teams to track onboarding progress, identify engagement gaps, and take action before any potential issues arise.

With June, customer success managers can personalize onboarding based on real usage data. If a new account is actively exploring key features, teams can reinforce those behaviors with additional best practices. If engagement is low, targeted outreach can help guide customers back on track. Instead of relying on assumptions, onboarding becomes a data-driven strategy that ensures every customer reaches their first moment of value as quickly as possible.

By surfacing key insights and automating critical touchpoints, June empowers customer success teams to be proactive rather than reactive. This results in a smoother onboarding experience, higher product adoption rates, and ultimately, stronger customer retention.

The Impact of a Customer Onboarding Process on Growth, Engagement, and Retention

A well-executed onboarding process has a direct impact on a company’s bottom line. Customers who experience a smooth introduction to a product are far more likely to stay engaged, renew their subscriptions, and expand their usage over time. Onboarding influences retention by ensuring that customers achieve early success, reinforcing their decision to invest in the product.

Beyond retention, strong onboarding also drives expansion revenue. When customers fully understand the product’s capabilities, they are more open to exploring advanced features or upgrading their plans. The relationship established during onboarding lays the groundwork for future upselling and cross-selling opportunities.

From a customer engagement perspective, onboarding shapes the way users interact with a product long after the initial setup. A positive experience leads to stronger product adoption, while a confusing or frustrating one can lead to disengagement. Companies that prioritize onboarding as a strategic initiative see higher levels of engagement across their customer base, leading to long-term success.

Final Thoughts: Why Companies should Treat Onboarding as an On-going Process

Customer onboarding is not just a technical process—it’s the foundation of customer success. For B2B SaaS companies, an effective onboarding strategy ensures that customers achieve early value, remain engaged, and continue to grow with the product. By leveraging customer analytics, CRM integration, and real-time insights from platforms like June, customer success teams can create a structured, data-driven onboarding experience that drives retention and long-term success.

Companies that treat onboarding as an ongoing process rather than a one-time event set themselves apart. When customers feel supported, informed, and confident in their decision, renewal conversations become easier, product adoption accelerates, and overall customer satisfaction improves. With the right tools and approach, onboarding becomes not just an introduction to the product, but the start of a long and successful partnership.

title: Product Usage Metrics: How to Use Embedded Dashboards to Close More Renewals
html:
Customer renewals in B2B SaaS rely on one fundamental principle: demonstrating ongoing value. If customers clearly see how a product impacts their business, retention becomes a natural outcome. The challenge, however, lies in effectively showcasing that value in a way that resonates.

Many companies struggle with providing tangible evidence of how their software improves workflows, saves time, or increases efficiency.

This was the exact challenge faced by TrueClicks, a PPC optimization platform designed to help agencies and advertisers maximize their Google Ads performance. While their product delivered actionable insights and automated recommendations, they needed a way to prove its long-term impact to customers.

Their solution came in the form of product usage metrics and embedded dashboards, built with June, to reinforce the platform’s value, improve engagement, and drive more renewals.

What we'll cover today:

  • Product usage metrics help B2B SaaS companies drive retention by providing visibility into customer engagement, feature adoption, and overall product impact. Tracking these insights allows customer success teams to proactively address churn risks and strengthen renewals.
  • TrueClicks improved its renewal process by embedding dashboards that combined product usage data with CRM insights, ensuring customers continuously saw the value of their platform. By making performance metrics easily accessible, they reinforced ROI and made renewals a data-backed decision.
  • Integrating CRM data with product analytics enables proactive customer success, allowing teams to track customer health, personalize outreach, and identify expansion opportunities. This combination ensures retention strategies are based on real user behavior rather than assumptions.
  • June played a critical role in helping TrueClicks scale renewals, providing real-time insights, automated customer health tracking, and embedded analytics that kept customers engaged. By leveraging June’s capabilities, TrueClicks turned retention into a seamless and predictable process.

How Product Usage Metrics Improve Customer Retention

Product usage metrics offer a way to understand how customers interact with a SaaS platform. They provide visibility into key behaviors such as engagement levels, feature adoption, and the overall impact of the product on customer workflows.

Many companies track these data points, but the real difference comes from how they use them. For customer success teams, these insights help predict churn risks, identify expansion opportunities, and tailor engagement strategies to ensure customers continue finding value.

Some of the most insightful usage data focuses on activity trends over time, showing whether customers are increasing or decreasing their engagement. Other indicators, such as the frequency of feature usage, reveal whether customers are fully utilizing the product’s capabilities or only scratching the surface.

Understanding these patterns helps teams intervene early when engagement drops or highlight underutilized features that could enhance the customer experience.

For companies focused on renewals, the ability to connect product usage with business impact is crucial. Rather than simply tracking logins or time spent in the platform, customer success teams need to measure how the product contributes to efficiency gains, cost savings, or strategic improvements.

TrueClicks recognized that proving these benefits in a clear and accessible way would strengthen customer retention and create a more seamless SaaS renewal process.

The Role of Embedded Dashboards and Product Usage Metrics

Embedded dashboards play a key role in connecting product analytics and CRM data, creating a seamless way to track and present customer insights.

By embedding key usage metrics directly into customer portals, internal dashboards, and renewal reports, companies provide customers with real-time visibility into how the product is benefiting them.

TrueClicks adopted this approach to reinforce its value proposition. By embedding live performance data into analytics dashboards, they allowed users to track their campaign improvements, optimizations, and efficiency gains without needing to log into multiple systems.

This continuous exposure to success metrics meant that customers weren’t just reminded of TrueClicks’ value during renewal conversations—they saw it every day.

Internally, the TrueClicks team also built a usage tracking system that combined CRM data with product analytics. This allowed their customer success managers and sales teams to monitor engagement patterns, detect early signs of churn, and identify accounts that were ready for expansion.

With a data-rich internal dashboard, their team could engage proactively, addressing issues before they escalated and reinforcing the platform’s impact with personalized customer insights.

How TrueClicks Used Product Usage Data to Close More Renewals

TrueClicks recognized that renewals weren’t just about having a good product or customer success renewal playbook but about ensuring clients consistently saw the value in the product itself.

Instead of relying on traditional renewal reminders or periodic check-ins, they built a system that kept product impact front and center throughout the customer lifecycle.

Internally, they developed a comprehensive dashboard that provided real-time data on customer engagement. They tracked active users, measured feature adoption rates, and analyzed how often customers leveraged the platform’s most impactful tools.

By monitoring these trends, their customer success team could pinpoint which accounts needed intervention, whether through additional training, product recommendations, or proactive support. This meant that rather than reacting to churn risks, they could address them before they became real issues.

Beyond their internal tracking, TrueClicks took it a step further by embedding personalized performance dashboards for customers. Each user had access to a tailored view of their success metrics, showing exactly how the platform was optimizing their advertising spend, improving campaign efficiency, and delivering measurable results.

Instead of manually gathering proof points before renewal discussions, customers already had that information at their fingertips. This transformed the renewal conversation from a negotiation into a natural continuation of the value they had already experienced.

By continuously reinforcing the impact of their platform, TrueClicks removed uncertainty from the renewal decision. Customers didn’t need to be convinced to stay—they could see the results for themselves. This shift significantly improved retention, strengthened customer relationships, and positioned TrueClicks as an indispensable tool for their users.

Why CRM Data and Product Usage Metrics Are Critical for Retention

An effective customer retention strategy depends on more than just a good product—it requires a data-driven approach that combines CRM insights with real-time product analytics.

While a traditional CRM tech stack stores account details, contract history, and supports interactions, it often fallsshort when it comes to tracking how customers are actually using the product. Without this visibility, customer success teams are left guessing about which accounts are thriving and which are at risk.

By integrating product usage data directly into the CRM, companies gain a holistic view of the customer journey. They can monitor engagement trends, identify the specific features driving value, and personalize outreach based on actual user behavior.

This kind of integration ensures that every interaction is based on real customer needs rather than assumptions.

For SaaS businesses focused on retention, a CRM-product analytics integration provides actionable insights. Customer success teams can see when engagement drops, enabling them to step in before a customer loses interest.

Sales teams can identify upsell or cross-sell opportunities based on feature adoption patterns. Even marketing teams can refine messaging by understanding which features resonate most with different customer segments.

TrueClicks saw the impact of this approach firsthand. By combining CRM data with real-time product insights using June, they created a system that empowered every customer-facing team with the information they needed to drive renewals and engagement.

How June Helped TrueClicks Improve Retention with Embedded Analytics Capabilities

June played a central role in TrueClicks’ renewal success strategy, providing the data and analytics capabilities needed to track product engagement, surface key usage trends, and integrate those insights into both internal dashboards and customer-facing experiences.

With June’s CRM integration, TrueClicks’ customer success team gained a real-time overview of customer health, enabling proactive engagement strategies that addressed risks before they escalated. They could easily see which accounts were highly engaged, which needed more guidance, and which were prime candidates for expansion opportunities.

Beyond internal tracking, June’s embedded analytics capabilities allowed TrueClicks to provide customers with clear, easy-to-understand usage reports. Customers didn’t just receive renewal emails—they had ongoing access to performance data that reinforced why TrueClicks was a valuable part of their workflow.

By leveraging June’s analytics to bridge the gap between CRM data and product usage insights, TrueClicks made renewals a data-backed decision rather than a subjective discussion. This approach strengthened customer trust, improved retention rates, and ultimately helped them close more renewals with confidence.

Final Thoughts on Product Usage Metrics and Embedded Dashboards

Customer retention in SaaS depends on more than just having a good product—it’s about continuously proving its value. TrueClicks’ success with embedded dashboards and product usage metrics highlights the importance of making impact visible at all times, rather than just at renewal discussions.

By integrating product analytics with CRM data, SaaS businesses can move beyond traditional customer success strategies and build a retention model that is proactive, personalized, and data-driven. With solutions like June, companies can ensure that their customer success teams always have the right insights to drive engagement, improve adoption, and make renewals a natural and seamless process.

title: Customer Success Enablement: Empowering Teams to Drive Retention
html:
Customer success has become a fundamental aspect of B2B SaaS companies, ensuring that customers not only see value in a product but remain engaged and committed to it over time.

However, as businesses expand, having a dedicated customer success team alone is not enough. These teams need structured knowledge, efficient processes, and the right tools to function effectively.

This is where customer success enablement comes into play.

What we'll cover today:

  • Customer Success Enablement ensures CSMs have the training, tools, and processes needed to improve customer retention, reduce churn, and drive expansion.
  • Key Components include structured workflows for onboarding and renewals, CRM and analytics integrations, and standardized playbooks for customer engagement.
  • Differences from Sales Enablement lie in the focus on customer retention and growth rather than lead generation and deal closing.
  • Challenges & Future Outlook involve cross-functional alignment, scaling enablement for growing teams, and leveraging technology to enhance proactive customer management.

What is Customer Success Enablement?

The idea behind customer success enablement is to equip customer success managers with the training, data, and resources required to proactively engage with customers, reduce churn, and drive revenue expansion.

In the same way that sales enablement empowers sales teams to close deals more efficiently, customer success enablement ensures that CSMs can provide a seamless and high-value customer experience at scale. For any company looking to build a sustainable and efficient customer success function, investing in enablement is no longer optional—it’s a crucial part of the strategy.

CS Enablement: Standardizing Processes for Consistency

At its core, customer success enablement is about establishing standardized processes and frameworks that ensure CSMs can consistently deliver value. Without these structures, teams often rely on individual expertise or ad-hoc customer engagement strategies, leading to inconsistencies and inefficiency. A well-implemented enablement approach supports CSMs in developing strong product knowledge, refining engagement techniques, and mastering best practices that foster long-term customer satisfaction.

Defining Key Workflows and Tools for Customer Success Enablement

Customer success enablement defines structured workflows for key activities like onboarding, renewals, and expansion, making these processes more predictable and efficient.

Technology plays a crucial role in this equation, providing teams with a CRM tech stack consisting of analytics tools, and automation features that allows them to monitor customer health, track engagement trends, and identify potential expansion opportunities. Additionally, access to detailed content, such as renewal guides, customer success frameworks, and objection-handling playbooks, further streamlines their work and ensures a consistent approach across the team.

Beyond Training: Building a Scalable Infrastructure

More than just training, customer success enablement establishes a scalable infrastructure that allows teams to deliver measurable results. This means designing robust training programs that equip CSMs with the necessary skills to manage accounts efficiently and defining engagement frameworks that set clear expectations for onboarding, renewals, and expansion. It also involves integrating CRM and product analytics tools to provide a comprehensive view of customer health, automating repetitive tasks to free up time for more strategic activities, and fostering collaboration between customer success, sales, and marketing teams to ensure alignment across the organization.

Customer Success vs. Sales Enablement

Although customer success enablement shares some similarities with sales enablement, their objectives differ significantly. While sales enablement is geared toward acquiring new customers by optimizing lead generation, deal acceleration, and closing processes, customer success enablement is focused on customer retention and growth.

The emphasis is on fostering adoption, mitigating churn risks, and uncovering opportunities for upselling and cross-selling. Instead of prioritizing deal closure, the goal is to cultivate long-term relationships, ensuring that customers derive ongoing value from the product.

Getting Started with Customer Success Enablement

Implementing a strong customer success enablement function requires a strategic approach. The first step is to assess the current challenges facing the customer success team, whether it’s inconsistent onboarding experiences, declining renewal rates, or difficulties in tracking customer engagement.

From there, companies need to define and formalize key processes that every CSM should follow. This includes developing clear playbooks for renewals, onboarding, and expansion strategies, alongside training programs that reinforce best practices.

Leveraging Technology for Better Insights

Technology should be a central component, with well-integrated CRM and product analytics platforms providing CSMs with real-time insights into customer health, engagement levels, and potential risks.

Beyond initial implementation, enablement must be treated as an ongoing initiative. Regular training sessions, iterative process improvements, and continuous feedback loops ensure that CSMs stay effective and adaptable to changing customer needs.

Measuring the Impact of CS Enablement

Measuring the impact of customer success enablement is essential for refining strategies and improving outcomes. Companies should track customer retention rates to determine whether enablement efforts contribute to increased renewals.

Monitoring customer health scores can reveal trends in engagement and satisfaction, while evaluating CSM productivity helps assess whether structured processes and tools are driving efficiency. Another critical metric is expansion revenue, which indicates whether enablement initiatives are facilitating upselling and cross-selling opportunities. Time-to-value, which measures how quickly customers realize the benefits of a product, is also an important indicator of an effective enablement strategy.

Challenges in Implementation

Despite its advantages, customer success enablement comes with challenges. One of the primary difficulties is ensuring cross-functional alignment, as customer success teams rely on data and insights from sales, marketing, and product teams.

Successful enablement requires coordination across these departments to maintain a unified strategy. Another challenge lies in driving adoption among CSMs. Providing training and tools alone is insufficient—teams need to see the tangible benefits of structured workflows and data-driven decision-making. This requires continuous reinforcement, coaching, and leadership support.

Scaling Customer Success Enablement as Companies Grow

Additionally, as companies scale, the complexity of enablement grows. A framework that works for a small team may not be sufficient for a global organization managing thousands of accounts, necessitating constant evolution and adaptation.

The Role of CRM and Product Analytics

Technology plays a pivotal role in making customer success enablement effective. A well-integrated CRM and product analytics platform eliminates data fragmentation, allowing CSMs to operate with a comprehensive view of customer behavior.

Without these tools, managing customer relationships becomes reactive rather than strategic. With a platform like June, which seamlessly integrates product analytics with CRM systems, CSMs gain access to real-time insights on customer engagement, health scores, and expansion potential.

The Future of Customer Success Enablement

Looking ahead, customer success enablement will continue to be a key differentiator for B2B SaaS companies.

Businesses that prioritize structured training, integrated technology, and data-driven decision-making will be well-positioned to drive retention and expansion.

More than just supporting CSMs in their daily tasks, enablement transforms customer success into a scalable and strategic function that directly contributes to long-term business growth.

By removing obstacles and ensuring teams have the right tools and insights at their disposal, companies can build a proactive, high-impact customer success operation that fosters loyalty and sustainable revenue growth.
