title: Customer Success Analytics: How to Leverage It for Maximum Impact
html:
Customer success (CS) analytics have become critical for B2B SaaS companies.

In a world where maintaining and increasing existing customers is less expensive than gaining new ones, understanding customer behavior and engagement is the cornerstone for long-term growth. CS analytics gives actionable insights that enable organizations to make better decisions, assisting customers in meeting their objectives, renewing subscriptions, and exploring chances for upselling or cross-selling.

To get the most out of customer success analytics, you must first understand the various types of data accessible, how to create a playbook to act on it, and the special benefits it provides to a B2B SaaS company.

What we'll cover today:

  • Customer Success Analytics Overview: CS analytics focuses on post-sale customer behavior, providing actionable insights to reduce churn, boost satisfaction, and identify upsell opportunities. It is transformative for B2B SaaS companies aiming to enhance retention and growth.
  • Key Data Types: Metrics like product usage, health scores, time-to-value, and customer feedback offer both quantitative and qualitative insights. Together, they enable prioritization and resource allocation for optimal customer engagement.
  • Effective Playbook Creation: Building a customer success playbook involves setting clear goals, centralizing data, segmenting customers, and proactively addressing issues. Continuous monitoring and adaptation are crucial for success.
  • Role of June: June simplifies customer success analytics by integrating product data with CRM systems, enabling precise tracking of key metrics like engagement patterns and health scores. This integration enhances team efficiency, supports revenue growth, and strengthens customer relationships.

What is customer success analytics?

Customer success analytics aims to understand customer behavior after the sale. It entails gathering, evaluating, and acting on data in order to boost customer satisfaction, reduce churn, and drive growth.

CS analytics focuses on specific customer interactions, answering questions such as whether customers are actively utilizing the product.

Are they getting the results they hoped for? How probable is it that they will renew or expand their accounts?

These insights are not only beneficial to a B2B SaaS company, but also revolutionary.

CS analytics not only strengthens customer connections, but it also helps uncover growth potential by improving revenue through upselling and cross-selling methods.

Key Data Types from Customer Success Analytics

The variety of data provided by CS analytics is one of its most effective features, since each one delivers unique insights into client behavior. Understanding this data can change the way you prioritize tasks and allocate resources.

For example, product utilization data indicates which features customers utilize the most and which they neglect. This can demonstrate how engaged customers are and if they are receiving the value they expected. Similarly, customer health scores use many data points such as product usage, support issues, and survey responses to provide a real-time view of an account's performance.

Time-to-value (TTV) data measures how quickly customers receive the promised benefits of your product. Shorter TTV corresponds with higher retention and pleasure. Customer feedback and sentiment analysis offer qualitative insights that complement quantitative data, allowing you to better understand customer emotions and views.

Finally, revenue measures such as churn rates, renewal rates, and expansion revenue provide a financial perspective on the performance of your customer success initiatives. Together, these datasets provide a comprehensive view of your client base, allowing you to focus on what is most important.

Creating an Effective Customer Success Playbook

To turn data into action, you must follow a disciplined method that is consistent with your company's goals. Setting defined objectives is the first step in creating a successful customer success playbook. For example, do you want to reduce churn, increase value realization, or find upselling opportunities? Your goals will influence how you prioritize and interpret data.

Centralizing your data is also important. All important information—whether it's product consumption, health scores, or consumer feedback—should be consolidated into a single platform for simple access. Tools like June, which connect product analytics with your CRM, are extremely useful in this area.

Once your data is centralized, categorize your consumers based on characteristics such as industry, account size, and usage trends. This allows you to customize your engagement techniques to varied demands, resulting in more tailored and successful outreach.

Take proactive activities based on a deep understanding of your clients. For example, if a customer's health score declines, contact them to identify and solve their issues before it is too late. Finally, continually assess your impact and adjust your approach as appropriate. Analytics is a continuous process of learning and improvement.

Benefits of Customer Success Analytics in B2B SaaS

The advantages of customer success analytics extend beyond lowering turnover. They have a broad and direct impact on B2B SaaS enterprises.

By identifying at-risk accounts early, CS analytics enables you to conduct targeted re-engagement initiatives. For example, if you see a customer's product consumption has decreased, you might provide additional training or resources to help them get back on track.

Analytics also speeds up value realization by identifying and removing impediments to success. The sooner customers perceive value, the more likely they are to remain loyal and advocate for your product.

Furthermore, by evaluating product usage and engagement trends, you can identify chances for upselling and cross-selling. For example, a customer who already uses numerous key capabilities may profit from additional modules or services.

The insights gained by CS analytics also improve the efficiency of your customer success team. With a clear understanding of priorities, your team can focus on actions that will have the most impact. This targeted strategy guarantees that resources are allocated properly and that no accounts are overlooked.

Growing the Martech Ecosystem: Additional Tools in the Stack

Customer success analytics is an important element of the jigsaw, but it works best when combined with other martech technologies. CRMs, for example, act as a central repository for customer data and interaction tracking.

Product analytics solutions offer more detailed insights into user behavior, whilst customer feedback tools assist you analyze consumer sentiment and satisfaction. Data visualization tools help simplify complex datasets, allowing for faster decision-making. Additionally, marketing automation technologies ensure coordination between your customer success and marketing teams, resulting in a seamless customer experience.

When these technologies work together alongside a fully equipped CRM tech stack, they form a strong ecosystem that boosts the effectiveness of your CS analytics efforts.

How June Supports Customer Success Analytics

For B2B SaaS enterprises, managing the nuances of customer success statistics can be difficult.

That is where June comes in. June integrates product analytics with CRM to create a unified platform for tracking important indicators such as health scores, TTV, and engagement patterns.

This integration streamlines data collecting while also providing useful insights. June can help you make the most of your analytics initiatives, whether it's detecting at-risk clients, boosting revenue growth, or improving customer happiness.

Some Final Thoughts

Customer success metrics are a game changer for B2B SaaS companies.

It gives the information you need to strengthen connections, reduce churn, and increase revenue. You can maximize the potential of analytics by understanding the many types of data accessible, developing an effective playbook, and integrating the appropriate technologies into your martech stack.

Using platforms like June makes it easier to leverage these information than ever before.

The future of customer success is data-driven; are you prepared to accept it?

title: CRM or Customer Success Software: What’s Best for Your B2B SaaS Business?
html:
In the fast-paced world of B2B SaaS, tools are more than just desired; they are required for growth.

It is critical to monitor, understand, and optimize every connection with a customer. This is where the clash between customer success software and customer relationship management systems emerges. Choosing the right tool can be like traversing a maze, even if both instruments serve different objectives.

So, how do you decide which choice is best for your business?

We'll look at how each works, why it's important, and how you may make a decision to improve your customer success. Spoiler alert: by combining analytics-driven solutions like June, you can ensure that both work seamlessly.

What we'll cover today:

  • CRM vs. Customer Success Software: CRMs excel at managing pre-sales activities, organizing customer data, and facilitating sales processes. However, they often lack the depth needed for post-sales engagement, such as tracking health scores, renewals, and time-to-value metrics, which are strengths of customer success software.
  • Integration for Growth: Combining CRMs and customer success tools bridges gaps in the customer lifecycle. Integration ensures seamless data sharing, enabling more effective team collaboration and holistic customer insights.
  • Role of June: June integrates CRM and customer success functionalities by combining product analytics with customer data. This allows B2B SaaS companies to track usage patterns, identify upsell opportunities, and enhance customer retention.
  • Strategic Adoption: Early-stage SaaS companies should prioritize CRMs for foundational sales management, while established companies benefit from integrating customer success solutions like June to optimize retention and long-term growth.

Understanding CRM: The Foundation of Customer Database

A CRM is usually the first software investment made by a company that wants to manage customer connections. A CRM is fundamentally a storehouse for consumer data that tracks interactions from the first marketing touchpoint to the final sales transaction. It is vital for increasing client acquisition since it helps teams manage contacts, track prospects, and automate procedures.

CRMs also help B2B SaaS organizations organize their client lifecycles, notably in managing long sales cycles and identifying upselling and cross-selling opportunities. CRMs are particularly adept at centralizing information and streamlining sales processes; yet, they do not typically go into great detail on post-sale consumer engagement.

This constraint marks the point at which CRMs begin to show their shortcomings. They frequently lack the granular details required by customer success teams to calculate customer health scores, evaluate time-to-value, and create renewal playbooks. Without these capabilities, it may be impossible to track your consumers' satisfaction.

The Post-Sales Specialist: Customer Success Software

Customer success software, unlike CRMs, is specifically built for the post-sales portion of the customer journey. These technologies are intended to proactively handle risks like churn, track engagement, and build customer connections.

This emphasis is critical for SaaS companies that rely on growth income and renewals. Customer success software typically contains characteristics such as:

  • Health Scoring: Tracking indicators like product usage and support interactions to assess customer health.
  • Onboarding and Engagement Tracking: Measuring time-to-value and ensuring customers see ROI quickly.
  • Renewal and Upsell Insights: Identifying opportunities for account growth or risks of downgrades.

These technologies are suitable for teams who want to maximize value realization and long-term consumer retention. Nonetheless, they typically fail to effectively manage pre-sales operations or integrate them into larger sales and marketing campaigns. This can cause data continuity gaps between the pre- and post-sales stages.

The Primary Difference Between Customer Success Software and CRM

The fundamental difference between CRMs and customer success software is their separate areas of focus. CRMs are useful for centralizing data and managing client acquisition, whereas customer success software excels at post-sales interaction and retention.

For B2B SaaS companies, retention and acquisition are both equally important; thus, the best approach typically entails combining the assets of both.
CRMs are crucial for sales teams because they provide the structure for monitoring sales pipelines and automating operations. In contrast, customer success software enables proactive interaction and more profound insights into customer behavior, both of which are critical for customer success teams.

The problem occurs when these instruments are used in isolation. Data silos, misaligned teams, and missed opportunities are all possible outcomes of a disconnected technological infrastructure. This is why it is critical to combine CRMs with customer success tools.

Why June is a sensible option: The Integration Solution

June now enters the picture.

June aims to bring the best of both worlds by merging product data with CRM tech stack and customer success systems. This hybrid strategy helps B2B SaaS enterprises to gain a more thorough insight of their clients and ensure seamless data transmission throughout the customer experience.

Consider the following scenario. June tracks product usage patterns, customer engagement, and crucial milestones like value realization, whereas your CRM keeps a detailed record of sales interactions.

By combining several data sources, KPIs like customer health scores and time-to-value may be precisely measured. Sales and customer success teams may interact more effectively when they have this degree of visibility, whether it's to secure a renewal or close a transaction.

June also helps to identify chances for upselling and cross-selling by evaluating actual product usage, which is an important customer success use case. For example, your team can send a targeted upgrade offer to a customer who frequently uses a feature contained in a premium tier at the right moment.

CRM o Customer Success Software: which tool should you prioritize?

Starting with a CRM is often the most sensible decision for a SaaS company in its early stages. CRMs provide the underlying framework for lead management and sales monitoring. As your customer base grows, the need for specialist client success software becomes more evident.

Incorporating a customer success solution like June into your CRM can provide the best of both worlds for more developed SaaS organizations. This strategy ensures continuity throughout the customer lifecycle, from acquisition to retention, while preserving efficacy and insights.

The Comprehensive View: Using the Right Instruments to Achieve Success

In the end, the question is not whether a CRM or customer success software is required, but rather how the two may be integrated. B2B SaaS companies' growth depends on acquiring new customers and retaining existing ones.

A well-integrated technological platform, with solutions like June at its core, ensures that you not only manage but also optimize client relationships at all stages.

June helps you organize your teams, uncover opportunities, and deliver value to your customers by bridging the gap between CRMs and customer success tools. This alignment is more than just a desired feature; it is a competitive advantage in a crowded SaaS marketplace.

By investing in the right tools and effectively integrating them, you'll be well-positioned to create long-term customer success as well as revenue.

title: CRM Tech Stack: Building the Foundation of Your B2B SaaS Business
html:
Often used in debates about company scalability is the phrase "CRM tech stack".

But specifically what does it mean, and why is it so important for B2B SaaS businesses? Your CRM tech stack may be the one most crucial collection of tools you will ever set whether you run a SaaS company managing customer success, sales, or product.

It's the basis that guides your relationship management, customer data analysis, and cross-selling, upselling, and retention-based expansion push.

Let's start with what a CRM tech stack is, why it's so important for business success, and which elements would be most helpful for B2B SaaS enterprises much like yours.

What we'll cover today:

  • A CRM tech stack is a collection of integrated tools centered around a CRM platform, helping B2B SaaS businesses manage customer relationships, analyze data, and streamline operations.
  • Key components for SaaS companies include a CRM platform, product analytics tools, marketing automation, customer success platforms, support systems, and billing integrations, all working together to drive customer engagement and retention.
  • A well-built CRM tech stack enables proactive strategies like monitoring customer health scores, reducing churn, improving time-to-value, and driving upselling, cross-selling, and expansion revenue opportunities.
  • Success lies in integrating tools effectively, keeping the customer journey in focus, and empowering teams with centralized data and training to leverage the stack fully.

Define a CRM tech stack

A CRM tech stack is a collection of tools, software, and integrations centered around a Customer Relationship Management (CRM) platform.

Although the CRM is the center, the stack consists of other technologies that improve its capability like data analytics tools, marketing automation systems, and product usage trackers. These solutions taken together form a seamless system that lets you control the whole customer lifetime—from lead generation and onboarding to retention and expansion revenue.

The software stack for B2B SaaS companies sometimes transcends conventional CRM capabilities. To offer a complete picture of every consumer, it must closely relate to product analytics, support ticketing systems, and even financial tools.

Consider it as your company's central nervous system, aggregating data from many sources and rendering it easily available and useable.

Why Does the CRM Tech Stack Matter for B2B SaaS?

Particularly in the B2B sector, SaaS firms find that their customer connection does not stop after the first sale.

As we all know, the true effort starts at that point. Retaining customers, enabling them to see the value of your product, and seeing prospects development via cross-selling or upselling will determine your success.

In several key ways, a well-designed CRM tech stack helps these initiatives.

1. Organizing Information to Support Improved Decisions

Customer data often resides in silos without a CRM software stack—product use metrics in one tool, marketing data in another, and financial data in yet another.

This fragmentation makes it challenging to see your whole customer's path. By combining all of these data elements, a strong CRM stack lets teams view everything from one location.

Monitoring important benchmarks such customer health scores, churn risk, and time-to-value depends on this.

2. Promoting Active Customer Success

A strong CRM tech stack allows you to go beyond reactive support.

For example, integrating product analytics tools like June with your CRM enables you to identify engagement trends and potential issues before they become problems.

This empowers Customer Success Managers to take a proactive approach, improving customer satisfaction metrics and retention.

3. Simplifying Multidisciplinary Cooperation

Sales, customer success, and product teams in a SaaS company sometimes demand close coordination.

Acting as a single source of truth, the CRM tech stack makes sure everyone agrees on consumer wants, behaviors, and chances for renewal or expansion revenue.

4. Encouraging Scalability

Managing customer interactions personally becomes impossible as your company expands.

A properly structured CRM tech stack automates repetitive procedures, allowing your team to scale operations while maintaining quality.

It also allows for more complex methods like individualized renewal playbooks and targeted upselling efforts.

What Should a B2B SaaS CRM Tech Stack Include?

Understanding your company needs will help you to build the appropriate CRM tech stack. Although there is no one-size-fits-all solution, B2B SaaS firms especially benefit from several technologies and integrations.

1. Platform for CRM Management

Your tech stack revolves mostly around the CRM itself.

HubSpot, Salesforce, and Attio are among the often used B2B SaaS products. Among other basic features, these systems track sales pipelines, handle contacts, and provide reports. Your team size, budget, and particular needs will all affect the ideal CRM for you.

2. Tools for Product analytics

Knowing how users of SaaS products engage with your offering is really vital. Tools like June immediately interact with your CRM to provide you understanding of user behavior, feature adoption, and engagement patterns.

Early problem addressing helps you lower turnover and increase time-to-value.

3. Automaton for Marketing

Marketing automation technologies like Marketo or HubSpot Marketing Hub constitute part of a good CRM tech stack. These systems let you launch campaigns, manage leads, and monitor consumer contacts across several channels.

The information gathered here returns into your CRM and offers a whole picture of the client path.

4. Platform for Customer Success

Customer success tools are priceless for handling renewals, health scores, and expansion income. These products provide capabilities catered to the needs of customer success teams, therefore complementing your CRM.

One of the greatest advantages of using June to complement your CRM Tech Stack is precisely that our software is able to offer those involved in customer success data and insights on the use of the product which are essential in B2B Saas environment.

Best Practices for Constructing Your CRM Tech Stack

Although the correct tools are crucial, your configuration and usage of them just as much define them.

These are some ideal behaviors worth giving thought:

Start with the fundamentals. Start with putting a basic CRM into use and progressively expand integrations depending on your needs. Starting a too complicated stack from day one could cause inefficiencies.

Emphasize data integration since the ability of a CRM tech stack to consolidate data defines its power. Make sure data moves naturally between all the integrated tools.

Remember the Customer Journey: Every instrument in your toolkit should help to enhance the customer experience. Every element, including tracking health metrics or running automated upselling initiatives, should complement your aims for customer success.

Train Your Team: Should your team lack effective knowledge of the tech stack, even the best one will not yield outcomes. Make training investments to guarantee everyone knows how to make use of the tools at hand.

Why the CRM Tech Stack Is Key to Business Success

The CRM tech stack is not only a nice-to-have but also a need for B2B SaaS businesses.

It helps you to better know your clients, simplify processes, and use retention and expansion income to spur development. In addition to helping you track KPIs like customer health scores and time-to- value, a well-designed stack offers proactive initiatives meant to lower turnover and raise involvement.

Fundamentally, the CRM tech stack is about forging closer bonds with your clients. You position your company for long-term success by making wise tool investments and properly combining them. The foundation of your efforts will be the CRM tech stack, whether your team is growing, you are introducing new features, or you are looking at cross-selling chances.

So, if you haven't already, closely examine your present tech stack.

Find holes, investigate integrations, and make sure any tool you employ is moving you toward your objectives. Strong CRM technology is not just a competitive need but also a benefit in the fast-paced B2B SaaS environment.

Appendix - Common Q&A about "CRM Tech Stack"

What is the CRM stack?
A CRM stack is a collection of tools and technology for managing customer interactions, which often includes software for sales, marketing, customer service, and analytics.

What is CRM technology?
CRM technology refers to software and technologies that assist firms manage customer interactions, data, and relationships throughout their lifecycle.

What are some examples of CRM tools?
Examples include Salesforce, HubSpot, Attio, Microsoft Dynamics 365, and Pipedrive.

What are the three forms of CRM?
There are three forms of CRM: operational (sales and marketing automation), analytical (data analysis), and collaborative (team and customer engagement).

What is the finest CRM tool?
The finest CRM relies on your requirements. Salesforce, HubSpot, and Attio are popular choices, with each having strengths in distinct areas.

What exactly does CRM mean?
CRM stands for Customer Relationship Management, which refers to the tools and tactics used to manage customer interactions and data.

Is CRM a tool or a skill?
CRM is both a technology (software) for managing customer data and a talent that requires its efficient application to promote customer success.

Audiences and company profiles

We redesigned the sidebar and made reports easier to set up, making it faster and simpler for teams to find the insights they need.

In 2025, our focus is clear: helping our customers get more customers. We work with Customer Success teams, solving activation and retention challenges so they can deliver amazing customer experiences and drive business growth.

Here’s how we’ll bring this vision to life:

  • Become the 360° customer platform: Centralize ticketing, revenue, calls, and notes into one place, giving CS teams everything they need. We want June to be where you can go where you want to answer the question "How are my users doing?".

Thank you

To our amazing customers, team, and everyone who’s been part of our journey this year: thank you for believing in June and pushing us to be better every day.

2024 was all about progress, and 2025 is where we turn that into even bigger wins. Let’s keep building, creating unforgettable customer experiences, and growing together. We can’t wait to see what’s next! 💜

— Enzo & the Team

title: Customer Success Account Number: How Many Accounts Should a CSM Manage?
html:
One of the most typical customer success queries is not about tools or methods, but about capacity.

How many accounts should a Customer Success Manager manage at any given time? The answer, unsurprisingly, is not simple. It depends on your company model, the complexity of your product, the clients you serve, and the objectives you've established for your customer success team.

Getting this balance correct is crucial. A customer success manager might not be able to give each customer the care they need if they are in charge of too many accounts. This can result in disgruntled consumers, missed opportunities for upselling or cross-selling, and, eventually, churn.

If you give out too few accounts, on the other hand, it might seem like you'll get better service, but this isn't always possible for small SaaS businesses with limited resources.

What we’ll cover today:

  • The ideal number of accounts a Customer Success Manager (CSM) should handle depends on factors like customer segmentation, product complexity, and the responsibilities assigned to the CSM.
  • High-touch models typically limit CSMs to 5–15 accounts, while low-touch or tech-touch models, supported by automation, can scale up to 50–100+ accounts.
  • Tools like June help CSMs manage workloads effectively by automating tasks like tracking customer health scores, churn risk, and time-to-value, enabling more strategic customer interactions.
  • Balancing account loads ensures customers achieve value realization, leading to higher retention, renewal rates, and opportunities for upselling and expansion revenue.

To calculate the ideal account load, consider the overall picture of client success

A CSM's primary responsibility is to assist customers in realizing value from your product. This includes delivering a seamless onboarding experience, maintaining engagement over time, and renewing their memberships when the time comes.

Along the way, a CSM may uncover potential for revenue growth, such as upselling or cross-selling, but this must be consistent with the customer's objectives.

It is not about driving sales, but about ensuring that the customer receives continuous value.

#1. Customer segmentation is a crucial aspect in determining how many accounts a CSM can manage

Not every customer is the same. Enterprise clients with complicated requirements can require far more attention than small-to-medium firms with simple use cases.

For example, a CSM working with high-touch enterprise clients may only manage five to ten accounts, whereas someone working with smaller, lower-touch customers may manage fifty or more. This segmentation is critical to ensuring that each customer receives the appropriate degree of help without overburdening the CSM.

#2. Your product's complexity is also an important consideration

A simple product that clients can rapidly adopt requires significantly less intervention than a complex solution with several integrations or a high learning curve.

If your product requires extensive onboarding and continuing education, a single CSM cannot effectively manage dozens of clients.

#3. Another concern is the extent of responsibility allocated to your CSMs

In some SaaS businesses, CSMs are solely responsible for assisting clients in achieving their objectives, doing activities such as monitoring customer health scores, minimizing time-to-value, and developing bespoke renewal playbooks.

Others provide CSMs additional responsibilities, such as managing contract renewals or discovering chances for upselling and cross-selling.

If your CSMs are performing numerous responsibilities, they will naturally have less capacity to manage accounts.

#4. Technology and automation can also make a significant impact

CSMs may use tools like June to track key indicators such as customer health scores, churn risk, and engagement levels without having to manually evaluate data.

By automating regular duties, these solutions allow CSMs to focus on high-value activities such as strategic check-ins and debugging complex issues.

This implies they can handle more accounts while maintaining high service standards.

#5. Your engagement model is an important part of the picture

If your organization follows a high-touch strategy, with CSMs involved in every step of the customer experience, fewer accounts will be manageable.

However, under a low-touch or tech-touch approach, where automation and self-service resources are more prevalent, each CSM can handle much more accounts.

Experimentation and data-driven decision-making are critical for achieving the ideal team balance. Begin by reviewing your historical metrics, notably attrition and retention rates.

Data-Driven Decisions for Account Allocation

If clients aren't realizing value soon enough, or if you notice signs of disengagement, it's possible that your CSMs are overworked.

Consider launching pilot projects in which you gradually increase the number of accounts that each CSM manages while assessing their performance.

It can also help you create a detailed customer journey map. Break out the major actions needed to support each account, such as onboarding sessions, regular check-ins, or health score evaluations, and estimate how much time each requires. Once you understand your client base's needs, you'll have a better notion of how many accounts a CSM can actually handle within their available capacity.

Striking the Right Balance

Although each SaaS company is unique, several common benchmarks can provide a starting point. Companies that offer high-touch corporate SaaS may find that their CSMs work best with five to fifteen accounts.

On the other hand, companies that offer low-touch SMB services may find that their CSMs can handle fifty or more accounts. A single CSM might even be in charge of hundreds of accounts for companies that use a tech-touch model, in which automation is key. It is important to remember that these standards should always be changed to fit your goods and customers.

Giving your customers something of value is the ultimate goal of customer satisfaction. Whether a CSM manages five or fifty accounts, their first responsibility should always be to ensure that customers are successful with your product. In order to do this, you need to build strong relationships with customers, deal with possible problems before they happen, and help them get the most out of their subscription.

When done right, customer success doesn't just keep customers; it creates brand fans who keep buying from you, open new accounts, and tell their friends about your business.

It's important for B2B SaaS companies to find the right account load for their CSMs in order to scale well. It's a balancing act that takes constant review and adjustment, but the results are worthwhile.

Businesses will do well when their customers are pleased and successful.

title: The Key to Unlocking Growth in B2B SaaS: SaaS Analytics
html:
Though SaaS analytics might not seem like the most exciting subject, trust me—if you run a B2B SaaS firm it will alter everything. Having the correct analytics in place will either help or destroy your plan whether your goals are customer retention, new upsell or cross-sell potential, or product optimization.

I will explore in this post what SaaS analytics is, why it is important for your company, and some of the main KPIs every B2B SaaS team should monitor.

Subtle alert: SaaS analytics it's about turning numbers into useful insights that propel development, not only about tracking numbers.

TL;DR - What you'll learn today:

  • SaaS analytics is the process of collecting and analyzing data to understand customer behavior, product performance, and revenue trends in B2B SaaS businesses.
  • It helps you track critical metrics like customer health score, time-to-value, retention, and expansion revenue, enabling better decision-making for growth and retention.
  • By integrating tools like June with your CRM, you can streamline insights into key metrics like churn, upselling, and renewal strategies without complexity.
  • SaaS analytics isn’t just about tracking numbers—it’s about turning data into actionable insights that improve customer success, product optimization, and revenue performance.

SaaS Analytics: Definition

Let's start with the foundations. SaaS analytics is the act of gathering, evaluating, and using data to better know how clients and your company are doing.

Consider it the foundation of every choice you make, from choosing which features to give top priority to spotting at-risk accounts using consumer health data to calculating the return on investment of your customer success initiatives.

The truth is, though, SaaS analytics goes beyond spreadsheets full of data. It's about tying your revenue, customers, and product together. This frequently entails gathering data from several sources—your product analytics, CRM, billing systems, and even customer feedback—for B2B SaaS firms to acquire a 360-degree view of your organization.

Why SaaS Analytics Count

Running a tiny B2B SaaS firm most likely means you are deprived of the luxury of throwing darts in the dark. Every decision counts, hence SaaS analytics guarantees that you are making the correct decisions.

First of all, analytics clarifies your clients for you.

Most users of your product are who? Whose search for worth is challenging? And whose ready for a change?

Value realization becomes very important here; it's all about knowing when and how clients reach the results they registered for. Without this realization, you start to wonder and may lose chances or, worse, cause unwanted turnover—that is, the phrase used to describe consumers quitting your good or service.

Regarding maximizing your product, it is also your friend. Analyzing usage data helps you to pinpoint which features are failing and which ones inspire involvement. This lets your product team concentrate on what counts most instead of squandering time on things that have little effect on the needle.

Not to overlook income either. SaaS analytics lets you monitor important benchmarks such lifetime value (LTV), customer acquisition cost (CAC), and monthly recurring revenue (MRR).

Knowing these indicators helps you to clearly see your financial situation and guides your sustainable development planning. It also directly relates to ideas like expansion revenue, derived by cross-selling or upselling your current customer base.

Important KPIs to Track in Business-to- Business Software-Based Products

Let us now delve right into the specifics. Although your own company goals will determine the metrics you monitor, here are some ones you should overlook as B2B SaaS companies.

Retention Rate of Customer

This one is obvious. Particularly in the B2B SaaS market, keeping clients typically proves to be more affordable than gaining new ones. Retention rate reveals your ability over time to keep clients. Whether it's your product, support, or onboarding process, a decline in retention raises concerns about something not functioning.

MRR, or monthly recurrent revenue

Any SaaS company lives on MRR. Key for forecasting and budgeting, it shows you the consistent monthly income you are producing. To better understand what's driving expansion or decline, though, break out the entire amount into new MRR, cross-selling or upselling revenue, and churned MRR.

Health Score for Customers

A strong customer health score aggregates several indicators—such as account activity, product use, and support interactions—into a single number that captures a client's overall "health." It's a great tool for spotting upsell chances and churn risks. Using it alongside time-to- value measures—the speed at which consumers cross their first significant milestone—you can guarantee that you are monitoring long-term success as well as current pleasure.

Net Revenue Retention (NRR)

After adjusting for upgrades, downgrades, and turnover, NRR gauges the income you are keeping. Congratulations if your NRR exceeds 100%; you are clearly indicating product-market fit since your current clients are generating income.

Activation Pace

Often the first major turning point in a customer's path in B2B SaaS is activation. It is the first time they really value your stuff. Monitoring activation rates lets you know how successful your onboarding program is and whether consumers are soon enough reaching that "aha" moment. This directly relates to developing a winning renewal plan that guarantees consumers remain interested long after their first contact with your offering.

Using SaaS Analytics to Fit You

The good news is that SaaS analytics can be made without either a large analytics staff nor a data scientist. Integration of your product analytics with CRM systems like HubSpot, Attio, or Salesforce is simple with tools like June.

This means you can start making data-driven decisions without drowning in complexity by seeing all of your important measures in one location.

The secret is to concentrate on issues that really affect your company. If you are experiencing turnover, explore retention statistics, time-to- value analysis, and customer health ratings closely. Look especially at MRR, NRR, and upsell trends if you want to increase income. And to gauge the impact of a new feature or product introduction, apply activation rates and engagement measures.

SaaS analytics seeks the ones that inspire action rather than monitoring every data under the sun. Start small, iterate, and as you develop keep improving your method.

Final Notes

One of those things that can first seem daunting is SaaS analytics, particularly if you're just starting out. Once you get it, though, it's rather empowering. It provides the clarity you need to grasp your company, enhance your offering, and strengthen ties with your clients.

For B2B SaaS businesses, where every customer interaction counts, this clarity can make all the difference between inertia and expansion. Including tools like June into your workflow can help you streamline procedures and concentrate on what really counts: providing value to your clients and promoting steady expansion for your company.

SaaS analytics ultimately transcends numbers at the end of the day. It's about wise choices, improved experiences, and establishing a company that survives in a cutthroat industry. All set to dig in? Let's do it.

title: What makes working at Intercom special
html:
I left Intercom four years ago, so some of what I’m sharing here might have changed. Yesterday, Lenny Rachitsky published a study ranking the companies that accelerate PM careers the most—to positions like Head of PM or founder.

Intercom is where I started in product management, reading Intercom on Product Management and learning the craft. It’s also the reason I eventually left that role to start my own company, June. Since then, we’ve built a company and stayed connected with people at Intercom. Some of their C-levels and one of the founders have even become angel investors, supporting us through both highs and lows.

People often ask me what makes Intercom special. "Special" is a nuanced word. No company is perfect, and Intercom isn’t either. But there’s something undeniably unique about it, and that’s why you see it ranking so highly in studies like Lenny’s—even ahead of companies like Palantir, Uber, and Square.

Here’s my take on what makes Intercom special, from the humble perspective of someone who worked there as a PM and now runs a company where two-thirds of the team have Intercom roots.

Five Things That Make Intercom Unique

1. Think for Yourself

Intercom expects its people to think independently, and this was one of the things that hooked me when I worked there. The company uses very few frameworks (almost none in product management) and avoids relying on tools for everything. When I was there, product development ran on Google Docs and GitHub tasks. That’s it.

This focus on first-principles thinking runs deep. If you’re not familiar with the concept, it’s about breaking problems down to their root causes and addressing those directly. At Intercom, this means really understanding the problem you’re solving.

For example, during my first quarter, I was working on a feature with a designer. In a planning meeting, an engineer said

“Can’t we just ask the support team to record a video and link to it?”

Boom—problem solved with zero engineering effort, and the CS team was happy to help. It was an elegant, low-effort solution.

PMs at Intercom are also encouraged to focus solely on discovery, leaving delivery to designers and engineers. This approach allows PMs to spend their time talking to customers, refining focus, and articulating problems. Once a problem is prioritized and well-defined, the delivery is owned by the engineering and design teams.

2. Focus

Intercom prioritizes specialization and focus. PMs focus on discovery, designers go deep into problem-solving but step back during delivery, and engineers own the delivery process. This clear separation of roles allows everyone to get really good at their part of the process.

This focus extends to leadership as well. For example, the VP of Product wasn’t deeply involved in every product team’s work. Instead, he focused on public communication and being a strong external voice for the company. Instead of trying to do everything, he excelled at one thing.

Another key element of focus at Intercom was the shared commitment to product excellence. Everyone—whether engineers, designers, or managers—was deeply invested in the roadmap and product decisions. This collective product focus created a culture where every craft contributed meaningfully.

3. Expose Yourself

At Intercom, the structure is lean, and you’re expected to show up and take responsibility—whether for kudos or failures. The company encourages visibility and vulnerability.

  • Roadmaps with founders: Two weeks after I joined, I presented a roadmap to one of the founders. That’s how it works—no middle management buffer.
  • Company-wide visibility: Intercom’s “Show and Tell” Fridays let anyone share their work. If you haven’t been on stage for a while, your manager will make sure you step up.
  • Vulnerability: This culture of openness starts at the top. Just watch the founders’ recent videos—their willingness to show vulnerability is clear.

The leaders—Eoghan, Des, Paul Adams, Emmet—were top-notch and accessible. You could learn a lot just by observing them, and they set the tone for the company’s culture.

4. Take Yourself Lightly

At Intercom, talent shines, not grind culture or politics. It’s a place where people take their work seriously but not themselves.

  • MC at Show & Tell: The MC—usually just a funny employee—adds humor and energy to the meetings.
  • Irish culture: Intercom’s Irish roots mean there’s often good “craic” (fun and banter) in meetings.
  • Assume best intent: One of the founders, Eoghan, encouraged everyone to assume best intent when disagreements arise. This principle fosters better conversations and outcomes.

The people at Intercom were highly ambitious and creative. Many had side projects or collaborated on cool things outside of work, adding a unique energy to the environment.

5. Be Efficient

Intercom is incredibly efficient, even as it scales.

  • Ruby on Rails: Betting on Rails allowed Intercom to iterate quickly, proving skeptics wrong as their product scaled to billions of daily pings.
  • Feature flags: PMs and anyone else can release features without involving engineering, speeding up the feedback loop and release process.
  • Demo culture: Show and Tell Fridays are a forcing function to keep the organization shipping. It’s a tradition that’s been the beating heart of the company for years.

Efficiency also means adaptability. Look at how quickly Intercom embraced AI and rolled out a complex brand redesign. The culture of “every day counts” ensures momentum even when energy dips.

Conclusion

Intercom is just different. The culture, the people, the focus on product—it all comes together in a way that’s hard to replicate. You meet some of the most ambitious and creative people there, all driven by a shared commitment to building great things. The leaders are accessible, the energy is contagious, and the product-first mindset runs deep.

These five elements—thinking for yourself, focus, visibility, lightheartedness, and efficiency—make Intercom special. It’s not just a workplace; it’s a place where people grow into leaders and founders. And even years later, it’s clear that Intercom’s culture continues to shape the people and companies connected to it.

title: Boosting SaaS Expansion through Customer Health Scores
html:
Customer health scores have emerged as the most effective technique for comprehending and enhancing relationships with your clients in B2B SaaS, where expansion and retention are crucial.

They are your compass for navigating growth, churn, and all in between; they are not simply another metric.

As your small SaaS business expands, it becomes more and more crucial to have a clear understanding of your customers' levels of involvement and happiness. A high health score eliminates the need for guesswork. It allows you to see how your clients are performing in real time and, more crucially, whether they are likely to stay with you or go.

But let's get beyond the basics.

While everyone agrees that health ratings are important, it can be challenging to design one that works for your business. For small SaaS companies, the dangers are much greater. Every customer matters, and losing one can have a significant effect on income.

Health scores can be a lifesaver for spotting dangers early on and creating opportunities for improvement when they are developed and used correctly.

What you'll learn today:

  • Customer health scores are vital for B2B SaaS companies to track client engagement and predict retention or churn, offering a clear view of customer success in real-time.
  • Building effective health scores requires identifying key behaviors and data points, such as feature usage, login frequency, and customer success interactions, tailored to your product and audience.
  • Health scores benefit all teams: customer success can mitigate churn, sales can identify upselling opportunities, and product teams can enhance features based on user engagement.
  • Common pitfalls include overcomplicating metrics, relying on averages, and overlooking context, but tools like June simplify data integration and analysis, fostering a customer-centric approach.

Why Customer Health Scores Matter for SaaS

Managing relations with customers at scale may appear like a chaotic process, but customer health scores provide structure and insight. It gets more difficult to monitor everyone's performance as your clientele expands. While some consumers may be prospering and utilizing each aspect of your product, others may discreetly cease to log in or interact.

You can see exactly where each consumer is with a well-designed health score. It helps you identify issues before they become worse, much like an early warning system. For instance, your team will be prompted to check in and resolve any worries if a customer's contribution drastically lowers and their health score reflects it. Conversely, clients with high ratings frequently offer chances for advancement or upselling.

Health scores are more than just a churn control instrument for B2B SaaS companies. They also serve as a roadmap for growth initiatives, assisting you in determining which clients have the capacity to move ahead with plan renewals or feature adoption.

Building a Health Score That Works for Your Business

It's not as easy as it would seem to put together a health score. Since every SaaS company is unique, the indicators of a customer's health will change based on your product and target market.

The first step is to figure out what success means to your clients. Success for certain cloud-based applications may require high use of particular features or frequent logins. Others can interpret it as a steady increase in the number of users in an account. In the bigger picture of your product, you will need to determine which behaviors and signs actually indicate health.

Using the product is frequently a smart place to start.

Do your clients frequently log in? Are they utilizing workflows or important features? Don't stop there, though. Think about more subtle cues as well, such if they've communicated with your customer success team, attended a training session, or replied to requests for feedback. The strength of your relationship may frequently be inferred from these touchpoints.

Collecting this data can be daunting for small SaaS teams, particularly if they are using disjointed platforms or manual methods. June can help with that. All of these data points may be gathered in one location by combining your product analytics with programs like Salesforce or HubSpot.

Leveraging Health Scores Across Teams

Health ratings are a tool for your entire business, not just customer success teams. Everyone can operate more efficiently in a SaaS company with limited resources if they have a clear picture of customer health.

The customer success team should intervene when a customer's health score declines. Perhaps they have ceased using a crucial feature or run across an issue that they haven't yet disclosed. Proactively contacting them can frequently mean the difference between retaining and losing that client.

Health scores show the sales team where they can improve. Consumers that often receive good ratings are probably getting a lot out of your product, which makes them perfect prospects for cross-selling or upselling. Instead of cold pitching an upgrade, you may adjust your strategy according to their engagement levels and usage trends.

Product teams can learn a lot from health scores as well. You may determine which features encourage the most involvement and which ones may require enhancement by examining consumer trends. You can improve your product and make sure it's providing the most value by using this kind of feedback loop.

Avoiding Common Pitfalls

Health scores have drawbacks despite their potential for great power. A common mistake made by SaaS companies is to overcomplicate the process by attempting to monitor too many metrics simultaneously. As a result, the score may become more difficult to understand and less useful.

Over-reliance on averages is another frequent error. An account's overall health score may not be sufficient to identify underlying problems. In a customer account, for example, one team may be flourishing while another is not. More useful insights can frequently be obtained by delving deeper into user-level data.

It's also critical to keep in mind that not all changes in health ratings warrant concern. Context is important. A decline in engagement could just be the result of a brief change in priorities or a seasonal slowdown.

The Bigger Picture

Customer health scores are a competitive advantage for SaaS companies. They give you the information you need to improve relationships, lower attrition, and spur expansion. Perhaps more significantly, though, they assist you in concentrating on what really counts—making sure your clients are successful.

You may streamline the recording and analysis of client health by incorporating June into your workflow. You'll have a clear, real-time picture of how your customers are performing rather than having to manage spreadsheets or disparate data sources.

This goes beyond merely increasing productivity or saving time. It involves establishing a customer-centric culture within your company. Your team can collaborate more successfully if everyone has access to the same insights.

In the end, having a high health score is more than just a score. It serves as a catalyst for progress, a conversation starter, and a problem solver. It's an essential tool for small SaaS companies who want to outperform their competitors.

title: What is Customer Advocacy and Why Does it Matter in SaaS?
html:
In the world of SaaS, success depends on making sure customers are happy.

People who love your goods so much that they tell other people about it are even better than happy customers. That is what it means to advocate for a customer.

Customer advocacy is when a happy customer goes out of their way to tell others about your product, share their good experiences with it, or even defend your brand if someone has questions. It's kind of like having a group of super-fans who help spread the word about your business because they really believe in it.

Customer support is gold for B2B SaaS companies. Advocates not only keep their clients longer, but they also often bring in new clients by recommending others. They also make your image stronger, which can help you stand out in a crowded market.

What you will learn from today's writing:

  • What is it? When happy customers tell others about your product because they had a good experience with it, that's called customer support.
  • Why it's important: Advocates give you more authority, get more people to recommend you, and lower your cost of acquisition. They also stay with you longer and are more likely to improve.
  • How to get people to advocate: Provide consistent worth, use data to find advocates, and give them chances to share their success stories.
  • June's part: June helps SaaS companies find happy customers, measure success, and make proactive advocacy strategies possible by connecting product data with CRMs.

Are you ready? Let's begin.

Why is it important for customers to speak out in SaaS?

Being in the SaaS business is very tough because it's tough to earn customers' trust.

In comparison to traditional ads, people are 92% more likely to believe a recommendation from someone they know. Word-of-mouth from people who already use the SaaS product can be very important for new buyers, especially for products that take a long time to sell, like those for big teams or businesses.

As an example, we saw in June how great customer support can be. One of our regular clients, a SaaS company that was growing, loved how easily our product analytics worked with HubSpot, Salesforce, and Attio.

They told another team about their success, which led to a tip and a brand-new customer for us. But you might be thinking what makes someone a great customer advocate?

Fans of your business don't just appear out of thin air. They are built over time by consistently offering a product that meets or beats expectations. Think of it as putting down a seed. You must first offer something of value. This could mean finding a solution to a certain issue, providing excellent customer service, or making teams more productive.

One of June's clients was having a hard time with churn—they couldn't figure out why some of their best users were leaving. With June's help, they found important patterns in how users acted before leaving by integrating product data and CRM systems. This helped them fix the issue and keep more people pleased. They quickly became strong fans of our product since it helped them save time and money.

How to Set Up a Program to Get Customers to Speak Out

It takes some thought to turn customers into advocates. You need to give people something of value, find champions, and give them the tools and the drive to talk about their experiences.

  • Offer value first: A customer won't tell others about a product they don't trust Make sure that your offering does what you say it will do. In June, this means giving customers clear views into their product data and helping them use it to keep customers or get them to buy more.
  • Look for your supporters: Pay attention to the people who are very happy. Net Promoter Score (NPS) questions are a great way to find people who really like your business. If someone gives you a 9 or 10, they will probably tell other people about it if you ask them to.
  • Give people chances to speak out: Your clients need a little push every once in a while. Ask them to take part in webinars, case studies, or share feedback. As an example, at June, we've helped customers write blog posts about their successes, which helps them show off their accomplishments and helps us build our image.
  • Thanking someone for their help goes a long way. Rewarding supporters shows that you value them. You can do this by giving them discounts, special access to features, or public praise.

How June Helps To Get Customers To Spread The Word

The June product isn't just about numbers; it helps people do things. So that customer success managers can turn normal users into brand advocates, we connect product data to CRM systems such as HubSpot, Salesforce, and Attio.

One of our users used June to find accounts that used advanced features a lot but hadn't upgraded their plans. With this information, their team reached out to those users, made personalized upsell ideas, and turned them into higher-paying advocates who told others about their good experience.

June was used by another customer to look at details about onboarding. They discovered that people who skipped an important training step were less likely to stick around for a long time. By making the onboarding process better, they were able to keep more people and get great feedback from those who had a better experience.

What Advocacy Does in the Long Run

A customer's support causes a chain reaction. Advocates bring in new customers through word of mouth, lower the cost of getting new customers, and improve the image of your brand. They also care more about the success of your product, resulting in them more likely to remain engaged with it and keep using it.

At June, we learned that people don't become advocates by chance. It occurs when you give others what they are interested in, earn their trust, and make it easy for them to share their personal experiences. Customers who talk about your business favorably can be one of the most effective instruments you use to grow.

Begin to get supporters right away

Delivering value is the first thing you should do if you want your best customers to become supporters. Know their goals, help them with their issues, and make your offering simple so they can achieve their goals. Tools like June can help you find advocacy chances by giving you the information you need to plan your next move.

It's not just about making more money when you have loyal customers; it's also about building real, long-lasting relationships with those who believe in your goods. When your clients win, you win too.

title: Houseplant: Database Migrations for ClickHouse
html:
At June, we use ClickHouse as our analytics database to process billions of user events and generate real-time insights for our customers. While ClickHouse is incredibly powerful for analytical workloads, managing database schema changes has been a pain in our dev workflow.

Unlike traditional relational databases that have mature migration tools (like ActiveRecord for Rails), ClickHouse lacks a robust solution for managing schema migrations. We'd accumulated a lot of migrations and rake tasks to manage the schema of our ClickHouse cluster, but over time, it became hard for one person to make sense of all of it, let alone four.

We love working with ActiveRecord and how easy it makes checking the database schema, generating, applying, and rolling back migrations (if needed!). We wanted something similar for ClickHouse, so we built it ourselves.

Today, we're excited to announce Houseplant, a Python-based CLI tool that brings ActiveRecord-style migrations to ClickHouse!

Why Houseplant?

  • Schema Management: Houseplant automatically tracks and manages your ClickHouse schema changes, making it easy to evolve your data model over time
  • Developer Experience: Write migrations in YAML format, making them easy to read, review, and maintain
  • Environment Support: Different configurations for development, testing, and production environments
  • Rich CLI: Comes with an intuitive command-line interface for all migration operations

Getting Started

You can install Houseplant using pip:

$ pip install houseplant

Then you can initialize your project, and use it to generate and apply migrations just like how you would do it with the rails db:migrate command.

You just need to set up the correct environment variables which you can find in the project README.

Open Source

Houseplant is open source and available on GitHub. We believe in the power of community-driven development and welcome contributions from anyone who wants to improve ClickHouse schema management.

Check out the README to get started, and feel free to submit issues or pull requests!

We're excited to share Houseplant with the ClickHouse community and hope it makes your database management as enjoyable as tending to your houseplants! 🪴

title: The Power of Customer Marketing: Driving Loyalty & Growth
html:
In the B2B SaaS industry, customer marketing plays a pivotal role in fostering engagement, loyalty, and advocacy.

While it intersects with customer success and product marketing, customer marketing has its own unique focus: nurturing long-term relationships with existing clients to boost retention, inspire advocacy, and drive revenue growth. 

By emphasising the value customers already experience with the product, customer marketing provides in fact meaningful ways to reinforce satisfaction, helping turn satisfied clients into real brand promoters. 

In this article, we’ll explore what makes customer marketing distinct in SaaS, its strategic benefits, and how it integrates with other customer-focused roles.

Defining Customer Marketing

Customer marketing is a strategic approach focused on engaging existing customers to increase their loyalty, drive retention, and foster advocacy.

Unlike acquisition-based marketing, customer marketing centers on campaigns that provide ongoing value to current users—such as loyalty programs, educational content, user groups, and customer success stories.

Through these tactics, B2B SaaS companies can cultivate a loyal customer base that actively advocates for the brand, creating a virtuous cycle of organic growth.

In B2B SaaS, where retention and expansion are essential for sustainable growth, customer marketing plays an increasingly critical role. By building deeper relationships, companies can amplify brand value, proactively prevent churn, and secure valuable referrals, all while strengthening customers’ commitment to the platform.

How Customer Marketing Integrates with Customer Success and Product Marketing

Customer marketing, customer success, and product marketing are interconnected, each contributing to an enhanced customer experience but with distinct focuses:

  1. Customer Success is tasked with helping customers achieve their desired outcomes with the product. By working closely with customers, the customer success team helps them maximize the product’s value, resolve challenges, and adopt the most useful features. Their primary goal is retention through hands-on support and strategic guidance.
  2. Product Marketing, in turn, is usually responsible for communicating the product’s value proposition, features, and benefits to both new and current customers. This team often focuses on product launches, positioning, and customer education, aiming to increase product understanding and initial adoption rates.
  3. Customer Marketing, meanwhile, focuses on building long-lasting customer relationships by reinforcing the product’s value through targeted engagement initiatives. Rather than supporting or troubleshooting product issues, customer marketing emphasizes brand loyalty, customer advocacy, and retention by fostering a community around the brand and celebrating customer achievements.

In practice, these functions complement one another: customer success supports customer needs directly, product marketing informs customers about product innovations, and customer marketing strengthens brand affinity and community engagement.  Together, they deliver a cohesive customer experience that balances practical assistance, product knowledge, and long-term loyalty.

Why is Customer Marketing Essential in B2B SaaS?

In the B2B SaaS sector, retaining customers is often as important as acquiring new ones. Customer marketing is becoming more and more critical because it drives significant ROI by reducing churn, increasing customer lifetime value, and generating referrals and case studies.

Here’s why customer marketing can be crucial:

  1. Improves Customer Retention: By actively engaging with existing customers, SaaS companies can improve retention rates. Through tactics like loyalty programs, tailored content, and exclusive webinars, customer marketing fosters a sense of belonging and reinforces the product’s value, making customers less likely to churn.
  2. Encourages Upselling and Cross-Selling: Customer marketing teams leverage data insights to identify users who would benefit from upgrades or additional services. By nurturing these relationships, SaaS companies can effectively introduce higher-tier plans or complementary products to satisfied users, leading to revenue expansion.
  3. Builds Brand Advocacy: Satisfied customers who feel valued are more likely to become advocates. Through referral programs, case studies, and social proof, customer marketing creates opportunities for happy customers to promote the brand, bringing in new customers organically.
  4. Leverages Customer Feedback for Improvement: Customer marketing initiatives often involve gathering feedback through surveys, NPS questions, and direct interactions. This feedback loop allows SaaS companies to refine their offerings, improve product experiences, and address customer pain points proactively.

Leveraging Product and Customer Analytics with CRM Integration

Creating a customer marketing strategy begins with understanding what will drive the most value for existing customers. 

Data-driven insights are vital for optimizing customer marketing strategies, and integrating product analytics with CRM systems offers unique advantages. B2B SaaS companies can leverage this integration to understand customer behaviors, identify needs, and personalize engagement campaigns. 

There are so many ways CRM-integrated analytics empower customer marketing! Here are just some, but the limit here lies in the imagination:

  • Personalized Campaigns Based on Usage Data: Product analytics offer insights into how customers use the product, helping customer marketing and customer success teams understand which features deliver the most value. By connecting these insights with CRM data, companies can tailor campaigns to introduce underutilized features or drive higher engagement among specific user segments.
  • Identifying Expansion and Upsell Opportunities: CRM data, combined with product usage insights, enables companies to identify users who might benefit from an upgrade or additional features. Customer marketing and customer success can then create personalized messages or offers to present these opportunities, maximizing the chances of conversion.
  • Reducing Churn Through Early Engagement: Customer analytics can reveal signs of disengagement or frustration, allowing customer success functions to act early with re-engagement tactics. By proactively reaching out to at-risk customers, companies can reduce churn and ensure customers continue to see the product’s value.

The Future of Customer Marketing in B2B SaaS

As the B2B SaaS landscape continues to evolve, customer marketing will become increasingly essential for competitive differentiation.

By focusing on delivering value beyond the initial sale, customer marketing builds lasting customer relationships and promotes a sense of community and brand loyalty.

For SaaS companies, creating a strong customer marketing strategy supported by an integrated product and customer analytics software is a smart investment in sustainable growth. By leveraging CRM systems like HubSpot, Attio, and Salesforce to connect analytics with customer interactions, companies can engage more effectively, anticipate needs, and foster advocacy.

In doing so, customer marketing creates a ripple effect that extends well beyond individual customers, driving brand loyalty, referrals, and long-term business success

title: Cross-Selling vs. Upselling in B2B SaaS: Empowering Teams to Drive Growth
html:
Expanding income from current clients is a key growth tactic in the B2B SaaS sector.

Two of the best strategies to reach this are cross-selling and upselling, different but complimentary ways to improve client connections and income. Though their goals and implementation differ, both approaches center on raising customer value.

While upselling motivates consumers to accept higher-tier plans or extended versions of their current subscriptions, cross-selling exposes consumers to complimentary items or services that enhance their experience.

These techniques taken together help SaaS firms to strengthen ties and match their products to changing client needs. Product analytics combined with CRM systems allows account executives (AEs) and customer success managers (CSMs) to precisely identify and seize opportunities, hence increasing customer happiness and business growth.

Cross-selling vs. Upselling: Their Differences

Cross-selling emphasizes breadth and provides consumers with extra options to go along with their main good. A SaaS provider providing workflow management tools, for example, might advise a time-tracking module to increase output. This method covers related needs, therefore providing a complete solution catered to the operations of the client.

On the other side, upselling stresses depth by improving the present product line. An analytics system might advise, for instance, moving a client to a plan with enhanced reporting features or more data processing limits. Offering more features that enhance the value of a product, upselling fits a customer's development or growing dependability on it.

Cross-selling expands the range of the relationship; upselling digs deeper. When data-driven insights direct the timing and relevancy of these offers, they jointly give a dual strategy to satisfy consumer needs—especially.

The Part AEs and CSMs Play in Cross-selling and Upselling

Driving cross-sell and upsell programs mostly falls on AEs and CSMs. Their different roles enable a coordinated effort that optimizes possibilities without overloading the customer.

Often concentrating on increasing revenue  during renewal cycles  or spotting strategic chances to upsell, account managers also Accessing product use data linked into CRM systems allows AEs to identify times when a customer can benefit from more advanced plans or features. If an AE discovers, for example, that a customer routinely exceeds their use restrictions, they can approach the conversation with facts showing the possible return on investment of an upgrade.

Conversely, CSMs keep up continuous relationships and are positioned to spot cross-sell potential. Regular check-ins let CSMs find out whether a client is exporting data to outside tools. This could hint to a want for the kind of integration the SaaS provider provides, so facilitating cross-selling from logical starting point. The CSM can create a proposal that shows value and builds trust by employing CRM-integrated data, therefore addressing the particular workflow difficulties of the customer.

Working together, AEs and CSMs guarantees the consumer a flawless experience. During a success review, for instance, a CSM may highlight a possible upsell opportunity, transferring the lead to an AE capable of handling the commercial concerns. This cooperation guarantees that upsell and cross-sell interactions feel natural and fit for the demands of the customer.

Uses of Cross-selling and Upselling Practically

Imagine a SaaS project management company for a medium-sized business. Although the customer often exports data for team reporting, she mostly depends on basic task management capabilities.

The CSM notes this behavior during a regular check-in and recommends a reporting add-on that streamlines the procedure, therefore saving team hours per month. Through customizing the recommendation to the customer's workflow, the CSM effectively cross-sells the add-on, so improving the customer's experience and raising income.

In another case, a SaaS analytics tool detects via product analytics that a client routinely uses more than their allocated data consumption allows. Equipped with CRM data on consumer business goals and usage patterns, the AE advises a change to a strategy with more data restrictions and sophisticated visualization capabilities. The AE closes the upsell and strengthens the relationship by orienting the discussion on how the upgrade meets the expanding needs of the customer.

Upselling for a marketing automation system could entail guiding an SMB client toward an enterprise plan including AI-driven campaign ideas. Cross-selling might meantime concentrate on including a social media integration that enhances the email marketing capacity of the platform. Both approaches show the provider's dedication to the customer's success since they help them to reach their objectives.

Using CRM and Product Analytics to Advance Revenue

Effective cross-selling and upselling in B2B SaaS finds their roots in the integration of product analytics with CRM systems.

Teams have a complete picture of every account by aggregating behavioral data with customer lifecycle data.

Product analytics might demonstrate, for example, that a customer regularly interacts with complex features offered in a higher-tier plan while CRM notes indicate they are getting ready for a significant product introduction. These revelations taken together make a strong argument for an upsell, backed by statistics that explicitly connect the recommendation to the aims of the consumer.

Analyzing usage trends together with support requests or feedback entered into the CRM helps one to find cross-sell chances. Should a client constantly ask for integrations or capabilities not included in their present package, these signals direct CSMs in suggesting complementary options to meet unmet demands.

Integration of real-time data guarantees that both AEs and CSMs may seize chances at the correct moment and provide tailored offers that appeal to consumers. This strategy not only boosts income but also helps the consumer view the provider as a partner committed in their achievement.

Creating a Consistent Growth Strategy

Approached as part of a consistent plan, cross-selling and upselling are most successful. Data-driven insights help AEs and CSMs to collaborate to make sure every recommendation fits the customer's objectives and schedule.

This involves encouraging a culture of teamwork between teams, making investments in systems that combine CRM and product data, and giving customer-centricity first priority in every contact for SaaS firms. When cross-selling and upselling are done with accuracy and care, they improve the customer experience and transform happy consumers into devoted champions rather than only increasing income.

SaaS companies may fully utilize their customer relationships by arming AEs and CSMs with the insights they need, therefore attaining expansion that benefits the company and its customers both.
