title: The First 90 Days as a Product Manager: Sink or Swim
html:
The first 90 days as a product manager can make or break your career. It’s a sink-or-swim situation, and those who tread water risk being forgotten. You’re not just learning a new product; you’re being sized up by stakeholders, your team, and leadership. Everyone is watching—waiting to see if you can deliver or if you’ll fall short.

So, how do you not just survive, but thrive in this critical period? It’s about more than just understanding the product or showing up at meetings. You need to own your role, deliver results, and prove that you’re the leader the company needs.

This isn’t the time to play it safe. It’s the time to step up, take bold actions, and show that you’re ready to drive impact from day one. In this guide, we’ll break down how you can master your first 90 days, from making a killer first impression to delivering on the promises that will define your future in product management.

Phase 1: Days 1-30: Listen, Learn, and Integrate

The first 30 days in any new role should be spent absorbing as much information as possible. You’re here to learn the lay of the land, understand the company’s culture, and grasp the nuances of the product. But more than just getting up to speed, this phase is about establishing relationships and credibility with your team.

Step 1: Meet with Stakeholders

As a product manager, your success depends on how well you understand the needs of your stakeholders and how effectively you collaborate with them. Schedule one-on-ones with your immediate team, cross-functional partners (such as engineering, marketing, and sales), and leadership.

Take this time to listen closely to their pain points and aspirations. Steven Haines, in his LinkedIn article, emphasizes the importance of asking the right questions in these meetings, such as:

  • What are the main challenges the product faces right now?
  • Where do you see the product going in the next six months?
  • What would success look like to you?

Your goal here is to build rapport and gather insights that will inform your decision-making later on.

Step 2: Understand the Product Inside and Out

Before you can make any changes, you need to know the product intimately. This means spending time with product analytics, diving into customer feedback, and reviewing the product roadmap. If the company doesn’t already have robust data and analytics in place, now’s the time to start organizing that information. ProductPlan’s guide on how to approach the first 30 days recommends using this time to identify where the product is excelling and where it's falling short.

You also need to become the voice of the customer. This means reading user reviews, analyzing support tickets, and paying close attention to any feedback loops in place. You can’t deliver a great product unless you deeply understand the problems users are trying to solve with it. This user-centric approach is explored in depth by Merit, offering practical advice for onboarding smoothly.

Step 3: Integrate into the Company Culture

During your first month, you should also be actively integrating into the company’s culture. This means understanding not just the formal structures but also the informal networks of influence. Who are the decision-makers? Who tends to resist change? Who are the early adopters you can rely on to help evangelize your vision?

In his blog post, LogRocket highlights how understanding the company culture can help you avoid missteps early on. Get to know the unwritten rules and expectations, as these will help you navigate the inevitable challenges ahead.

Phase 2: Days 31-60: Strategize and Plan

Now that you’ve spent a month listening and learning, it’s time to start formulating a strategy. This second phase is crucial because it’s when your stakeholders will begin to look to you for direction. The pressure is on to show that you have a plan and that you can steer the ship.

Step 1: Conduct a Gap Analysis

One of the first things you should do is conduct a gap analysis. Where does the product stand now, and where does it need to go? Identify the major gaps that are holding the product back, whether it’s technical debt, UX issues, or missed opportunities in the market. The Pragmatic Institute’s checklist offers a step-by-step approach to identifying these gaps, particularly for product leaders stepping into new roles.

A good gap analysis looks at three main areas:

  • Product performance: Are users happy with the product? What are the churn rates, and what feedback are customers giving?
  • Internal processes: Is the team functioning well? Are there bottlenecks in the development process or communication issues across departments?
  • Market positioning: How does the product stack up against competitors? Are there opportunities in the market that the product isn’t currently capitalizing on?

Your analysis here will directly inform your priorities in the next phase.

Step 2: Prioritize Projects

Once you have a clear understanding of where the product stands, it’s time to prioritize the most important projects. The key here is to strike a balance between quick wins that will demonstrate early success and longer-term initiatives that will drive significant impact. As you define your roadmap, make sure it’s closely aligned with the company’s broader business goals.

A great resource for prioritizing and balancing short- and long-term wins is the guide from Idea Shortcut. It outlines how to approach this phase with a critical eye on both what’s immediately achievable and what will deliver the most value in the future.

Step 3: Deepen Relationships with Cross-Functional Teams

By this point, you should have built some initial rapport with your stakeholders, but now it’s time to deepen those relationships. This means working closely with your engineering, design, and marketing counterparts to make sure everyone is aligned around the same goals.

For example, if you’re pushing for a UX improvement but haven’t aligned with the design team, you’ll likely face resistance. The best product managers understand that cross-functional collaboration is at the heart of successful product development. GoPractice offers insightful advice on how to foster these relationships by focusing on shared outcomes and mutual respect.

Phase 3: Days 61-90: Execute and Deliver

By the time you hit the 60-day mark, you should have a well-formed strategy, a prioritized roadmap, and the buy-in of your key stakeholders. Now it’s time to start executing and delivering results. This is where the rubber meets the road.

Step 1: Ship Something

Execution is where product managers prove their value. By now, you should have identified a few key areas for improvement that can be tackled relatively quickly. Whether it’s a new feature, a UX improvement, or a bug fix, make sure you’re delivering something concrete. The goal is to show that you can take an idea from inception to launch.

As LogRocket advises, shipping doesn’t have to be monumental in scope—it just needs to move the needle. Even small wins can create momentum, build confidence with your team, and signal that you’re a PM who can deliver.

Step 2: Track and Iterate

Once you’ve launched something, it’s critical to track the performance closely. Whether you’ve shipped a new feature or fixed a major issue, you’ll want to keep an eye on the relevant KPIs to measure the impact. Did the changes improve customer satisfaction? Did they reduce churn? Whatever metrics you defined in your strategy should now be closely monitored.

In the product world, the ability to iterate quickly and improve based on feedback is just as important as the initial launch. Stay agile and ready to make adjustments as needed. The Product Coalition offers some great tips on how to use early feedback to refine and enhance your product decisions.

Step 3: Communicate Progress Regularly

During this final phase, communication becomes even more critical. Keep your stakeholders in the loop with regular updates on your progress. Highlight both your wins and your learnings, and don’t be afraid to ask for feedback. Transparency helps to build trust, and by sharing both successes and challenges, you show that you’re focused on long-term improvement.

Joni Hoadley’s article on crushing your first 90 days emphasizes the importance of visibility and clear communication. It’s not enough to just do the work—you need to make sure your team and leadership understand the value of what you’re delivering. Having a regular product changelog is also a good way to make sure your team communicates releases publicly and frequently.

If you don't have one yet, you can use this open-source changelog. It lets you create stunning changelogs like illustrated such as Linear, Vercel or Framer.

Beyond the First 90 Days

Once you’ve completed your first 90 days, the real work begins. These three months were about building a foundation—now it’s time to scale. Having established credibility and delivered early wins, you’re in a strong position to push for larger, more ambitious initiatives. But don’t forget that product management is a marathon, not a sprint. To ensure continued success, there are several key areas you should focus on as you move beyond your onboarding phase.

1. Continue Building Relationships

The relationships you cultivated in your first 90 days will continue to be your most valuable assets. Keep fostering a collaborative environment by regularly meeting with cross-functional teams, deepening the trust and alignment you’ve built. Maintaining strong relationships with your stakeholders will not only help you execute better but will also position you as a product leader they can depend on for strategic insights.

As you move forward, consider applying the lessons learned from this phase to build partnerships that support long-term product success. For more strategies on developing and maintaining key relationships, check out The Product City’s guide.

2. Strengthen Your Product Vision

With the immediate pressure of the first 90 days behind you, now is the time to take a step back and think bigger. What’s the long-term vision for the product? How does it fit into the company’s broader strategy? Being able to articulate a compelling product vision is one of the hallmarks of a great product manager.

Start working closely with leadership to understand the company’s long-term goals and ensure your product roadmap aligns with these. A well-defined vision will not only guide your decisions but will also inspire your team.

This article provides insight into how product managers can drive a vision that resonates with both the team and the business.

3. Keep Learning and Adapting

Even after you’ve made your mark, continuous learning should remain a priority. The best product managers are lifelong learners who actively seek out feedback and new information. Stay curious about your customers, the market, and your team. As new data comes in, don’t hesitate to adapt your strategy and make adjustments as necessary.

One way to ensure you’re consistently improving is by setting up regular feedback loops. Conduct regular retrospectives, ask for candid feedback from your team, and keep a close eye on the product metrics that matter most. This iterative approach will help you refine your processes and ensure your product continues to grow in the right direction.

For more on adapting to new insights and refining your product strategy, you can refer to Lauren Chan Lee's guide.

4. Build a Culture of Innovation

Now that you’ve built a foundation, your next challenge is creating a culture where innovation thrives. This doesn’t mean coming up with radical new ideas every week—it’s about encouraging your team to experiment, iterate, and learn from failure.

Set the stage for a culture where trying new approaches is not only encouraged but supported. This helps drive continuous product improvement, enables rapid prototyping, and positions your product team as forward-thinking leaders in the company. For ideas on fostering innovation in your team, check out Ant Murphy’s guide.

Conclusion: Thrive, Don’t Just Survive

Your first 90 days as a product manager are your proving ground. It’s where you either make a name for yourself or fade into the background. But to thrive, you need to be bold, strategic, and relentless in execution. Stakeholders won’t remember the person who played it safe—they’ll remember the one who stepped up, took risks, and delivered results.

If you’re looking to amplify your impact even further, having the right tools in place can accelerate your success. june.so equips product managers with the analytics needed to track performance, understand user behavior, and make data-driven decisions. As you strategize and execute, june.so provides the insights you need to stay ahead, spot opportunities, and ensure your product makes waves, not ripples.

So, will you sink or swim in your first 90 days? With the right approach—and the right tools—you can be sure you’ll thrive.

Finally, don’t forget to enjoy the journey! Product management is an incredibly fulfilling career. While it comes with its fair share of responsibilities and occasional pressure, the reward of solving real-world problems for real people is unmatched. At the end of the day, making a tangible impact is what makes this role so special.

title: The Crazy Story of Command AI – How to Get to 25 Million Monthly Users By Accident
html:
Some startup stories are all about coincidence. This is one of them.

This is the crazy story of Command AI.

I flew out to San Francisco to meet James Evans, the co-founder and CEO of Command AI. I wanted to find out how he managed to get to 25 million monthly users almost by accident, and despite having launched during a tech crisis.

What Is Command AI?

If you’re unfamiliar, Command AI is user assistance software. Anyone who’s building any kind of web app, desktop app, or mobile app has essentially the same goal: To make their product easy for their users to use, without annoying them.

Command AI started off as a search bar built into web apps. End-users could use it to discover and execute commands. Think of it as “cmd+k”, but for any app.

Now Command AI offers a bunch of user assistance tools designed to make every aspect of a product easier to use and understand. These tools include non-intrusive nudges, intuitive product tours, AI copilots, and more.

Before Command AI

Before Command AI, James was working on an entirely different project: A platform for teachers to review students’ codes. But his business had a problem. It was an incoherent product. Yet one day, he introduced a feature that changed everything…

James and his co-founders studied computer science at an Ivy League school. Even then, they knew they had to start a company together. They were always tinkering with ideas in college, and even built a few prototypes (which James now describes in… less than glowing terms.)

Leaving college, they joined a crypto startup which “burned fast and bright”. After that collapsed, James and his co-founders were “unburdened by employment”, so they were free to explore certain ideas.

Their original idea was a tool that computer science teachers could use to give their students feedback on their code. They already had a prototype, and they were working to solve a problem they knew well, having just graduated as computer science students.

They worked on solving this problem for a year, before they hit a dead end.

Too Much Of A Good Thing

In those days, James and his co-founders were “young, scrappy, and eager”. In other words, they weren’t very good at saying “NO”.

Users would request features, and James and his team were always happy to comply. Anything anyone requested, they’d build it straightaway.

While this made their users happy, there is such a thing as being too receptive to user feedback. James was left with a Frankenstein product, with dozens of features which hardly anyone would ever use. This, of course, made their product totally baffling for new users.

James isn’t a designer, nor were any of his co-founders. They knew they had to fix the complexity problem, but they didn’t want to redesign the whole app from scratch.

So instead, they created a searchable menu of functionality within the product itself (CMD+K!). And this was the birth of Command AI.

What Do You Want To Do Today?

Say you login to an app. There’s something you want to do, but you’re not quite sure how to do it.

James created a system that allowed users to search for the very thing they wanted to do, without having to navigate through the UI.

The system worked. It worked so well that James and his team wondered:

Why don’t more products have this interface?

Was this a good enough idea to focus on? James decided to let someone else decide.

They turned to Y Combinator (YC), the program that provides funding, mentorship, and community for startups. Unfortunately, they’d already missed the YC application deadline by two weeks. Never mind: James and his team applied anyway. If we get accepted, they thought, then we’ll focus on this search bar idea as our business.

They decided to work on Command AI over the summer, to see what happened. But as anyone who’s taken part in the YC process knows, the moment you start, things get very serious, very quickly. You immediately start to build a company.

James and his team found themselves working with numerous startups that were far more advanced than they were. They’d written a few lines of code. They had zero customers and zero revenue, but they were rubbing shoulders with startups who were pushing a million in ARR within their first week. This made James realize – we’ve got a lot of work to do.

Prototyping, and Customer Acquisition Strategies

James and his team spent their first month of the YC program building a prototype. They made the “classic” YC move of trying to convince their batchmates to use their product.

Command AI started off as a Chrome extension, allowing users to inject the functionality search bar into any website build. This prototype was “semi-useful”, but Command AI has never been a very visual product. It’s the sort of product you need to see in action if you’re to get any idea of its value.

So, James started creating short, five-minute Loom videos. Essentially, James would assess a product, and identify areas where he thought that Command AI could help users access certain features. He’d explain how Command AI could help the products with upselling or converting through addressing areas where he felt there was too much friction.

James would then build the Command AI that could help solve these specific problems, before emailing certain founders so as to build up some interest. They were very clever in who they sent these outreach emails to. They intentionally picked people who already knew what command palettes are, and how they work. These were the sort of people who’d quickly see the value in what James and his team were building.

They used a function in the Superhuman email service to identify other Superhuman users, who they reasoned would be familiar with command palettes. It was then simply a case of sending an email which explained that they’d built a version of command palette that the founder could add to their own product, with an example of how it might look.

They got a 30% reply rate on these initial emails, making this Superhuman “hack” a highly effective early customer acquisition strategy.

They Got Lucky…

James readily acknowledges the huge role that luck played in this early success. Not many founders use Superhuman. Yet between their seed and their series A, they were lucky enough to reach high quality companies who happened to be a good fit for their product.

James estimates that around 80% of their ARR throughout their series A was essentially random – just the result of people who happened to sign up, or who messaged him on LinkedIn. They acquired a lot of leads without doing too much to cultivate them. “It just sort of happened,” James says.

Yet while luck played a huge role, they continued with their initial customer acquisition strategy, of creating custom product demos as Loom videos which they’d send to carefully chosen founders. And in this way, they acquired an encouraging number of champions, and all signs indicated that they’d achieved product-market fit (PMF).

Key Takeaways From Command AI’s Early Days

If you build a product that can:

  • Demonstrate a “proof of work” at a reasonable cost.
  • Deliver actual value to users.

…and if this is 100% repeatable…

Then you’re probably on the right track. You’re probably on course to PMF, and $1m AAR, just like Command AI were.

But things don’t always work out the way you expect them to…

PROTIP – Don’t Launch a Tech Business During a Tech Crisis

It wasn’t exactly smooth sailing for James and his team from this point on.

First of all, while they were very lucky in their initial customer acquisition, they had the tremendous misfortune to launch their business during a tech crisis. Remember 2020? The pandemic, the stock crash, and the worst crypto decline in years? TechCrunch summed up the crisis with an image of a dumpster fire, and the words “Well, that was terrible”.

Not the best time to launch a tech business, you might think. And sure enough, James and his team soon found that they had plenty to worry about.

They’d primarily been selling to high growth SAAS companies, so there were concerns that people were suddenly going to turn away from their product. Thankfully, this didn’t happen. Yet still, Command AI started to find it harder and harder to encourage people to prioritize what they were offering.

Losing PMF? Then It’s Time To Pivot

James recalls the moment when they knew that they had to change course. They were on the verge of selling to a company which, on the surface, looked to be a perfect fit. They had a bunch of UX problems which Command AI could easily solve.

Then, just as they were getting ready to close, their product champion got in touch. “Hey,” he said. “Leadership keeps asking me whether your tool would be a good replacement for Pendo.”

A good replacement for Pendo? You mean, the digital adoption product that uses pop-ups to onboard users? No! Command AI is something completely different. It’s a totally new building block for the internet.

“OK,” said this champion. “The thing is, unless you can tell me that your tool can replace Pendo, then I can’t take this deal any further.”

Largely thanks to the wider tech crisis, the summer had been tough for Command AI. James felt as if they had to work a lot harder to hit the same growth targets that they were seeing just before the series A. He now says that it almost felt like people were doing them a favor by trying their product. They’d do anything to get deals over the finish line, often building new features at the last minute.

But then someone simply asked, can your product just replace this other product?

This was a wake up call. It made it clear that it was time to pivot.

How To Go From 100k to 25 Million End Users in Just Two Years

Up until now, James and his co-founders had been trying to compete in their own category. The “Pendo Question” made them realize that they could make life much easier for themselves if they instead tried to compete in an existing category.

The keywords were “digital adoption”. Instead of trying to sell people on the benefits of Command AI, why not instead describe their product as a “digital adoption” tool? That way, they’d be able to sell to people who already knew what they wanted.

They didn’t forget their original insight, which is that products can be confusing, and that users don’t really like intrusive popups telling them what to do. The Command AI way is to help users by figuring out what they truly care about, through their intent.

So, James and his co-founders repositioned Command AI to compete in the digital adoption category. They had to build new features, and they had to reconsider how they marketed and sold their product.

Long story short, it worked: Over the course of the next two years, Command AI grew from 100k to 25 million end users. They went from failing to build their own category to disrupting and reinventing an existing one. Rather than selling themselves as a completely new idea, they can sell themselves as a better version of a product that people might already be using.

As a measure of how successful this strategy is, James refers to his sales calls. Before they pivoted, initial sales calls might have lasted 30 minutes, 20 minutes of which would be spent explaining just what Command AI is, and how it works. Now the Command AI sales team can explain their offering, and hint at their value, in just two minutes.

Marketing and Sales Tactics

Effective Use of Sales Decks 

James and his team do a lot of iteration. They tweak their sales decks every week to ensure they can strike a chord with certain audiences. Also, today’s sales decks are tomorrow’s marketing. They allow you to tell the story of who you are, what you’re building, and what problems you’re solving.

Leveraging Industry Terminology 

Command AI did not start out as a “digital adoption” tool. But once James and the team learned the power of the words “digital adoption”, they found a means of attracting and retaining customers who already knew what they needed.

Using Market Maps For Visibility and Credibility

James and his team made a conscious effort to get Command AI included in market maps, as they knew it would boost both their credibility and their visibility among people who cared about the problem they were trying to solve. They also found that market maps acted as a powerful social proof visual for use in sales decks.

Build Competitor Pages

Many startups tend to wait until they feel, well, competitive before they build competitor pages. But James sees a lot of value in building competitor pages when as a startup. They can say a lot about how you view your product, and about the specific problems you’re trying to solve.

Conclusion – Key Takeaways From The Command AI Story

  • You don’t have to change the world. Command AI failed to build their own category. Instead, they chose to reinvent an existing one. Once they found their category, they embraced it fully, being sure to use the terms that would resonate with the customers who count.
  • Build the minimum as fast as you can. A workable prototype lets you demonstrate your value, which is essential for achieving PMF. Plus, the sooner you get the prototype out there, the sooner you can start gathering invaluable user feedback.
  • Iterate quickly. Listen to your users and iterate based on what they tell you so that you can continue to strike a chord.

But perhaps the biggest takeaway from the Command AI story is that you make your own luck.

James acknowledges that he and his co-founders were very lucky in the early days, in that they tended to attract highly valuable customers without doing all that much to cultivate them. Yet at the same time, they were unlucky enough to launch in the midst of a crisis in the tech world.

Good luck will only get you so far. Bad luck can scupper you completely. What really matters is how you react to situations. When things aren’t going your way, reflect on what you can do to get back on track. This might involve pivoting in a way you never imagined you’d have to. But as James and Command AI demonstrate, you can radically change your business without losing sight of your core values.

Want To Get 10x More Users For Your SAAS?

Imagine being able to find out exactly who’s using your product and using that information to make people stick around.

title: How to increase client retention in B2B SaaS: using data to enhance client relationships
html:
In the competitive landscape of B2B SaaS, retaining clients is just as critical as acquiring new ones. 

High client retention not only leads to consistent revenue streams but also fosters a community of loyal customers who can advocate for your brand. 

In this article, we will explore effective strategies to enhance client retention in the B2B SaaS sector and we’ll see a couple of different approaches you can test right away to leverage your product data usage for this purpose. 

By continuing to read you will:

  • Learn why retaining clients is crucial for long-term profitability and the cost-effectiveness of nurturing existing relationships.
  • Discover how to foster loyalty and reduce churn by offering value and support throughout the client journey.
  • Explore how integrating product analytics and CRM data helps anticipate client needs and improve engagement.
  • Understand the importance of continuous improvement in meeting evolving client needs and staying ahead of expectations.

Understanding the Importance of Client Retention in B2B SaaS

Client retention is a key performance indicator for any B2B SaaS business that, at its core, reflects how well a business fulfils the needs and expectations of its clients. 

Retained clients often yield higher lifetime values, which significantly contributes to long-term profitability. Retaining clients is also typically more cost-effective than acquiring new ones, since the marketing and sales expenses associated with bringing in new customers can be substantial while nurturing existing relationships often requires fewer resources. 

By focusing on client retention, businesses can thus allocate budget more efficiently but - in addition to financial benefits - strong client retention also fosters deeper relationships, which can in turn lead to invaluable feedback and insights. 

It’s when clients feel valued and heard that they are more likely to share their experiences and suggestions for improvement.  

Clients retention’s foundations: building strong relationships with clients

Building strong client relationships in the B2B SaaS industry is essential for driving long-term success, fostering loyalty, and reducing churn. 

These relationships are built not only on the quality of the product but also on the value and support offered throughout the customer journey. In an industry where competition is fierce and switching costs for clients are often low, maintaining a proactive and customer-centric approach becomes vital. 

Companies need to focus on creating trust through transparent communication, regular check-ins, and consistent value delivery. This includes personalised onboarding to ensure clients are set up for success from the start, as well as ongoing support and training to help them achieve their evolving goals.

In today’s data-driven world, the ability to deeply understand client needs and behaviour is more important than ever. By building strong client relationships, SaaS companies can better anticipate challenges, adapt to specific requirements, and provide solutions that deliver immediate value. 

Understanding the nuances of each client’s business also allows for more tailored recommendations, making the relationship feel more like a partnership than a transaction. 

Further reading:

  • How to calculate retention rate
  • No BS retention metrics to reduce churn

Enhancing client retention with Product Analytics and CRM integration

As SaaS products become increasingly complex, clients rely on their providers not only to solve problems but also to guide them in maximising the full potential of the platform.

However, simply maintaining relationships through regular interactions can be not enough. 

The next step to deepen these connections lies in leveraging product usage and CRM data to gain insights into client behaviour and anticipate their expectations. 

By analysing how clients engage with the product, SaaS companies can identify patterns, uncover opportunities for improvement, and proactively address issues before they become major problems. 

Product data reveals how clients interact with the platform, showing which features are used most, which are underutilised, and where clients may be encountering friction. This information allows SaaS providers to identify patterns of successful engagement, as well as potential red flags, such as a drop in usage or a lack of engagement with key features. 

Armed with this data and following a proper customer retention analysis, companies can take proactive steps to re-engage users, offer additional training, or introduce relevant features that better meet the client’s needs.

CRM data complements product usage insights by providing a holistic view of the customer journey, including interactions with support teams, feedback provided, and any issues raised. 

By integrating these two data streams, companies can build a more complete picture of each client, allowing for personalised outreach based on their specific behaviour and needs and increase expansion. For example, if a client has reached out frequently for support with a certain feature, but their usage data shows they aren’t fully utilising it, a targeted training session or tutorial can be offered to help them gain more value from the platform.

Client retention and continuous improvement: adapting to changing clients expectations

Continuous improvement is essential in maintaining strong client relationships, especially in the dynamic B2B SaaS industry where users' expectations are constantly evolving. 

As businesses grow and their needs shift, their requirements from a SaaS provider also change. 

What worked for a client initially may no longer be enough as they scale or adopt new strategies and this is (again) where the ongoing analysis of product usage and CRM data becomes crucial. 

Product analytics provides detailed insights into how users interact with a platform, uncovering trends, pain points, and feature adoption rates.  When this data is combined with a CRM,  customer success teams gain a comprehensive view of client behaviour, allowing for more personalised communication, targeted feature updates, and data-driven recommendations. 

This synergy helps SaaS companies proactively address client needs, ensuring that every interaction is relevant and tailored to their changing goals and business objectives. 

It’s by consistently delivering on this promise that SaaS companies can strengthen relationships, reduce churn, and foster enduring partnerships with their clients.

Conclusion: how to increase client retention in B2B SaaS

In conclusion, improving client retention in B2B SaaS requires a comprehensive approach that blends personalised client support with data-driven insights. 

By integrating product usage and CRM data, companies can better understand client behaviour, anticipate their needs, and address potential issues before they escalate. 

Continuous improvement is key to staying relevant and ensuring that a software solution evolves alongside its clients' growing businesses. 

By maintaining this proactive, customer-focused strategy, SaaS companies can build stronger, longer-lasting client relationships, ultimately driving loyalty and long-term success.

title: Understanding Retention Rate: What It Is and Why It Matters for Your B2B SaaS Business
html:
In the rapidly evolving world of SaaS, understanding and optimising retention rate is essential for long-term success. 

Retention rate, simply put, refers to the percentage of customers who continue to use a product or service over a given period of time. 

This metric is of utmost importance as it directly affects the growth, revenue, and overall health of a SaaS business, so let’s see exactly what we mean when we talk about retention in a SaaS context and why maintaining a high rate of customer retention is of critical importance in this industry (especially for B2B focused companies).

What you’ll learn:

  • A high retention rate indicates satisfied customers, leading to stable revenue, reduced churn, and growth through customer referrals, especially crucial for B2B SaaS businesses.
  • Retention is calculated by dividing the number of customers at the end of a period by the number at the start, providing insight into customer behaviour.
  • Strategies like enhancing user experience, analysing product usage data, and offering robust customer support can improve retention.
  • Continuous analysis of retention rates using analytics tools is critical for refining customer success strategies and fostering long-term loyalty.

Defining Retention Rate in SaaS Context

Before exploring what retention rate means, let's first establish a solid understanding of what it entails in the context of SaaS. 

The basics of retention rate involve tracking how many subscribers remain active within a specified time frame. It helps gauge customer loyalty and the efficacy of a SaaS product in meeting their ongoing recurring revenue needs.

Understanding retention rate in the realm of Software as a Service (SaaS) is crucial for businesses looking to assess the long-term success and sustainability of their customer base. 

By analysing retention rate metrics, companies can gain valuable insights into customer behaviour, satisfaction levels, and the overall health of their subscription-based business model, whether it’s B2C or B2B focused.

The Basics of Retention Rate

Calculating retention rate is relatively straightforward. 

It involves dividing the number of customers at the end of a specific period by the total number of customers at the start of that period. The resulting figure is then multiplied by 100 to obtain the retention rate as a percentage. 

For example, if a SaaS business had 1000 customers at the beginning of a month and 900 customers at the end, the retention rate for that month would be 90%.

Furthermore, retention rate analysis can provide SaaS companies with actionable insights for improving customer engagement and reducing churn. 

By identifying patterns in customer behaviour and preferences, businesses can tailor their product offerings and customer success strategies to enhance customer satisfaction and drive long-term loyalty.

Key Components of Retention

Retention in the SaaS industry refers to the ability of a business to keep its customers coming back to use its product or service over a given period of time. 

It's a critical metric that reflects customer satisfaction, product value, and long-term business sustainability. One of the key components of retention is understanding returning users, which refers to customers who have already used the product in the past and continue to engage with it over time. Tracking these users helps identify trends in customer loyalty and product engagement.

Another important aspect is the cohort definition, where users are grouped based on specific characteristics or behaviours, such as the time they signed up, their location, or product usage patterns. Cohort analysis allows businesses to understand how different groups of users behave over time, providing deeper insights into retention rates across various segments.

Finally, determining the best time period for user retention analysis is crucial for accurate insights. Depending on the product's nature and customer lifecycle, businesses may need to analyse weekly, monthly, or quarterly retention rates: identifying the optimal time frame ensures that the analysis reflects meaningful user behaviour, allowing businesses to make informed decisions on customer retention strategies.

The Importance of Retention Rate for SaaS Businesses

Now that we have a solid grasp of what retention entails, let's explore why retention rate holds such high importance for SaaS businesses.

Retention rate has a direct correlation with a SaaS business's revenue and growth prospects. Acquiring new customers can be in fact an expensive and time-consuming process, making retaining existing ones significantly more cost-effective. 

High retention rates contribute to a stable and recurring revenue stream as satisfied customers continue to renew their subscriptions and potentially upgrade to higher pricing tiers. A high retention rate is also often indicative of satisfied customers who find value in a SaaS product or service. Happy customers are more likely to become loyal advocates, referring others and thereby helping to fuel organic growth. 

By building long-term relationships based on trust and continuous improvement, SaaS businesses can benefit from enhanced customer satisfaction and loyalty.

Calculating Retention Rate in SaaS

Understanding how to accurately calculate retention rate is crucial for SaaS businesses. Let's delve into the formula and identify common mistakes that should be avoided.

Understanding the Formula

As mentioned earlier, the retention rate is calculated by dividing the number of customers at the end of a specific period by the total number of customers at the beginning of that period. 

This formula provides a straightforward approach to quantify customer retention and analyse trends over time but, when calculating retention rate, it's important to ensure accurate data collection and avoid common mistakes. 

Inaccurate customer counts, failing to account for upgrades or downgrades, and excluding churned customers from the calculation are errors that can skew the retention rate and lead to misleading insights. 

Here’s some examples of common situations that can lead to incorrect counts:

  • Imagine a customer who upgrades from a basic plan to a premium plan. If this upgrade isn’t correctly tracked, it may appear that there’s an additional new user rather than a continuation of an existing user, skewing retention numbers.
  • If churned customers are not included in retention calculations, a SaaS company might falsely believe it has a high retention rate. For example, if a business fails to track churn from annual subscribers and only looks at monthly users, the long-term picture could be significantly off.
  • Again, Incorrect customer counts may arise from duplicate accounts or improperly defined user categories. For instance, if a customer has both a trial and a paid account under different emails, it may be mistakenly counted twice, impacting retention metrics.

Diligence and attention to detail are therefore paramount in obtaining reliable data for calculating retention rate, otherwise the risk of making incorrect considerations can be particularly high.

Now that we understand the significance and calculation of retention rate, it's time to explore effective strategies for improving this critical metric within a SaaS business.

How to Improve Retention Rate

Providing a seamless and user-friendly experience is crucial for customer satisfaction and retention. Continually collecting feedback, analysing user behaviour, and iterating on the SaaS product helps ensure that it remains valuable and relevant to customers. 

Regular updates and feature enhancements can thus contribute to a positive user experience, leading to higher retention rates, but it’s a deep product usage analysis and robust customer support system that can significantly move the needle here. 

Product usage data, in particular, has often been a tool for guiding product decisions but, especially for B2B SaaS businesses emphasising a data-driven approach to the market, these data can be critical not just for product development, but also for analysing and anticipating accounts needs, applying solutions to engage and retain customers at a very granular level.

This can be at the core of effective customer success, the kind that builds trust and fosters long-term relationships with clients increasing the likelihood of customers remaining loyal to a SaaS business.

Monitoring and Analysing Retention Rate

Peter Drucker once said:

"What gets measured gets managed"

emphasising that the first step to improvement is measurement, as it's the only way to truly understand and manage progress.

To leverage retention rate effectively, SaaS businesses need to monitor and analyse it over time. This allows for data-driven decision-making and the identification of trends and opportunities.

Various tools are available to SaaS businesses to track retention rate efficiently, each of them providing insights into customer behaviour, churn rate, and retention rate trends and each of them with a different approach and perspective. 

Leveraging such product analytics platforms allows businesses to make informed decisions and implement targeted strategies to improve their customer retention.

But not all tools are created equal: at June, i.e., we want first of all to make sure that you have all the insights you need to fully understand how your customers are using your product, providing with features and reports specifically built to enhance not just the Product development but also your Sales and Customer Success strategies.

If you have a B2B SaaS business you can try it by yourself by simply starting to set up an account. We’ll guide you to activate the product in less than 30 mins and you’ll get our Pro plan free for one month. 

Conclusion

Interpreting retention rate data requires a comprehensive understanding of each specific SaaS business and its customer base. 

An in-depth analysis of retention rate data helps uncover actionable insights and provides a roadmap for optimising customer retention and engagement.

There are a number of tools on the market that can help you do that, but June’s unique approach can give B2B SaaS businesses a complete overview on a set of metrics and reports that can make life much easier, focusing not just on ways to develop their Product for success but also to help to really understand their customers and their behaviour, providing the data that customer success teams need to successfully improve clent’s retention.

It’s by understanding retention rate, calculating it accurately, and implementing an effective approach to customer retention improvement that B2B SaaS businesses can focus on enhancing the user experience, providing exceptional customer support, and leveraging data to drive growth and success.

title: Iconic brands stem from unrecognized truth
html:
This article began as an internal note I shared with the June team. After countless conversations with other founders, I realized it could be valuable to a broader audience. I hope you find value in it.

Writing is thinking. And to write well is to think well. Many say this and for good reasons. That's why it's so hard but that’s also why it’s valuable. For me, writing has never been second nature. But sometimes, I feel the need to spill my jumbled thoughts onto a blank page. Like a child dumping out Lego pieces all over the floor, trying to build something new, I try to make sense of everything going through my head, playing with the fragments of my ideas, recollecting and reshaping them into something coherent.

What you are about to read and (hopefully appreciate..) is the result of me going through some of the hardest questions I’ve faced at June so far. Questions that touch everything from customer-psychology and character-building, to positioning and brand identity, and how all of this ties back into June’s grand-scheme of things.

These are personal reflections that I’ve shared with my team and that today I wanted to share with you too. 

There are no shortcuts; to create a long-lasting company, you need to make something genuinely useful. As the old man from the orange company said: “...something they love.” While I think it’s fair to say that June hasn’t quite yet nailed PMF (or at least not in the original Andressen’s definition) and there are lots of margin for improvements on the product side, I think we can all agree that we DO have built something people want.

I mean... paying customers, and annualized revenue, if anything, means that we as a company have successfully crossed the early extinction chasm.

Then, why are we still here, doing more than okay-ish but definitely not AMAZING yet? And why am I in my bed at night listening to countless podcasts about brand and positioning knowing that, deep down, something’s still not quite there? And why are we so obsessed about finding the narrative™ for June? This sort of special thing that would make June, June?

Deep down we know the answer. It’s because most companies (within our target range) would probably benefit from something like June, but they don’t know it yet. But how would they know? June is just a small company in what looks like a well-defined market category, dominated by a few larger companies.

The old saying “Nobody has ever been fired for buying an IBM” seems to fit this case well. The current widely used alternatives, Amplitude or Mixpanel, work just fine—so, why would someone even bother finding or trying something else?

We know you are unlikely to be able to sell June as “a simplified Mixpanel” very well: there aren’t simply not enough people shopping for “simplified product analytics platforms” or a “new way of doing product analytics'' or a “product analytics that just work.” On June product analytics features, the cold truth is that Amplitude and Mixpanel analytics do actually just work.

So, if we’re not really selling an “analytics product” or the set of features June has in their specific implementation, what are we even trying to sell here?

Just as much as our job is about building something that is genuinely useful, our job is also about understanding what people think they want and then translating the value of June into their terms.

We know we have to come up with something better, more powerful, more exciting. Something that helps people reframe the question and see June as the obvious answer.

Narrative Building

When I think about companies and narratives I keep instinctively going back to the ideas of minerals and colors and their textures. Some have such bright and unique combinations that are easy to remember even if you took a single glimpse. Others have mild blends incapable of standing out from the rest. I think the same applies to companies and product identities. 

Some companies and products seem to have such unique and distinct characters. While others don’t. Some narratives are so powerful that they stay with us for months after we heard them for the first time, while others are completely forgotten the minute we close their website’s tab.

Is this something that we actually have some control over? And if so, to what extent?

Taken for granted that there is not a single way to approach this and, like mother History has taught us plenty of times, there are many examples that validate or invalidate what I am about to write. Nonetheless, under our specific circumstances I think it makes sense to follow 3 criteria that I see being at the heart of powerful narratives:

1. Fundamental, unrecognized truth

If you are looking to reframe a 20-year old industry problem you better start from the correct underlying premise or, at least, a very reasonable one. It doesn’t make any sense to even consider a wacky foundation or something that we don’t quite believe it’s (or it’s going to be) an absolute truth.

It’s also important that this “truth” isn’t as widely acknowledged (this, I think, crosses with Thiel’s infamous question). After all, if that were the case, there would be no need to tell people, and it likely wouldn't be relevant anyway. Often, these truths are held back by some pre-existing generational societal norms.

Think of Airbnb, the idea of people sleeping in other people’s beds was considered inappropriate and quite over the line for standard social conventions. Regardless they stood for a loud “we think it's okay to sleep in other people's beds.”

Or take Uber: “we think it’s okay to step in stranger’s cars”. Or Bumble “we think women can make the first move.”

All of these 3 were kinda considered taboos by the previous generations. Instead they counteracted and made that act the centercore piece of their identity. It’s how Airbnb became “the only app that allows you to live everywhere” and Bumble “the first feminist dating app”.

A strong “unacknowledged truth,” with the concrete yet unrealized potential to resonate with contemporary audiences, is the foundation for great products and iconic identities.

We talked about digital products’ identities, but we could also talk about physical products brand’s and (pretty much) all we’ve said would still apply. Take Levi’s, for example—the jeans were originally designed and marketed for labor and manual work. In the 1960s, it was considered inappropriate to wear Levi’s outside of blue-collar settings. But by the 1980s, a new generation embraced Levi’s in formal contexts, using them as a form of rebellion against the norms of the previous generation. And it was exactly during this cultural shift that Levi’s found the identity we all know today.

Clearly, in Bumble’s case, the shift was intentionally planned, while with Levi’s, it emerged organically from the ground up. Yet, the common thread between both is how they transformed cultural norms to define their identities.

"This feels like a crossroads where we could dive into adjacent topics—how trends emerge, their impact on sociology, semiotics, visual art, and (probably, hardest stuff on Earth) the complex evolution of fashion. But that would take us WAY too far off track. So, let’s bring it back to us…

Everything we said so far, can be distilled down to this idea: if people agree you have the correct code and the right framing of the problem, they will feel legitimate doing things your way. 

This raises the obvious questions for us: what’s that equivalent for June? Can we identify an unspoken truth in our category?

2. Narrative-Product fit

The product should fit and embody this unrecognized truth to the point it becomes its vessel. Airbnb is a short term rental website, Uber is a ride-hailing app where you tap and a black car picks you up, and Bumble is an app where only women are allowed to swipe.

These products are such great instances of that unspoken truth. To the point it looks almost impossible to come up with a different or better form-factor.

Back to June, if our “unacknowledged truth” isn’t practically embodied by the June product, then it will feel superimposed, manufactured, detached from reality and it will work against us.

3. Exciting and inspiring

Just because this “truth” is (might be) true and it's well embodied in your product, doesn’t mean it's an exciting thesis. If startups are “movements”, the narrative needs to be exciting, inspiring and make people want to be part of it.

At the intersection of the 3 is where, I think, we need to look for:

Character as a Texture

What we're looking for here is a “core idea” that can be eventually broken down at every sub-level, morphing into the different, required artifacts while still retaining the original meaning.

We’re looking for a material, a texture, a flavor. Whether with that we’re going to create a chair, a sofa, or table doesn’t really matter. If we go with marble, it might be an elegant, royal marble chair, if we pick wood it might be a warmer, friendly and rustic chair.

The core idea will take different shapes and orient to different meanings depending on context, but it will always stay true to its unique original traits and characteristics.

A new perspective

I have to zoom out for a moment and reflect on who we are and everything we've accomplished so far. When I step back and take in the broader picture, I see a team of intelligent, kind, and welcoming people, all united by one clear goal: to delight every customer who interacts with us

In a category space dominated by cold-looking, static, lifeless brands, June stands out as a warm, welcoming ally. This isn’t distorted or manufactured reality to role-play someone else’s character. It’s just plain truth; it’s who you are and your attitude is perfectly mirrored on the brand you have created.

To me the word that captures everything you do, did and are doing is “empathy”. And after that “customer-empathy”

Empathy because when we onboard customers we listen to their needs with a care and dedication that I have yet to see somewhere else. Empathy because Ferruccio doesn’t just share a list of features and bugs in the changelog but actually highlights and uplifts (with public tweets) the customers who requested them in the first place. Empathy because Alberto often emails people out of the blue when he guesses they are struggling on the docs page and they might have questions.

Empathy because we all of you share our personal Whatsapp numbers with customers, listen to their feedback, reply on the weekends and are willing to do everything possible to make them happy.

The kind of empathy that stems out of mutual recognition and deep understanding of someone' needs. The kind of empathy that eventually leads to digital proximity and–to some extent–intimacy. A connection on a deeper, more personal level. Person to person. Human to human.

I find it quite amazing that while you do this as the front-face men of the company, your product also helps others achieve the same results and embrace the same philosophy.

June is empathetic software. Software capable of generating customer intimacy. And it does that by creating a window in your customer world.

When we speak about data being generally available, I think we want to say “make your team more empathetic”. Because, if everyone in your team truly connects on a deeper, more meaningful level with your customers (their desires, their frustrations, their needs), if everyone in your team truly becomes more “customer-empathetic” then you’ll be more successful.

When you say “teams are disconnected from their product” you actually mean, product teams aren’t empathetic enough with their customers—and one of the core reasons is that analytics products for the last decade have made you think of customers in terms of clicks, numbers, steps and funnels.

June flips that with a human-first approach where people aren't flattened and reduced to metrics, stats and digits. June stands for customers being treated like they deserve.

If we go back to the previous 3 criterias and try to run the simulation with this idea instead:

For the last 20-years, analytics products have lost touch with people. Yet, your customers are the most important asset in your company. You wouldn't have a company without them afterall, and yet you are still treating them in terms of clicks, pageviews, and funnels. 

In that sense, the final form-factor can’t be anything else than June. A data tool that stands for a human-first approach, providing the right abstraction level (hence, a simplified, more streamlined approach to analytics) and that allows everyone (not just PMs) to be more customer-empathetic and connect with the people using your product (hence, Slack/Hubspot integration and customer-context reaching your team whenever they are)

If “data'' doesn't sound too exciting, maybe “customer-empathy” does. Or maybe, it does when we tell the world we are looking to build the most customer-empathy company on earth and in doing so we are building the best tool to also help you achieve that.

I hope this story helps anyone reflecting on their own narrative. If you're interested, the exercise I did to find ours evolved into what you see here. I believe it truly captures everything we stand for.

title: How to proactively reduce churn by building a Health Score using product data In HubSpot
html:
Product usage data, especially when integrated with the rest of your customer data in HubSpot is a powerful asset for reducing customer churn. By monitoring how customers interact with your product, you can identify early signs of disengagement and take proactive measures to reduce churn risks before it’s too late.

In this guide, we’ll cover:

  • How to define relevant product usage metrics that might signal churn risk.
  • How to integrate these metrics into a customer health score in HubSpot.
  • Best practices for interpreting the data and taking action to reduce churn.

Tracking customer health in HubSpot

Building a customer health score in HubSpot allows you to monitor key metrics that signal an increased likelihood for an account to churn - with the huge benefit of being able to combine signals from multiple sources in one place.

It’s important to keep in mind that any health score should not be viewed as a foolproof prediction of the future but as a directional guide on how to engage and prioritize your accounts.

By integrating product usage data and applying it to your customer health score, you can quickly identify which accounts are at risk. Below, we break down the four key metrics for building a robust customer health score and how you can track these metrics using HubSpot.

5 core components of an effective customer health score

Not all metrics contribute equally to customer churn prediction. By assigning weightings to each metric based on how predictive they are (e.g., product usage may have more weight than NPS), the health score becomes a more accurate tool. Regular review of these weightings and adjusting them based on trends helps in maintaining an up-to-date and effective health score.

Below, the most common building blocks of a healthscore for a B2B SaaS company.

1. Product Setup

💡 Has the product been implemented to a level that makes it possible to deliver the expected value.

In HubSpot’s health scoring tool, we can track Product Setup by creating custom properties mapped to June traits that measure the completion of critical implementation steps.

For example, if your product requires users to integrate third-party tools or set up specific features, these milestone completions can be tracked as individual boolean properties.

Here’s an example for a payment management app.

2. Product Usage & Feature Adoption

By integrating product usage data In HubSpot via tools like June.so, you can quickly incorporate usage behaviours into your healthscore definition. The most commonly used product usage fields are:

  1. The number of times a specific feature is used
  2. How much of a billed action or seat count an account is using
  3. How frequently users are using the product or specific features in a given period

👀 Consider normalizing usage metrics based on account size - to ensuring that large teams are compared equally with smaller ones when it comes to notating the health of an account.

3. Customer Satisfaction (NPS or CSAT)

HubSpot provides built-in functionality for tracking NPS and CSAT or you might be using an integrated 3rd party solution to survey your customers. You can automatically update the customer's health score based on their NPS feedback. Scores are typically divided into Promoters (9-10), Passives (7-8), and Detractors (0-6), and this data feeds directly into your health score model.

4. CSM Pulse (Qualitative Insights)

The CSM Pulse is a subjective (and qualitative) metric that provides a "gut check" on customer sentiment. Normally Customer Success Managers enter a categorical value for this metric after an interaction with a customer. Among the most common values used fot the CSM pulse we can find: “Healthy”, “Neutral” or “At risk”.

5. Customer Goal Achievement

Similar to the CSM pulse, this will be a manually updated measure of how well customers are meeting the goals they set when they started using your product. Tracking this metric involves regular check-ins and performance reviews with customers to ensure they’re getting the value they expect.

You can create custom properties in HubSpot to log goal progress, helping you assess whether customers are seeing success with your product that isn’t tracked in your product metrics.

Step-by-step: using product data to prevent churn

Enabling your team to most effectively reduce churn requires both identification of accounts with the highest risk of churning (as described in the last section) but also proactively surfacing them to our customer success or account management teams in HubSpot with a clear playbook for how to engage them.

With a health score (and associated health status) being calculated and automatically updated in HubSpot, it’s a good idea to build an active list of accounts that are currently At-Risk 🚨 to make it simpler to identify them consistently in automated workflows.

🚨 Create an active list of accounts (companies)
→ Add a filter: “Health Status” is “At Risk” → Edit columns: Based on your property preferences

Here’s how to use that list as the starting point for your churn playbook:

Part 1: Notify the team of falling health scores

⚡️ Create a company based workflow
Trigger Criteria: Enroll companies when they meet these filters:
→ List membership includes “At-Risk Accounts 🚨”

🤖 Action 1: Send Slack notification

→ Channel: #customer-success
→ Message: 🚨 {{ company.name }}’s health status was updated to At-Risk. It’s time to run a new playbook.
→ Properties to include: ARR, Health Score, Renewal Date, Seat Utilization, Total Seats, Active Seats

✅ Action 2: Create task

→ Name: Schedule re-alignment call
→ Type: Email
→ Associate to: Deal & Contact records
→ Assign to: Company owner

Deal tags

One of the most helpful use cases for any score is to inform how customers are engaged throughout their journey. In HubSpot, Health Score and Health Status are tracked at the company level, but there are many associated records through which a CSM or Account Manager could be engaging with a customer.

One example is renewal deals, to help visually identify deals where the account has an 🚨 At-Risk health status we can use a deal tag. Here’s how to create it:

  1. From your Deal Settings page click the “Deal Tags” tab and then “Manage Deal Tags”
  2. Create a new deal tag from scratch with the following properties: → Name: 🚨 At-Risk → Description: Identifies deals associated to a primary company with an “At Risk” health status. → Color: Red → Pipelines: All Pipelines → Filters: Deal is associated to: Any Company → AND associated Company has all of: → Health status is any of At-Risk

Part 2: Build proactive “At-Risk” playbooks

As accounts fall into our “At risk” health status we can enable our teams with a playbook to guide their engagement with customers.

Using playbooks in HubSpot we can:

  1. Present customer success managers, account managers, and renewal managers with contextual information about an account with real-time data from HubSpot personalization tokens for company record properties (including product usage data from June).
  2. Provide a guided way to ask questions and take notes about the interaction with customers.

Here’s how to use a HubSpot playbook for reducing churn step-by-step:

Step 1. Write the playbook

Navigate to Library → Playbooks → Create Playbook. This renewal call playbook includes 4 sections:

1. Account Overview: Provides a high level summary of the account using HubSpot personalization tokens to display relevant company properties.

→ Plan Type - The company property which represents the billing plan/tier this account is on. This property should be a dropdown select and could be populated manually by June or a billing integration.
→ ARR - The current annual revenue for this account. Updated based on closed-won deal amounts.
→ Next Renewal Date - The date of the next upcoming renewal for this account.

2. Product Usage: Includes real-time visibility into each account's product usage.

→ Usage Trend - A computed trait from June which displays the percentage change of events performed by a group in the last two periods. The period length can be customized. For example you could look at year over year, quarter over quarter or month over month change.
→ Total Seats - The number of users who have accessed the product for a given account. This should also be compared to the total number of purchased seats.
→ Active Seats - The number of users who have accessed the product for a given account in the last 30 days.

****We can also include counts of product usage events captured by June across all users within an account. This allows us to display feature usage information that can provide clarity to the rep about what each customer is using specifically and identify any usage gaps to address during renewal conversations.

→ KYC Complete - Include a key activation milestone. This may be turning on a key integration or importing data, and is generally a dependency for receiving value from a product.
→ Invoices Sent - A count of a key event needed to receive value from the product.
→ Payments Received - A count of the value realization event for an account.

If the activation milestone has not been achieved or the value realization event does not align with the precursor event count there is a high likelihood the account is at-risk.

3. Customer Goals - Prompt the rep to ask the customer about their goals with your product, and more importantly how they align with their current business objectives.

→ This should create a note on the account record in HubSpot.

4. Current Gaps - Prompt the rep to identify the biggest gaps between the current state and the goal state so they can suggest and action plan to close them.

5. Product Feedback - Prompt the rep to ask the customer if they are experiencing product friction or missing features in their critical workflows.

→ This should create a note on the account record in HubSpot but also enable the rep to escalate any relevant issues to the product team for triage through the standard product feedback process.

6. CSM Pulse - The rep should refresh their assessment of the accouyt and update the company property used as an input to the health score.

7. Next Steps - Based on this conversation with the customer, what is the next action that needs to happen - ideally this should be created as a task and assigned to the rep.

Step 2. Configure playbook settings

The next step is to ensure our At Risk playbook is available to our customers success managers and account managers when it’s needed.

In the playbook settings we need to:

  1. Select the checkbox to log playbook submissions as activities → Engagement type: Call
  2. Set the playbook recommendation to display on company records with an At Risk health status

→ Filters: Deal is associated with a Company that is a member of the list → At-Risk

We can also customize our company records to display:

  1. Recommended enablement at the top of the center panel by adding the “Recommended Enablement” card.
  2. The Health Score by adding the Health Score card at the top of the right sidebar

In this guide, we’ve shared how to use product usage data to identify churn risks by building an effective customer health score in HubSpot by integrating June.so.

By defining key metrics for 4 health scoring categories: Product Setup, Product Usage Rate, Net Promoter Score (NPS), CSM Pulse, and Customer Goal Achievement. You can create a holistic view of customer health that balances both qualitative and quantitative data. Integrating these metrics into HubSpot allows you to automate the monitoring of customer engagement, enabling proactive churn prevention.

Remember the best health scores are the ones your team understands and iterates on to help the score match the reality of account outcomes.

title: How to increase expansion opportunities using product data
html:
The top performing SaaS companies generate more revenue from expansion of existing customers than their peers.

“Companies growing in the top 40% of their cohorts are seeing at least roughly 20% of their revenue coming from expansion and a high end of nearly 40% expansion revenue.” - Patrick Campbell, Paddle

Providing your sales, and customer success teams access to product usage data offers them the opportunity to proactively engage users based on their specific product behavior, which can be used to personalize upsell and expansion strategies.

→ Frequent usage of limited features: if a customer regularly hits the limits of their current plan (e.g., maxing out user seats or data storage).

→ Increased engagement with advanced features: customers who begin using more advanced features or tools might be trying to solve new business problems.

→ Cross-product interactions: if you company offers multiple products or services, track how customers interact with them. For example, a customer heavily using one product might benefit from integrating another complementary product, providing a cross-sell opportunity.

Product usage data provides a window into how customers derive value from your product. By tracking signals such as feature usage, login frequency, and engagement patterns—it becomes possible to identify which aspects of the product are critical to specific users and accounts.

This understanding is crucial for pinpointing opportunities for growth.

Delivering personalized experiences that genuinely resonate with users drives higher customer satisfaction and loyalty. When customers feel seen and valued, they're more likely to stay with your service and explore additional offerings.

Recognizing patterns that indicate expansion opportunities

Product usage data can reveal patterns that signal when a customer might be ready to upgrade to new features or expand their usage. We can use computed traits in June and surface them in HubSpot via the June integration to identify these expansion patterns and make them actionable to our team.

Step 1: Create computed traits in June

Calculated traits allow you to go beyond simply counting events to display in CRM properties. A calculated trait in June can:

  • run a total count on the selected events e.g number of invoices created, number of teammates invited etc
  • run a unique count of the users that performed the events you've chosen e.g number of active seats in a company, number of new users in a company etc
  • set a boolean on whether a specific event has happened or not e.g user has completed their account verification
  • first seen / last seen the timestamp of the last or first time a given event happened e.g invoice created first seen on July 18th 2024

Computed traits are particularly useful to create audiences and cohorts which improve your team’s ability to action in HubSpot and report more accurately on their impact.

Here are 2 examples of how you could use June Computed Traits to identify expansion opportunities:

High number of active seats
If you have a seat based (or other form of consumption based) pricing model, you could use a computed trait with the “User Count” output type to identify the number of users in an account who have been active in a defined period.

👀 In this example we are tracking how many users in each workspace were active in the last 30 days


Increased engagement over time
Sudden spikes in specific feature usage or rapid adoption of a feature by additional account users could signal a change in business priorities and an opportunity to expand an account.

👀 In this example we are tracking the Event count change of subscriptions being created over the last 30 days.

Cross-product interactions
Tracking the usage of specific product features and how that usage increases over time can be a helpful signal not only for linear expansion using more of the same feature but also as an entry point into complimentary features or services.

In our example: If we see an account is creating more subscriptions instead of only sending invoices or collecting one-time payments an expansion opportunity could be to sell a revenue recovery feature that helps reduce the impact of expired cards causing churn on subscription plans.

Step 2: Map your June traits to the equivalent custom properties in HubSpot

When you are setting up your product usage data integration you’ll need to create a custom company or contact property in HubSpot for each Trait in June.

In our example we’ll create properties for our 2 computed traits: → Active Seats - The number of users at a company who triggered an event in the last 30 days. → Subscriptions Created Change - Event count change of the subscriptions created in the last 30 days vs the previous period.

We may also create a property for:

→ Seats purchased - The number of seats included in the accounts billing plan. This could be updated manually when a deal closes or also synced from your billing tool.

Step-by-step: how to engage expansion opportunities with product usage data in HubSpot (via June)

Now that we have our account and user product usage data flowing into HubSpot contact and company records using June, we can start building a workflow in HubSpot to automatically prompt engage with accounts that have the highest chance of expanding.

In this example we are going to use increased usage of a specific feature from a user at an ICP account as an expansion signal.

Here’s how it works step-by-step:

Step 1. Identify accounts exceeding their expected usage

Create an active list of accounts with expansion potential (companies):

→ Add a filter: “Subscriptions Created Change” is greater than 100% → AND “Number of Employees” is greater than 50 → AND “Active Seats” is greater than 3

💡 The combination of product usage signals and your regular ICP definitions will help to ensure only accounts likely to be hot leads for sales are being surfaced.

Step 2. Create an automated email template to engage them

  1. Create an automated email template using the “Simple” template type
  2. Add the following content to your email (copy+paste):

Subject:

Hi {{contact.first_name }}

I noticed your usage of our { key feature identified in data } has really increased in the last month or so (up { company.subscriptions_created_change }%). Typically when I see that happening it's because of { x,y,z pain point or business milestone being reached }. Typically our { recommmended pricing plan } is a better fit for that use case.

I'd love to connect and make sure you're in the plan that's the best fit for your needs at { company.company_name }.

Feel free to grab some time on my calendar.

Best,
{{owner.full_name}}

Step 3. Prompt the outreach process in HubSpot

⚡️ Create a company based workflow
Trigger Criteria: Enroll companies when they meet these filters:
→ List membership includes “Accounts with expansion potential”

🤖 Action 1: Send Slack notification
→ Channel: #sales
→ Message: 📈 {{ company.name }} increased usage of { feature name }
→ Properties to include: ARR, Health Score, Renewal Date, Seat Utilization, Invoices Utilization, Total Seats, Active Seats, Invoices Sent

✅ Action 2: Create task
→ Name: Send upgrade notification
→ Type: Email
→ Associate to: Deal & Contact records
→ Assign to: Existing sales owner

Providing teams access to product usage data inside HubSpot surfaces valuable insights that can drive smarter upselling, cross-selling, and customer retention efforts.

Segmenting your customer base by usage patterns allows for more personalized automated campaigns that ensure timely and relevant customer interactions that drive revenue growth.
